### ADR-056, Amendment 20 (1 October 2026) — the stage 0b dry run counted through types ArcadeDB does not have

**Seen.** The first real stage 0b dry run passed the vault check ("going on with 8 id(s) stored twice") and then died
counting the shared graph: `SELECT count(*) FROM V` fails on ArcadeDB (`Type with name 'V' was not found`). Nothing was
deleted (the dry run deletes nothing); the Conduit was stopped and started again as designed.

**Class.** The same one as Amendment 18: the count was never exercised against anything that refuses what the real store
refuses; the earlier tests used a stand-in for the whole graph object, so the class that talks to ArcadeDB had no test at
all. The count is now a traversal (`g.V().count()`, `g.E().count()`), and `ArcadeShared.counts` is tested with a client
that refuses the SQL form and treats an empty answer as an empty graph. `reset` (drop, create, apply the schema) is the
same code the `--reset-graph-database` option has already run on the real store, and was not changed.

### ADR-056, Amendment 21 (1 October 2026) — the demos show the same defect, and the seeds no longer point at a repair that does not exist

**Seen.** After stage 0b, `make seed-hmp` and `make seed-fixture-corp` both reported "4 id(s) stored more than once" over
the whole shared graph. The Fixture Corp count is the same four, so the HMP load wrote them and the Fixture Corp load
added none that the check could see (the check does not say which load wrote an id; this is read from the two counts).
So the defect is not specific to the PaySim load or its size: a small synthetic load (400 people, 10 yards) shows it.

**Fault in my own work.** Every seed's check still told the owner to "remove the strays with `--repair-strays`", the
command Amendment 19 withdrew. The check now says what the position is (a known ArcadeDB defect with no repair; the
product does not count the strays), through one shared text, and `repair_command` became `advice`. A test asserts the
line neither says "remove the strays" nor names the withdrawn command (red first).

### ADR-056, Amendment 22 (1 October 2026) — the corpus total is read once per call, not once per edge

**Seen.** The first Enron load (233,890 links, shared graph) slowed as it went: 146 s per 1,000 links at the start,
about 230 s per 1,000 at 82,000 links, a projected 17 hours for the link phase. The owner interrupted it at 82,040
links. It left 21,932 addresses and about 82,000 links in the shared graph, and no events.

**Why.** Every edge written asked the store three questions to compute its weight: the source's degree, the target's
degree (index lookups, cheap) and the total weight of every edge of its type (a whole-corpus traversal). The third ran
once per edge, so the cost of a write grew with everything already loaded: quadratic in the load. Two causes, one mine:
the whole-corpus query is older than this record, but Amendment 19 made it a vertex traversal (visiting all 21,932
addresses on every write) and that fixed cost was never measured on a real store. PaySim's 13k edges hid it. Rule 15's
point again: a test double does not show cost.

**Change.** `upsert_edges` reads the total once per call, per edge type, and carries it forward: after each write the
total is the weighed total with that write's delta in it, which is what the store would answer for the next edge. Each
edge is therefore weighed exactly as if written one at a time. Nothing is kept between calls, because anything may
write or revert between them. `_corpus_edge_stats` and `_weigh_edge` accept the total when the caller holds it and
otherwise ask the store as before. A load of 40-edge batches does one whole-corpus traversal per batch instead of 40.

**Tests (red first).** `tests/adapters/graph_arcadedb/test_corpus_total_read_once_per_call.py`: forty writes cost one
total query (was 40); the batch and the one-at-a-time loads give identical stored weights and components, with a
repeated pair in the batch so the merge path is exercised; a second call reads the store again. Planted faults: carrying
the total without the write's delta fails the weight comparison; keeping the totals on the adapter between calls fails
both the weight comparison and the second-call test.

**Not changed.** The weight formula, the ontology, the stray-record handling of Amendment 19, and the order of the
statistics. A per-batch traversal still grows with the corpus; the expectation is a link phase of well under an hour,
which is unmeasured until the Enron load is rerun.

### ADR-056, Amendment 23 (1 October 2026) — Amendment 22 held its test but not its prediction: the load is no faster

**Seen.** The Enron load was rerun with Amendment 22's change in. Elapsed seconds for 1,040 and 10,040 links were 150
and 1,522, against 146 and 1,489 before. The first 10,000 links are no faster.

**What was wrong in Amendment 22.** Its "expectation of a link phase of well under an hour" was a prediction from the
first run's growth alone. The cost per link was already about 0.15 s at the very start, when the corpus was almost
empty, so the corpus total could account for the *growth* but never for that baseline. The change is still right in
what it does (one whole-corpus traversal per 40-link batch, not 40; weights identical to one-at-a-time writes, which the
tests show) and it removes the growing part: the time per 1,000 links stays flat at about 150 to 157 s where the first
run climbed to about 230 s by 82,000 links. It does not touch the baseline.

**Not known.** What the baseline is spent on. A hypothesis, not a finding: several of the per-link queries embed the
address as a literal in the Groovy script text (`_find_existing_edge` and the two degree queries), so the server may
compile a new script for every link, where the insert uses bound parameters. It is unmeasured. A measurement needs the
store idle, since timing against a running load is contaminated (rule 14).

**Position.** The owner is letting this load run to completion (projected about 10 hours if the time per 1,000 links
stays flat; that is a projection from 10,000 links). The cost is then to be measured on an idle store, one query kind at
a time, before anything is changed.

### ADR-056, Amendment 24 (2 October 2026) — a correction to Amendment 23: the cost per link still grows, and the load will take about 18 to 19 hours

**Seen.** Amendment 23 said the time per 1,000 links "stays flat at about 150 to 157 s". That was read from the first 10,000
links only and is wrong. At 154,040 links (36,376 s elapsed) the time per 1,000 links is about 330 s, against about 156 s
at 10,000: it grows by about 1.2 s with every thousand written, the same growth as the first run. The change in
Amendment 22 neither removed it nor made it worse. The link phase is projected at 18 to 19 hours (about 8 to 9 hours
still to run at that point), no better than the first run's projection of 17.

**What is known and not known.** Known: the cost has a baseline of about 0.15 s per link from the start, and a part that
grows with the graph, and neither is the per-edge corpus total. Not known: what either part is spent on. Two guesses so
far were wrong because neither was measured; `scripts/probe_write_cost.py` is written to measure it on an idle store, and
is not yet run.

**Also seen, and the reason for ADR-058.** `services/ingest/engine.py` writes one element per `GraphPort` call (one
`upsert_nodes([node])` after one `find_node`, one `upsert_edges([edge])` per edge). The per-call carry of Amendment 22
therefore saves nothing for an Ingest Studio publish, and `03_CONDUIT_MIDDLEWARE.md` §5.1's "batched writes through
`GraphPort`" is not what the engine does. ADR-058 proposes a bulk-load path.

## ADR-058 — Bulk loading is the default write path for ingest; `upsert_*` is for low-volume writes

**Status: PROPOSED, 2 October 2026. Awaiting the owner's decisions D1 to D10 below. Nothing is built.** Each decision
carries a recommendation; none is taken until the owner says so. The spec notes this record adds (`00_ARCHITECTURE.md`
§2.1, `01_DOMAIN_MODEL.md` §6.1, `03_CONDUIT_MIDDLEWARE.md` §5.1, `04_VAULT_BACKEND.md` §6, `09_INGEST_STUDIO.md` §6)
are marked "PROPOSED" and are not the design until this record is accepted.

### Context: what was seen

- **The Enron load.** 233,890 links through `GraphArcadeDBAdapter.upsert_edges` cost about 0.15 s per link at the start
  and about 0.33 s at 154,000 links, a projected 18 to 19 hours (ADR-056 Amendments 22 to 24). Two fixes aimed at the
  per-edge corpus total did not change the baseline.
- **Why the path is slow by design.** For each edge `upsert_edges` asks the store for the type of both endpoints, for an
  existing edge between them (to merge, `01_DOMAIN_MODEL.md` §3), for both endpoints' weighted degree and, per call, for
  the corpus total (`01_DOMAIN_MODEL.md` §6.1), then writes the edge. That is about six round trips per edge, each a
  separate Groovy script. It is built for correctness on a live graph, one write at a time, which is the right shape for
  an analyst's edit and the wrong shape for 234,000 pairs the loader already holds in full.
- **The Ingest Studio is worse off than the seeds.** The engine writes one element per call (`services/ingest/
  engine.py`: `find_node` then `upsert_nodes([one])` per node; `upsert_edges([one])` per edge), so even the batching a
  seed can do is not used. `03_CONDUIT_MIDDLEWARE.md` §5.1 already says "load: batched writes through `GraphPort` and
  `AnalyticsPort` in one logical transaction per document". The spec and the code disagree (rule 11); this record
  settles which way.
- **ADR-056's context already named the cost** ("every edge write scans all edges of its type") and answered it with a
  vault per dataset, which bounds what a write scans but does not change the number of round trips.
- **Unknown, and to be measured first:** what the baseline and the growing part of the per-edge cost are made of
  (`scripts/probe_write_cost.py`, to be run on an idle store); and which bulk transport is fastest and avoids the stray
  records of ADR-056 Amendment 19 (stage 0).

### The proposal

1. **Two write paths, named for what they are for.**
   - **Bulk load** (new): the default for everything that arrives as a set: an Ingest Studio publish, a seed, a re-load.
     The loader has already resolved, deduplicated and aggregated its elements, so the store is asked to write them,
     not to rediscover them.
   - **`upsert_nodes` / `upsert_edges`** (existing, unchanged): for low-volume and interactive writes where merge-on-
     write and a weight against the live corpus are the point: an analyst's edit in the Glass, a supersede, a
     retraction, a watch's output, and any element a bulk load hands back because it collides with what is stored (D3).
2. **The Ingest Studio publish becomes** (the staging steps are unchanged): resolve rows in memory, aggregate by
   (type, source, target), write nodes then edges in bulk chunks, append events, record the load. The engine calls
   `upsert_*` only for what the bulk call returns to it.
3. **Nothing about what a stored element means changes:** the same properties, provenance, handling, audit stub,
   `load_id` / `recipe_id` / `recipe_version`, validation, and the same revert (`revert_load`) apply. Validation parity is
   a requirement, not a choice: every element is validated against the ontology and handling scheme exactly as
   `upsert_*` validates it; the bulk path never trusts its caller.

### Decisions the owner needs to make

**D1. The shape on the port.** (a) A separate optional capability, `BulkGraphLoader`, in `packages/ports`, with its own
conformance section; an adapter that does not declare it is loaded through chunked `upsert_*` by the engine. (b) New
methods added to `GraphPort`, mandatory for every adapter. (c) A flag on `upsert_*`. *Recommendation: (a).* It keeps
`00_ARCHITECTURE.md` §2.1's promise that a new backend needs only a green suite (the second supported adapter,
`janusgraph`, is not forced to build one before it can load anything), and it makes the fallback explicit. (b) forces
every adapter to build bulk; (c) hides a different contract behind a flag and was the shape that let `upsert_edges`
never merge for a whole phase (rule 12).

**D2. What "low volume" means, and the studio's default.** (a) Bulk always for a publish; `upsert_*` only for collisions
(D3) and for writes that are not ingest. (b) A row threshold: a publish below N elements uses `upsert_*`, above uses bulk.
*Recommendation: (a), no threshold.* A threshold is a second code path to test at its edge and it sends small publishes,
the most common kind, through the slower path. The bulk path must therefore be correct for one element as well.

**D3. An edge for a pair that already exists in the vault.** (a) The bulk call refuses to write that pair and returns
it to the caller as a typed result (`collisions`, never silently dropped: rule 2's spirit), and the engine routes those
through `upsert_*`, which merges as today. (b) Bulk merges in the same call. *Recommendation: (a).* One merge
implementation stays the only one; a fresh vault, the common case for a first load, has no collisions and pays for no
lookups beyond one batched existence check per chunk.

**D4. What weight means for a bulk load.** Today each edge's weight is a snapshot against the corpus *as it stood when
that edge was written*, so the first edge of a load is weighed against almost nothing (`01_DOMAIN_MODEL.md` §6.1 already
says weight is "a load-time snapshot ... never frozen ground truth"). (a) A bulk load weighs every edge against the
corpus *as it stands at the end of the load* (existing edges plus the load's), with the formula, parameters and
`WeightComponents` fields unchanged and `computed_at` recording the end of the load. (b) Replay the sequential
snapshots. *Recommendation: (a).* It is order-independent and cheaper; (b) reproduces an accident of write order.
**Consequence to accept:** a bulk-loaded edge and the same edge upsert-loaded will not carry identical weight values
unless the load is a single edge; the equivalence test (below) compares the stored counts, not the float.

**D5. Where the merge rules live.** `_merge_provenance` and `_merge_interval` are private to the ArcadeDB adapter, and a
bulk load must aggregate repeated pairs by the same rules. (a) Move them to one shared pure module (for example
`packages/schemas`) used by both paths, with a test that the two paths agree on the same inputs. (b) Re-implement in the
loader. *Recommendation: (a).* Two implementations of one merge rule are how the two paths would drift.

**D6. A failed bulk load.** A 234,000-edge load cannot be one transaction. (a) A failed load is reverted (`revert_load`
by `load_id`) and re-run, not resumed, as ADR-055 Amendment 4 already decided for the seeds; chunk progress is logged for
the owner, not used to resume. (b) Build resumable loads with chunk checkpoints. *Recommendation: (a).* Resume needs
idempotent chunks, which is the merge-on-write cost the bulk path exists to avoid.

**D7. The stray-record tolerance for the bulk path.** ArcadeDB sometimes stores an edge twice (ADR-056 Amendment 19;
about 8 in 13,068 in the PaySim upsert load, 4 in each small demo). The cause is unexplained. The bulk transport may or
may not show it. (a) Acceptance: the stray count is measured and reported on every bulk load, and a bulk load is not
accepted if its rate is higher than the upsert path's on the same data. (b) Acceptance: no strays. (c) Not a criterion.
*Recommendation: (a).* (b) may be unachievable until the cause is found, and (c) lets a worse path in unseen.

**D8. Scope of the first slice.** (a) Edges first, nodes in a second stage under this same record. (b) Nodes and edges
together. *Recommendation: (a).* Edges are where the cost was measured; nodes have the same one-element-per-call shape
in the engine and are added once edges are proven.

**D9. The PaySim twin.** The owner's ask: a duplicate PaySim dataset to test the new method. (a) A second vault, same
source file, same graph sample (500 fraud rows and their neighbourhood, about 13,000 edges), loaded by the seed with
`--method bulk`, compared with the existing `paysim` vault by the equivalence test below; once it passes, a second
twin at the full neighbourhood (about 74,000 accounts) to prove scale. (b) The same, but loaded through an Ingest
Studio recipe so the real default path is proved, not only the adapter. *Recommendation: (a) first, (b) as stage 4.*
**To decide:** the vault id (suggest `paysim-bulk`, per ADR-056 decision 7's `vault_<id>` naming); whether to keep it
after the comparison (suggest keep until the Ingest Studio path is proved, then retire at the owner's word, as ADR-056
did for the original); and that the twin is synthetic, so ADR-053's real-data rules do not apply.

**D10. The measurement spike.** Before any adapter code, a throwaway spike on a scratch database (never `ospreyflow`,
never a real vault, run only when the store is idle) times three transports on the 13,000-edge PaySim sample and counts
strays for each: (a) one parameterised Gremlin script per chunk; (b) ArcadeDB SQL `CREATE EDGE` in batches; (c)
ArcadeDB's own importer, if this container offers it (unverified). *Recommendation: yes, about a day.* The spike's table
goes into this record as an amendment before the port is designed, so the transport is chosen on numbers.

### The equivalence test (the twin's acceptance)

A bulk-loaded vault and an upsert-loaded one, from the same source and sample, must match on: the set of node ids; the
set of edge ids and their (source, target, type); `occurrences` per pair; the provenance source references per edge
(every collapsed row retained); handling and `load_id` / `recipe_id`; the intervals; and the `WeightComponents` counts
(`occurrences`, `corpus_pair_count`, degrees, corpus total) recomputed against the end-of-load corpus, which for the
bulk vault must equal what the bulk call stored. The count of ids stored twice is reported for both, by scan and by
traversal. `revert_load` on the bulk load must leave the vault as it was, and a reload after it must match again.

### Staging (nothing started; each stage lands green before the next)

0. Spike (D10), once the Enron load has finished and the store is idle. 1. This record decided; `BulkGraphLoader`
Protocol and its conformance section written first (rule 1); the shared merge module (D5). 2. The ArcadeDB adapter's bulk
method. 3. `seed_paysim --method bulk`, the `paysim-bulk` vault, the equivalence report. 4. The Ingest Studio engine's
publish path through bulk with `upsert_*` fallback, recipe re-run and revert tests, and an acceptance row (owner-owned).
5. Nodes (D8), the full-size PaySim twin, and the Enron reload by bulk in place of the 18-hour upsert load.

### What this does not decide

Cross-vault loading (ADR-056); how this interacts with the vault resolver of ADR-056 stage 1 (a bulk load takes the same
per-vault graph port and has no default vault); the analytics-store side, which is assumed to be written in chunks
already and is to be checked, not assumed; a bulk path for the `janusgraph` adapter.

### ADR-058, Amendment 1 (2 October 2026) — the owner accepts D1 to D10 as recommended, and the build starts

**Owner's ruling:** "all as recommended, go ahead with the build", and a PaySim duplicate load to test the new build.
The record's status is now **ACCEPTED, with the decisions below**; the PROPOSED notes in `00_ARCHITECTURE.md` §2.1,
`01_DOMAIN_MODEL.md` §6.1, `03_CONDUIT_MIDDLEWARE.md` §5.1, `04_VAULT_BACKEND.md` §6 and `09_INGEST_STUDIO.md` §6 are the
design from this date, and their "PROPOSED" wording is lifted by the commit that builds the part they describe.

| | Decision taken |
| --- | --- |
| D1 | `BulkGraphLoader` is a separate optional capability in `packages/ports`; the engine falls back to chunked `upsert_*` where an adapter does not declare it. |
| D2 | Bulk for every Ingest Studio publish, no row threshold; `upsert_*` for non-ingest writes and for collisions. The bulk path is correct for one element as well as many. |
| D3 | A pair already stored is not written by the bulk call: it is returned to the caller as a typed `collisions` result, and the engine routes it through `upsert_*`. |
| D4 | A bulk load weighs every edge against the corpus as it stands at the end of the load; the formula and `WeightComponents` are unchanged. The equivalence test compares stored counts, not the float. |
| D5 | The provenance and interval merge rules move to one shared pure module used by both paths, with a test that they agree. |
| D6 | A failed bulk load is reverted by `load_id` and re-run, not resumed. |
| D7 | The stray count is measured and reported on every bulk load; a bulk load is not accepted if its rate is higher than the upsert path's on the same data. |
| D8 | Edges first; nodes in a second stage under this record. |
| D9 | The PaySim twin: vault `paysim-bulk`, same source and graph sample as `paysim`, loaded by `seed_paysim --method bulk`, then a full-neighbourhood twin; kept until the studio path is proved, retired only at the owner's word. Synthetic, so ADR-053 does not apply. |
| D10 | The transport spike runs on a scratch database, only when the store is idle. |

**What this changes about the order of work.** The Enron load is still writing to the shared stores, and a timing taken
against a busy store is not a measurement (rule 14). So what is built first is what needs no live store and no timing:
the shared merge module, the port and its conformance cases, the spike script, and the adapter and seed code with
test doubles that refuse what the real store refuses. The transport is **not chosen by guess**: the adapter is written
with the transport behind one small seam, the first candidate (a parameterised Gremlin script per chunk) is the one the
code starts with, and it is replaced by whichever the spike measures fastest with the fewest strays. No speed is claimed
until the spike and the twin have run on an idle store.

### ADR-058, Amendment 2 (2 October 2026) — the twin vault is named `paysim-perftst`

The owner asked for the duplicate PaySim to be called `paysim_perftst` in place of D9's suggested `paysim-bulk`. A vault id
may use only lower-case letters, digits and hyphens (ADR-056 decision 7; `vault_locations` refuses anything else, so an
underscore never reaches a path), so the id is **`paysim-perftst`**. Its graph database is `vault_paysim_perftst` (hyphens
become underscores), which is the name the owner gave. D9 is otherwise unchanged: same source and graph sample as `paysim`,
loaded by `seed_paysim --method bulk`, kept until the studio path is proved. Nothing had been loaded under the old name.
The name says what the vault is for (a performance test), not how it was loaded; the load method is recorded by `--method`
and the comparison, not by the name.

### ADR-058, Amendment 3 (2 October 2026) — seed containers take the checkout's packages as well as its scripts

**What was seen.** The first run of the transport spike, inside the deployment's network, died with `ImportError: cannot
import name 'BulkGraphLoader' from 'ports.graph'`. (Run from the host it had failed earlier because the graph store is not
published outside the deployment's network, which is why `seed_internal --spike-bulk-transport` exists.)

**Cause.** A seed runs in a one-shot container from the Conduit's image. `seed_internal` mounted the checkout's `scripts/`
over the image's, but not `packages/`, and the image's copy of `packages/` is as old as its last refresh. `seed_support`
now imports `BulkGraphLoader`, added to `packages/ports/graph.py` by this ADR, so it failed in every container run, not
only the spike: any seed, inspection, repair, comparison or stage 0b run built on the committed tree would have failed the
same way. Nothing had run in a container since that commit, which is why it was not seen sooner.

**Fix, at the class.** One function, `_checkout_mounts`, returns the read-only mounts every container run takes (`scripts/`
and `packages/`), and all six places that build a run use it. A test starts one container run of every kind (seed, bulk
seed, inspection, repair, comparison, spike, stage 0b clearing) and requires both mounts in each; with the packages mount
removed from one kind, it fails. `harness.apply`'s own seeds are unchanged: it builds the image from the checkout at the
time, so the packages are current.

**Open, to watch for.** Mounting `packages/` read-only replaces the image's copy for the run. A file the image holds under
`packages/` that is not in the checkout would be hidden; none is known.

### ADR-058, Amendment 4 (2 October 2026) — the first spike on a real store

**Run.** `seed_internal paysim --spike-bulk-transport`, 1,000 PaySim-shaped transactions (773 accounts, 671 distinct pairs),
each method on its own new scratch database, the store otherwise idle. Measured, not predicted.

| Method | Time | Edges/s | Stored | Ids stored twice |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Upsert, chunks of 40 (today) | 10.2 s | 98 | 671 | 1 |
| Bulk, Gremlin, chunks of 100 | 1.3 s | 794 | 671 | 1 |
| Bulk, Gremlin, chunks of 500 | 1.0 s | 1,045 | 671 | 4 |
| Bulk, Gremlin, chunks of 2,000 | 0.8 s | 1,190 | 671 | 4 |
| Bulk, SQL script, chunks of 500 (timing only) | 0.4 s | 2,617 | 1,000 | 0 |

**What it settles.** Every query shape `GremlinBulkTransport` sends (`within`, `project`/`by`, `coalesce`, the per-row
`addE` closure, `bothE`/`otherV`) runs on this ArcadeDB and returns what the loader expects. All three Gremlin runs
left the same stored edge ids and occurrence counts as the upsert path. So D1's first candidate transport works.

**What it does not settle.**
1. *The speed-up on a large graph.* Upsert here cost about 10 ms an edge on an empty database; the Enron load cost about
   150 ms a link from its first thousand and about 510 ms at its end (233,890 links, 69,647 s, no ids stored twice). The
   1,000-edge test does not reproduce that cost, so "8 to 12 times" is for a small empty graph and is not a forecast for
   Enron. A larger run (`--spike-edges 10000`) and the PaySim twin are the next measurements.
2. *Strays (D7).* Upsert left 1 in 671 and bulk 1, 4 and 4 by chunk size. The numbers are tiny and one run each, so this is a
   lean and not a finding; by D7 (bulk must not be worse than upsert's rate on the same data) only chunks of 100 passes.
   **The seed's bulk chunk is therefore 100**, raised only on a run showing no rise in strays.
3. *The SQL-script candidate* is not comparable: it wrote id and occurrences only and stored 1,000 edges because it does not
   merge repeated pairs. It is faster and left no strays, which makes it worth building to full fidelity (properties,
   provenance, dates, weights) and measuring, but it is not chosen and not built.

**Decision.** Gremlin at 100 per chunk stays the transport for the twin load. Nothing else changes.

### ADR-058, Amendment 5 (2 October 2026) — the 10,000-edge spike: where the time goes

**Run.** `seed_internal paysim --spike-bulk-transport --spike-edges 10000`: 10,000 transactions, 13,426 accounts, 6,713
distinct pairs, each method on its own new scratch database, the store otherwise idle.

| Method | Time | Edges/s | Ids stored twice | Same edges as upsert |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Upsert, chunks of 40 | 778.6 s | 13 | 0 | (reference) |
| Bulk, Gremlin, chunks of 100 | 161.1 s | 62 | 0 | identical |
| Bulk, Gremlin, chunks of 500 | 167.0 s | 60 | 2 | identical |
| Bulk, Gremlin, chunks of 2,000 | failed | | | `Timeout on locking http session` |
| Bulk, SQL script, chunks of 500 (id and occurrences only, no merge) | 2.9 s | 3,407 | 0 | not compared |

**What it shows.**
1. Bulk by Gremlin at 100 per chunk is 4.8 times faster than upsert here, left the same edges, and no stray: **chunks of 100
   stay the setting**. 500 is no faster and left two strays; 2,000 does not run (one transaction that long times out).
2. *Upsert's cost follows the number of accounts, not of edges.* It held at about 79 ms an edge from the first thousand edges
   to the last (the 1,000-edge run, with 773 accounts, cost 10 ms); writing the accounts themselves slowed from 463 to 97
   a second as they were added. The Enron load (21,932 addresses) cost about 150 ms a link from its start.
3. *The bulk Gremlin rate is also flat across chunk sizes* (43 edges/s over the loading phase, 100 or 500 per chunk), so the
   time is per row, not per chunk. A row is two `g.V().has("id", …)` lookups and an edge: about 23 ms.
4. *The SQL script did the same two lookups and the create in 0.3 ms a row* (`CREATE EDGE … FROM (SELECT FROM <type> WHERE
   id = :s) TO (… :t)`), about 80 times faster per row on the same data.

**Reading (a hypothesis, not yet isolated).** The Gremlin `has("id", …)` lookup costs about as much as scanning the vertex
type; the SQL `WHERE id = :s` uses the type's index. That fits points 2 to 4 and the Enron history, and the cheap way to
settle it is to time the two lookups alone on a scratch database (and a label-qualified Gremlin lookup, which may reach the
index). If it holds, the cost is in every Gremlin id lookup the adapter makes, `upsert_*` included, so the fix is at that
class and not only in the bulk path.

**Decision (D10: the transport is the one the spike measures fastest with the fewest strays).** The SQL script is the next
transport to build, **to full fidelity** (every property, provenance, handling, dates, weights, audit; repeated pairs merged
before writing, as the Gremlin loader does) behind the same `BulkTransport` seam, and to be compared against the Gremlin
runs with the same equivalence report. Until it is proved the Gremlin transport at 100 per chunk is the one the twin load
uses. The index experiment runs first because it decides whether upsert's lookups need the same change.

### ADR-058, Amendment 6 (2 October 2026) — the PaySim twin load, and the first comparison

**Seen.** The full PaySim twin (`paysim-perftst`, bulk Gremlin, chunks of 100) loaded 13,564 accounts in 93 s and 13,068
transactions in 300 s (131 chunks, 43 per s, steady), then 6,362,620 events. The load's own check reported 6 ids stored more
than once. `--compare-vaults paysim paysim-perftst`, run afterwards on the same stores, reported: 13,564 nodes and 13,068
edge records on both sides, no node or edge differences, the right vault's weight components all matching its own contents,
**0 ids stored twice by scan on both sides**, and "the vaults agree". (The left vault's 38,705 differing weight values are
information only: upsert weighs edge by edge, so its stored components differ from end-of-load counts; bulk weighs against the
end-of-load corpus, as D4 intends.)

**What this does and does not show.** Bulk and upsert produced the same graph from the same data (D5 met for this data). The
stray counts do not agree between two readings of the same store: the load check (`GROUP BY id`) saw 6 on the twin, the
comparison (a scan of all edge records, 13,068 of them, so no extra record) saw 0 on both vaults, and the original vault was
recorded earlier as 8. Either the stray is not present in what the comparison scans, or it was gone by then, or the two
queries do not see the same thing. That is not yet explained, so **D7 (bulk strays no more than upsert on the same data) is
neither passed nor failed here**: 6 against 8 was by the load check; by the comparison it is 0 against 0.

**Next.** Make the comparison run the load check's own `GROUP BY id` query on each vault as well, so one tool reports both
readings on the same stores. Events loaded without timers on this run (it predates `EventProgress`).

### ADR-058, Amendment 7 (2 October 2026) — the stray copies are still there; the comparison's own read was hiding them

**Seen.** Amendment 6 recorded 6 ids stored twice by the load check and none by the comparison, and asked which to believe.
The comparison now takes three readings of each vault (paged read, `GROUP BY id`, `count(*)`). On the same two stores:
original (upsert) vault: 13,068 records by paged read, 8 ids twice by `GROUP BY id`, 13,076 by `count(*)`; twin (bulk, 100 per
chunk): 13,068, 6 ids twice, 13,074. `GROUP BY id` and `count(*)` agree with each other exactly (13,068 plus the stray
copies); only the paged read did not.

**Reading (a hypothesis, from the three counts).** The paged read was `ORDER BY id`, which the store answers from the id
index, one record per id; so it could not see a stray copy. The strays did not go away between the load and the comparison
(Amendment 6's "0 on both" was the comparison's blind spot, not a change in the store). The paged read now has no ordering
and walks the records; the next real run is what shows whether the three readings then agree.

**D7 (bulk's stray rate no more than upsert's on the same data), for this data: met.** Bulk 6 of 13,068 against upsert 8 of
13,068 on the same data, both by the two readings that can see them. One run each, small counts, so this says bulk is not
worse here, not that it is better; the spike at 10,000 edges (upsert 0, bulk at 100 per chunk 0, at 500 per chunk 2) points
the same way. Strays remain the parked ArcadeDB defect (ADR-056 Amendment 19); nothing here repairs them.

**Equivalence (D5).** The edge comparison reads one record per id, so it compared the graphs as the product reads them
(a traversal reaches each edge once). Strays are therefore outside that comparison, and are reported separately.

### ADR-058, Amendment 8 (2 October 2026) — the three readings agree (confirms Amendment 7)

With the paged read no longer ordered by `id`, the comparison on the same two stores read 13,076 edge records on the
upsert vault and 13,074 on the bulk twin, 8 and 6 ids stored twice by the paged read, the same 8 and 6 by `GROUP BY id`, and
the same record counts by `count(*)`: "the three readings agree". The `ORDER BY id` reading in Amendment 7 is now an
observation, not a hypothesis (the id-ordered read returned one record per id; the unordered read returned them all). Node
and edge differences: none; the twin's weights match its own contents. D7 stands as recorded in Amendment 7 (bulk 6, upsert 8).

### ADR-058, Amendment 9 (2 October 2026) — the Gremlin id lookup the adapter sends scans the type; label-qualified ones do not

**Measured** (`scripts.probe_lookup_cost`, scratch database, one account looked up by id, median of 30 spread across the
set; the store otherwise idle):

| accounts | `g.V().has("id",X)` (the adapter's shape) | `hasLabel(T).has("id",X)` | `has(T,"id",X)` | SQL `WHERE id = :id` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1,000 | 1.64 ms | 0.93 ms | 0.64 ms | 0.68 ms |
| 5,000 | 4.01 ms | 0.52 ms | 0.52 ms | 0.59 ms |
| 15,000 | 11.17 ms | 0.63 ms | 0.58 ms | 0.80 ms |

The shape the adapter sends (`adapter.py` and `builders.py` send it 37 times) grows with the account count, 6.8 times slower
at 15,000 than at 1,000. The other three stay flat at about 0.6 ms. Amendment 5's hypothesis is therefore confirmed for the
lookup: the type's unique index on `id` exists and is used when the label is given, and is not when it is not.

**Fits the earlier figures.** At about 13,000 accounts two unlabelled lookups cost about 22 ms, against the 23 ms a row the
bulk Gremlin transport took; upsert's 79 ms an edge at 13,426 accounts is the same lookup several times over.

**Also seen, not yet understood.** The account type holds two indexes on every property (`mx_Endpoint[id]` and
`mx_Endpoint_0_<number>`, both unique on `id`; the same for `owning_unit`, `email`, `handle` and the rest). Whether that
doubles every node write, and whether it has any bearing on the stray copies, is not known. It is recorded, not acted on.

**Consequence.** The cost is in the adapter's read and write paths alike, not only in bulk loading. What fixes it is not yet
decided (the label is known on some paths and not on others); see the design choice put to the owner.

### ADR-058, Amendment 10 (5 October 2026) — the Enron and PaySim seeds load in bulk by default

Status: accepted 5 October 2026 (owner, in chat, re-seeding overnight after the deployment was lost: "can you enable to bulk load for Enron and Paysim").

Decision. `make seed-enron` and `make seed-paysim` (and `scripts.seed_enron`, `scripts.seed_paysim` run directly) write their edges through the bulk loader unless `--method upsert` is given. `seed_internal` always sends the method to the container for the two, so the script's own default never decides. The synthetic seeds (HMP, Fixture Corp) are unchanged and are refused `--method bulk`. `seed_support.write_graph` still defaults to upsert for its other callers.

Grounds. For PaySim, D5 (same graph) and D7 (no more stray copies than upsert) were met on the twin (Amendments 6 to 8: no node or edge differences; 6 ids stored twice against 8). **Enron has had no twin comparison**: its links go through the same loader at the same chunk size (`BULK_CHUNK`, 100), and the load's own stray check (`report_ids_stored_twice`) still runs after it, so a stray copy is reported, not hidden. The stray defect itself (ADR-056 Amendment 19) is unrepaired on either path.

Tests: `tests/test_seed_bulk_method.py` (`test_enron_and_paysim_load_in_bulk_unless_upsert_is_asked_for`, `test_the_synthetic_seeds_are_not_sent_a_method`, `test_method_is_refused_for_a_dataset_that_cannot_take_it` for HMP, `test_run_directly_the_enron_and_paysim_seeds_default_to_bulk`), red before the change. **Not run:** either seed with the new default against a real store.

## ADR-059 — The search box suggests as the analyst types: a separate prefix read, not a change to the exact search

**Status.** Accepted 2 October 2026, by the owner's choice of option B from the written options below. Built tests
first (see the friction row in `process/07_BUILD_PLAN.md`).

**Context.** Seen: typing `C` or a partial account id into the Glass search box found nothing, because `POST /v1/search`
is an exact match against a declared identifier by contract (`GraphPort.search_nodes`, `03_CONDUIT_MIDDLEWARE.md` §3.3).
An analyst who does not know the full value has no way in. (The full id also found nothing on that occasion, for a
different reason: the Glass reads the shared store until ADR-056 stage 1, and the PaySim accounts are in a vault.)

**Options put to the owner.** A: make the existing search match prefixes (breaks the exact contract and its tests, and
scans on every keystroke). B: a separate read and route for prefix suggestions. C: filter in the browser only (cannot find
anything not already on the canvas). **B chosen.**

**Decision.**

- `GraphPort.suggest_nodes(prefix, principal, *, limit=10) -> NodeSuggestions(nodes, more)`: nodes whose declared
  identifiers or indexed **string** properties start with `prefix`, case-sensitively. `search_nodes` is unchanged.
- The adapter scans label first (only the entity types that carry a suggestable field; an unlabelled lookup scans every
  vertex, ADR-058 Amendment 9) with `TextP.startingWith`, asks for `limit + 1`, returns `limit` and sets `more`. `more` is
  counted after the access filter, so it cannot reveal a hidden node (rules 2 and 3). An empty prefix is refused.
- `POST /v1/suggest {query, limit}` in the Conduit: `query` of at least 3 characters (`SUGGEST_MIN_CHARS`), `limit` from 1
  to 25 (default 10), audited as `suggest`. Response `{nodes, more}`.
- The Glass asks for suggestions from the third character, after a 250 ms pause, shows at most 10 and says when there are
  more ("keep typing to narrow"), and selecting one behaves exactly as selecting a search result does today.

**Cost and what would make it wrong.** A prefix scan is not an index lookup: it is bounded by the type's size (about
11 ms per 15,000 vertices measured for an unindexed id scan, ADR-058 Amendment 9) and by the 250 ms pause. It is
case-sensitive (a lower-case `c13` does not match `C13`), which is the next thing an analyst will notice; making it
case-insensitive needs a normalised, indexed form and is not decided here. If the Glass's first-use measurements show a
suggestion taking over about 300 ms on the largest case, the scan needs an index-backed form before it ships further.

**Not decided here.** Case-insensitive matching; ranking; suggestions that span documents or the index (OpenSearch is
not wired).

## ADR-060 — The working set settles into a force layout, and directed relationships carry an arrowhead

**Status:** Accepted, 3 October 2026. Appended; it supersedes nothing. ADR-002's "one parameterised program" for node shapes is
untouched.

**Seen.** An analyst expanding a node on the Enron case saw nodes scattered at fixed pseudo-random positions, so a network of any
size read as a hairball, with no sign of which way a relationship pointed. Edge labels had been worked out by
`computeEdgeAttributes` for the closest zoom band but were never drawn, because Sigma's `renderEdgeLabels` was off.

**Decision.**

- A force layout (`canvas/forceLayout.ts`: every pair of nodes repels, every edge attracts, a weak pull to the centre) runs a
  moment after the last node or edge is added and moves nodes to their settled places over `--dur-graph`. A node that arrives
  beside a settled neighbour starts next to it. Cluster members share their anchor's position, so only one node per cluster
  takes part and the rest follow it.
- It is bounded. Above `FORCE_LAYOUT_MAX_NODES` (1,000) it does nothing and the scatter stays, because freezing the page is worse
  than an unsettled picture. Passes are scaled down as the node count rises (60 to 200). Measured in the build environment:
  about 190 ms at both 500 and 1,000 nodes. That is the cost on one machine; it has not been measured on the analyst's.
- An edge type the ontology declares `directed` is drawn with an arrowhead (`EdgeArrowProgram`); a symmetric type, such as
  `SAME_AS`, and a type the ontology does not know are plain lines.
- Edge labels are drawn (`renderEdgeLabels`) at the closest zoom band, and at any zoom for an edge touching the node under the
  pointer.

**Not decided here, and not built.** ForceAtlas2 in a worker for the 50,000-node and 250,000-edge case (02_GLASS_FRONTEND.md
section 5), which is still unmeasured. Dragging a node by hand, and so a pin that survives a re-layout (the layout supports
a pinned node; nothing in the canvas pins one yet). A visual check in a real browser: the tests cover the layout's behaviour
(spreading, attraction, repeatability, a pinned node, the size cap), not whether it looks right.

### Amendment 1 (3 October 2026) — an expansion that would add more than 500 nodes asks first

**Seen.** A double-click on a busy Enron address added all 1,090 of its neighbours at once (1,091 nodes, 1,163 edges). That is
past the layout's own limit of 1,000, so no layout ran and the result was an unreadable disc. The double-click had been built
without the count-first check the owner had agreed.

**Decision.** Every way of expanding a node (double-click, a right-click menu entry, the Enter key) goes through one function
that first asks `/expand/preview` how many nodes it would add. Up to 500 it goes ahead. Above 500, or when the count could not be
obtained, nothing is added until the analyst chooses: a single relationship type (each shown with its own count), everything, or
nothing. The limit is `EXPANSION_CONFIRM_ABOVE` in `canvas/expansionGate.ts`.

**Not built.** "Add the strongest 100": the expand request has no limit field, so it needs a server change. Whether 500 is the
right number has not been tried on a real screen.


## ADR-061 — Type-ahead search takes options: match mode, ignore case, entity types

Status: accepted 3 October 2026.

Context. ADR-059 gave the Glass a type-ahead box that matched the start of a value, case-sensitively, across every entity type. The owner asked for filters: ignore case, entity type, match mode (starts with, contains, exact) and a scope limited to the graph on screen.

Decision.

1. `/v1/suggest` gains three optional fields: `mode` (`starts_with` default, `contains`, `exact`), `ignore_case` (false default) and `types` (list of entity types, at most 50). Defaults reproduce ADR-059 exactly.
2. The port takes a frozen `SuggestOptions`. An unknown entity type is a `ValueError` in the adapter and a 422 at the route; it is never silently dropped.
3. Case-sensitive forms use the predicates already proven on the store (`TextP.startingWith`, `TextP.containing`, `P.eq`).
4. Ignoring case uses `TextP.regex` with a `(?iu)` flag and the typed text quoted as a literal (`\Q...\E`), so characters such as `.`, `*` and `(` are text. This is unproven on ArcadeDB. Four live conformance cases (ignoring case, contains and exact, typed regex characters are text, access filtering with ignore case) were written first and must be run against a live store before this is relied on.
5. Contains and ignore-case cannot use an index. Their cost on the Enron data is unmeasured; ADR-059's 300 ms threshold applies once measured.
6. Searching only the graph on screen is client-side over the drawn nodes and does not call this endpoint.
7. The Filters panel in the Glass is not built by this decision; it follows as its own step.

Consequences. The audit record of a suggestion includes mode, ignore_case and types. Access filtering is unchanged and runs after matching.


## ADR-062 — The view can be tidied: remove selected nodes, or clear the view

Status: accepted 3 October 2026.

Context. After a large expansion the owner could not clear the graph and had no way to drop nodes they did not want ("I cannot clear out the graph once it is rendered").

Decision.

1. A **Remove selected (n)** button and the Delete or Backspace key take the selected nodes out of the working set. **Clear view** removes every node, after a confirmation that names the count and says the records stay in the store and History can restore them.
2. Both use the existing `DELETE /v1/investigations/{id}/nodes` route. No new endpoint. The server records a History step and publishes a remove delta.
3. The graph changes only after the server confirms (a reply with a sequence number). A refusal or a failed request shows the error and leaves every node where it was.
4. Removal is from the view only. No record, edge or assertion is deleted from the store.

Consequences. Delete and Backspace now act on the canvas when something is selected; they do nothing when nothing is selected. Removing an edge on its own comes with selectable links, not here.


### ADR-061 Amendment 1 — The Filters panel is built (3 October 2026)

Item 7 of ADR-061 said the Glass panel was not yet built. It now is: a **Filters** button under the search box opens a panel with an ignore-case tick box, the match mode (starts with, contains, exact), the entity types from the ontology (none ticked means every type) and "Only nodes on screen". The button shows how many filters are on. Changing a filter asks the question again.

With every filter at its default the request is exactly the one ADR-059 defined; a changed filter is sent under the Conduit's own names, and an unchanged one is left out. "Only nodes on screen" asks the Conduit nothing: it compares the typed text with the identifiers of the nodes drawn, as plain text (never a pattern), honouring ignore case, match mode and type, and it searches from the first character. It matches the same identifier properties the box already shows, which is not necessarily every field the Conduit searches.

Still unproven: ignoring case against the real store (the four live conformance cases from ADR-061 have not been run).


## ADR-063 — The analyst chooses how the working set is arranged

Status: accepted 3 October 2026.

Context. The owner found the graph unreadable after a large expansion ("no way to reformat the layout"), and a second review asked for several layout algorithms: organic by default, hierarchical, and grouping.

Decision.

1. A **Layout** menu on the canvas offers five arrangements: Organic (the force layout of ADR-060, the default), Radial around the selected node, Hierarchical, Circular and Group by type. Choosing one arranges at once and applies to nodes added afterwards until another is chosen. **Arrange again** repeats the current one, which re-centres a radial layout on whatever is now selected.
2. The four new layouts are pure functions in `canvas/layoutModes.ts`, behind one `arrange(mode, input, options)` interface. Positions are repeatable for the same graph. Above 6,000 nodes none is attempted and the positions stay.
3. **Hierarchical is our own small implementation**: edges that close a cycle are set aside, each node goes on the layer below its deepest parent, and four barycentre sweeps reorder each layer to reduce crossings. It is not a full Sugiyama layout (no optimal crossing minimisation, no dummy nodes for long edges). It sits behind `arrange`, so dagre or another library can replace it later without touching the canvas. No library was downloaded.
4. Radial uses the first selected node as the centre, or the most connected node when nothing is selected. Choosing a different node does not re-arrange by itself, so clicking around does not move the graph under the analyst's hands.
5. Nothing is stored: a layout is a view of positions, never a change to the data.

Not decided here. Communities (collapsing a group into one node) is a separate step.

Consequences. The layout choice is per session in the browser tab and is not remembered. Radial, hierarchical and circular ignore pinned nodes, which the force layout supports.


## ADR-064 — A link can be selected, and shown in the Inspector

Status: accepted 3 October 2026.

Context. The owner could not select links ("I am not able to select the links themselves"). A link was only inspectable through a popup that opened on hover, anchored at the pointer, so the click that followed landed on the popup. The drawn line is also one or two pixels wide, and the renderer picks a link only where it is drawn.

Decision.

1. A click on a link selects it: it is drawn thicker, in brass, with its label, and the Inspector shows its type, the direction between its two ends (or that it has none), how many records stand behind it, its dates, its provenance and its sources. Selecting a link clears the node selection and the other way round, so the Inspector shows one thing.
2. The click target is wider than the line. A click that the renderer did not attribute to a node or a link is checked against every visible link in screen space, with a reach of 6 pixels, before it counts as a click on empty space. The arithmetic is a pure function (`canvas/edgeSelection.ts`); a browser test proves a click 4 pixels off selects, one 16 pixels off does not.
3. Hovering a link opens nothing. The hover popup is removed; its component is left unused.
4. Keyboard (rule 13): with a node focused, `L` selects its next link and `Shift+L` the previous, wrapping round.
5. Delete (or Backspace) on a selected link, and a **Hide selected link** button, hide it from the view **in this browser tab only**. A **Show hidden links (n)** button brings them back, and a reload resets it. This is not recorded in History and nothing is sent to the server, because the server has no way to remove one link from the working set today. Hiding a link on the server, undoable through History, would need a new route and delta; it was offered and not chosen.

Not decided here. Deleting a link from the store; selecting several links.

Consequences. A hidden link still counts in the working set and in layout. The details panel for a link reads only what the working set already holds.

### ADR-064, Amendment 1 (28 October 2026): the unused hover overlay is removed

The owner's ruling of 28 October 2026, given with decision 3's history in front of them.
- **The finding.** Decision 3 removed the hover popup and left its component,
  `canvas/EdgeInspectionOverlay.tsx`, unused. It was still built, tested and kept current (ADR-130
  Amendment 2 gave it the sources-withheld words), but nothing mounted it, so no analyst could
  see it.
- **The decision.** The component and its test are deleted. A link's details are shown in one
  place, the Inspector (decision 1), which a click or `L` reaches.
- **Not changed.** Link selection, the Inspector's link details, and the keyboard walkthroughs.
  No keyboard case tested the overlay, because nothing opened it.


## ADR-065 — The top bar: menus for case and account, an application switch, Filters inside the search box

Status: accepted 3 October 2026.

Context. The owner looked at the Glass at about 1,000 pixels wide and found the top bar cluttered ("I don't think we need the case selector expanded here"): the case choice was a bare white box with `All cases` and `New case` stacked under it, `Filters` dropped below the search box looking like a stray button, and `Export`, `Sign out` and the long user id broke over two lines. Two causes were in the stylesheet, not the layout: `.select { composes: input; }` is CSS-modules syntax and does nothing in a plain stylesheet, so every `<Select>` was drawn with the browser's own white face (the same white boxes appear on the Ingest Studio's Connector and Handling marking choices); and the search box's Filters button and the header's buttons had no rules at all. The owner then asked for the Ingest Studio to stand apart from the Glass ("I want to distinguish clearly between the apps") and chose, from three offered designs, the application switch below.

Decision.

1. A shared dropdown panel (`design/primitives/DropdownPanel.tsx`): a button that opens a panel beneath it. Closes on Escape (focus returns to the button), on a click outside, and when keyboard focus moves outside it.
2. The case choice becomes `Case: <name> ▾`, opening the list of cases (the open one marked), `All cases` and `New case`. The Ingest Studio's "goes into" row uses the same component.
3. The account becomes one button, `<user name> · <clearance> ▾`, at the right-hand end. The user name may be cut short; the clearance is never cut short, so ADR-050's "always visible" holds. The panel shows the subject, clearance, unit and `Sign out`. `DisplayPrincipal` gains `username` from the token's `preferred_username` (empty when absent; the subject is shown instead).
4. Filters is an icon inside the search box at its right-hand end, with a small count when filters are on. Its accessible name is unchanged (`Filters`, `Filters (n)`).
5. An application switch at the far left, `[Glass | Ingest Studio]`, the open one filled in brass; while the Ingest Studio is open, a brass line under the bar and the Glass-only controls are not shown. Choosing Glass returns to the Glass view last open.
6. `.select` is given the input's own rules. Whole items of the bar wrap to a second line in a narrow window; labels never break.

Not decided here. A different accent colour per application (offered, not chosen). Removing the Ingest Studio's own case row now that the bar carries the case menu in both applications (both are kept).

Consequences. The bar is one line from about 1,440 pixels wide (measured in a browser with a stand-in for the slider's width); narrower windows wrap. The case name in the button is cut at 200 pixels. Existing tests were changed where the controls moved (the case switcher tests now open the menu first; the Ingest tab test names the button `Ingest Studio`). `App.test.tsx`'s fixture was also corrected: its handling-scheme stub had the wrong shape and its other answers did not suit the screens the new tests reach, so the new tests hold every request unanswered. Not exercised: the real `App` bar in a browser (the browser tests render the same components in a harness, `keyboard/top-bar-harness.tsx`); the light theme.


## ADR-067 — Upload from the analyst's computer into the ingest folder (amends ruling R6)

Status: accepted 3 October 2026.

Context. Ruling R6 (27 September 2026) gave Connect a list of the files in a read-only ingest folder and deferred any browser upload past the milestone. The owner opened the Ingest Studio and said: "I need a file picker, not just the bar saying file path." With an empty folder the screen offered only a text box, and a path typed from an analyst's own machine names nothing the Conduit's container can open. The owner chose "Upload from my computer".

Decision.

1. `POST /v1/ingest/source-files?name=<file name>` takes the file's bytes as the raw request body and writes them to `<ingest root>/uploaded/<name>`. `SOURCE_AUTHOR` only, checked before any byte is read. It returns the same shape as a listing entry, marked `uploaded`.
2. It refuses, with a sentence the Glass shows as given: a name with a folder part, a leading dot, a control character or over 200 characters (400); an extension outside the connectors' list (415); a name already used in the root or in `uploaded`, so nothing is ever overwritten (409); an empty file (400); a file over `OSPREY_INGEST_MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES`, default 512 MiB (413). The size is counted as the body streams and the declared length is checked first.
3. The bytes go to a hidden part-file and are linked into place only when complete; a refused or interrupted upload leaves nothing behind and a half-written file is never listed.
4. The audit record holds the name and the size, never the contents.
5. The renderer keeps the root's mount read-only (R6 is unchanged for operator-placed evidence) and lays one writable bind mount over its `uploaded/` sub-folder (`INGEST_UPLOAD_SUBDIR`, tested equal to the Conduit's own `UPLOAD_SUBDIR`).
6. The listing now includes the `uploaded/` folder (files only; a symlink or folder inside it is not offered; the same resolve-then-compare check applies), each entry carrying `uploaded: true|false`.
7. Connect shows **Choose file…** first (a real button that presses a hidden file input, so the keyboard reaches it), then the list of what is already on the server, and the typed path behind "Or type a path or address". The chosen file is selected as the data as soon as it has uploaded.

Not decided here. Deleting an uploaded file (nothing removes one yet); a quota across all uploads; scanning an upload for malware; uploading to a deployment whose ingest folder is on object storage.

Consequences. The Conduit can now write inside the ingest root, but only inside `uploaded/`. The write path is covered by module and route tests (names, no overwrite, size limit stopping the read, no leftovers, role, audit) and the mount by two renderer tests. **None of it has been run against Docker by the session that wrote it.** The known risk is Linux host ownership: Docker creates a missing host folder as root, and the Conduit runs as uid 10001, so the operator must create `uploaded/` and give that uid write access (`05_DEPLOYMENT.md`); Docker Desktop on macOS maps ownership itself. If the folder is not writable, the upload fails with a server error rather than a sentence, which is the first thing to check if the owner's first upload fails.


## ADR-068 — A blank classification on Connect is recorded as PUBLIC

Status: accepted 3 October 2026.

Context. Spec 09 §2 said none of Connect's three answers is optional. The owner looked at the Connect form and said the classification "needs to include public and also it does not need to be mandatory", and ruled "Blank means PUBLIC" when offered a scheme-named default instead (my recommendation was a default named in the scheme; the owner chose differently).

Decision.

1. The UK scheme (`packages/ontology/handling/uk-le.yaml`) gains `PUBLIC` as its lowest level: `[PUBLIC, OFFICIAL, OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE, SECRET]`. Dominance is by position, so every existing marking keeps its rank relative to the others, an `OFFICIAL` reader clears `PUBLIC`, and a `PUBLIC` reader does not clear `OFFICIAL`.
2. When a draft is created or edited with no classification (missing, empty or blank), the server records the scheme's lowest level, `PUBLIC` when the scheme has it and otherwise its first level. The Glass does not decide this; it only says "Left blank: recorded as PUBLIC" beside the box.
3. An analyst's own choice is never replaced. The other parts of the handling marking (handling code, originator, owning unit) and the legal basis stay required for Profile.
4. Spec 09 §2 is amended to say so.

Not decided here. Whether a blank classification should warn when the source was supplied by another unit; adding a `PUBLIC` level to the US scheme (it has its own lowest level, `UNCLASSIFIED`, which a blank marking takes there).

Consequences. A blank marking is the least protective marking, so a source loaded without thought is visible to every principal who clears `PUBLIC`. That is the owner's ruling and is why the screen says so rather than hiding it. Nothing in storage changes shape; a `PUBLIC` value is an ordinary classification string. Demo realm clearances (`harness/realm.py`) and every existing seed are unaffected because none carries `PUBLIC` as a clearance.


## ADR-066 — Communities on screen: boxes round groups of closely linked nodes, folded into one Group Node (appended after ADR-068; numbered earlier because the code cites it)

Status: accepted 3 October 2026.

Context. A busy view is a tangle: the owner asked for the nodes that belong together to be shown as groups the analyst can fold away and open again ("Communities"). Nothing in the spec described grouping on screen; ADR-029's Louvain (with a connected-components fix) runs in the compute tiers for the Metrics panel; the canvas does its own, lighter grouping of just the nodes in view.

Decision.

1. A `Communities` button on the canvas (reached by Tab, pressed by Enter or Space) switches the view on and off. When on, the nodes now in the view are divided into groups by Louvain with a fixed seed, so the same nodes fall into the same groups each time. A node with no link to another is in no group. Nothing is stored and nothing is sent to the server: it is a way of looking at the view, and switching it off puts everything back.
2. Each group is drawn as a box round its nodes, kept a fixed 16 pixels clear of them whatever the zoom. A box has a fold button (labelled `Fold group of N nodes`).
3. Folding turns a group into one Group Node: the group's best-connected member is drawn larger with a brass ring and labelled with what the group holds; the other members are drawn at the same place, too small to see, so a link from outside the group still reaches the Group Node, and links inside the group are not drawn. Opening it puts every member back where it was.
4. Ways to fold and open, all reachable by keyboard: the box's button; `G` on a focused node (folds its group, or opens it when it is the Group Node); `Collapse all` and `Expand all` beside the Communities button; a double-click inside a box folds it; a double-click on a Group Node opens it (and does not ask the server to expand anything).
5. While a group is folded: keyboard walking, ring walking and the lasso skip the members that are not drawn; a selected or focused hidden member is moved to the Group Node; Delete on a lone Group Node opens it rather than removing it, unless the whole group is being removed; the status bar says how many nodes are folded into groups (spec 02 §2: the bar never lies).

How a folded group is drawn. Sigma reads every node's position from the graph on each draw and ignores a position returned by a reducer (confirmed in `sigma.cjs.dev.js`, `process()`, and in a real browser, where the Group Node was drawn at the stand-in's own place). So the folded members' stored positions are really moved to the group's centre and their true positions kept aside; a position written afterwards (a layout, a drag) is noticed because it no longer matches where the member was put, and becomes its true position. Opening, switching Communities off, or a member leaving the group puts the true position back. The force layout starts from the true positions.

Not decided here. Naming a group by something other than its size; remembering which groups are folded between sessions; grouping by a property (the Layout menu's group-by-type does that for position only).

Consequences. While a group is folded the working set's stored x and y for its members are the group's centre, so anything that reads them directly sees the centre (the Metrics hulls do, which is right for a folded group). Not tested in a browser: a layout run while a group is folded (the logic above handles it, no test drives it). The on-screen Louvain does not apply ADR-029's connected-components split, so a group can in principle be made of two pieces that are not linked to each other. Louvain on a very large view is done on the main thread each time the working set changes; unmeasured, and the performance gate in spec 02 section 5 does not cover it.


## ADR-069 — Declutter, first part: the timeline's rarely used boxes behind buttons, and a quieter drawing for a crowded view

Status: accepted 3 October 2026.

Context. The owner found the workspace cluttered. Two causes are fixed here; the rest of the declutter list (the Metrics panel, the judgement badges, a light and dark theme, drawing three degrees out on a search selection) is not decided and is not built.

Decision.

1. The timeline's two boxes for typing exact dates (`from (ISO)`, `to (ISO)`) are behind a `Set exact dates` button in the timeline's own bar, closed until pressed (`aria-expanded` says which). Spec 02 section 3.4's "Brush endpoints are editable as text" still holds; the text boxes are one press away.
2. The `Overlay investigation` row above the timeline, a labelled box that was always showing, becomes an `Overlay another case` button in the timeline's own bar that reveals the same box (accessible name unchanged: `Cross-case overlay investigation id`). While a second investigation is overlaid, the button names it. The row above the timeline is gone, so the chart has that height back.
3. A crowded view is drawn quieter. Node size is multiplied, and link width multiplied, by a scale that is 1 up to 150 nodes (or links) and falls steadily on a log scale to 0.55 at 3,000 and beyond. A node is never drawn smaller than 2, nor a link thinner than 0.5, and a link on a found path keeps its width. The scale depends only on how many there are: nothing is hidden, so spec 02 section 1.1's "zoom never changes what exists" and the status bar's counts are unaffected.

Not decided here. The 150, 3,000 and 0.55 are first guesses to be tuned by looking at a real busy view; they are named constants in `canvas/nodeAttributes.ts`.

Consequences. The live scenario B specs press the two new buttons first (changed, not run: they need the owner's seeded stack). A drawing change cannot be judged by a unit test, so what is tested is the arithmetic (it shrinks, has a floor, leaves a small view and a found path alone) and not how it looks; the owner should look at a few hundred nodes and say whether it is quieter enough.


## ADR-070 — Declutter, second part: Metrics in closed sections, a count on nodes that have judgements, three steps drawn on a search selection, and a light and dark choice

Status: accepted 3 October 2026 (the four choices were put to the owner and each recommended option was taken).

Context. ADR-069 left four items of the owner's declutter list undecided. They were put to the owner as four questions and answered; this records the answers and what was built.

Decision.

1. **Metrics panel.** It opens closed. Inside it there are two sections, `Ranking` and `Communities`, and only one is open at a time (each heading is a button with `aria-expanded`). Neither metric is fetched until its section is opened, so a closed panel costs the server nothing. Spec 02 section 3.2's "ranked list, not a chart", "clicking a row selects and centres that node" and the hull overlay are unchanged.
2. **Judgement badges.** A node that has at least one judgement resting on it (listed as supporting or contradicting) carries a small brass count beside it on the canvas, labelled `N judgement(s)` for a screen reader. It shows that a judgement exists and nothing about the judgement: no probability band, no text. It is drawn only from the judgements the signed-in principal can already list, through the existing judgements route, so it opens no new read path and cannot reveal a judgement the principal may not see (`CLAUDE.md` rules 3 and 4; spec 02 section 9.2's hidden-judgement rule is therefore unchanged). The badge ignores the pointer, so it never gets in the way of a click or a drag.
3. **Choosing a search result.** The node is put on the canvas and drawn out three links (`SEARCH_DRAW_DEPTH = 3`) in one request, not one link as before. The server counts the result first, and above the existing 500-node gate the canvas asks before drawing and keeps the three steps in the answer; nothing is cut silently (`CLAUDE.md` rule 2). The expand request already carried a depth (1 to 4), so no server change was needed.
4. **Light and dark.** A button in the top bar (`Light theme`, `aria-pressed`) switches between the two themes already defined in `tokens.css`. The choice is kept in this browser only (`localStorage`, key `ospreyflow.theme`), never sent to the server, and is not part of the case. Dark stays the default and is what a new browser, an unreadable stored value or blocked storage gives. Text, panels and borders follow `data-theme` through CSS; what is painted to a canvas cannot read a CSS variable, so a hex palette (`color/palette.ts`, kept equal to `tokens.css` by a test) is chosen by the current theme, and the graph and the timeline draw again when it changes. Spec 02 section 10.4 is untouched: an exported chart still defaults to light whatever the analyst is working in.

Not decided here. The map's basemap is not made theme-aware (it keeps its own styling in both themes). The Timeline's light appearance and the Sigma label colour in light have not been looked at by the owner. Judgement counts for a folded group: a member hidden inside a folded group shows no badge, and the node standing in for the group shows its own count only, not the group's total. Whether the group should show the total is for the owner to say.

Consequences. Keyboard: the Ranking and Communities section buttons and the theme button are ordinary buttons reached by Tab and pressed by Enter; `keyboard/metrics-panel.spec.ts` and `keyboard/top-bar.spec.ts` prove them, and `keyboard/keyboard.spec.ts` proves the badge, the three-step draw (and its large-result prompt) and the repaint on a theme change. `live/scenario-a-a12-a15.spec.ts` presses `Ranking` first (changed, not run: it needs the seeded stack). What a unit test cannot judge is how it looks: the owner should look at the badge, the closed Metrics panel and the light theme.


## ADR-071 — Telling nodes apart, a right-click menu that names its node and closes, and a search hint and Filters panel laid over the page

Status: accepted 3 October 2026 (found by the owner on the Enron case; no choice among options was needed).

Context. On the Enron case the owner selected two addresses through the search box and saw two small unlabelled squares, a right-click menu that stayed open when clicked away from, and no way to say which node was which. Separately, the one-line top bar grew a second line as soon as the search hint "Showing the first 10; more match. Keep typing to narrow." appeared, and again when the Filters panel opened. The owner also said the light and dark button was found "almost by mistake", and that the large-expansion prompt "appears randomly".

Decision.

1. **Labels.** A view of 40 nodes or fewer (`SMALL_VIEW_LABEL_LIMIT`) names every node whatever the zoom or the node's links. A node that is selected, under the pointer or on a found path is always named, in any view. The zoom rule in spec 02 section 1.1 is unchanged for a larger view with nothing selected.
2. **The node menu** is headed with the node's type and name (`Endpoint: ` and the address, also its accessible name) and closes on a click anywhere outside it as well as on Escape. A click inside it does not close it.
3. **The search hint** ("more match") is laid over the page under the box, not part of the bar, and fades after four seconds (`SEARCH_HINT_MS`). It stays in the page for a screen reader. Only that nudge fades: "No match starts with that." and "Suggestions are unavailable." are answers and stay while the typed text stands. A new answer brings the hint back.
4. **The Filters panel** is laid over the page under the search box (it no longer pushes the bar down). While it is open it can cover the hint; only the order of the two is decided (the panel is on top).
5. **The light and dark button** is a worded button (`Light`, with the sun glyph) drawn like its neighbours, not a bare 28-pixel glyph. Any button with `aria-pressed="true"` (this one, and Graph, Map and Watches) now shows it: brass border and text on a raised surface. Before, none of them showed which was on.
6. **The large-expansion prompt** now names the node and the relationship being expanded and, when the size could not be counted, says nothing has been added. It was never random: it opens on a double-click on a node, on Enter with the canvas itself focused, on choosing a relationship in the node menu and on "Expand" by depth, and it opens whenever the size could not be counted (spec 02 and `expansionGate.ts`: not knowing is a reason to ask). On the Enron store the count calls do not answer, so every such gesture asks. The cause of the failed counts is not known (see below).

Not decided here. Why `/expand/preview` fails or does not answer on the large Enron store (the node menu's counts stay `(...)` and the prompt says `count unavailable`); a suspect is the parked lookup cost of ADR-058 Amendment 9, but nothing measured says so. The 40, the four seconds and the earlier crowding constants are first guesses to be tuned by looking at real views.

Consequences. `nodeAttributes.test.ts` (labels), `RadialMenu.test.tsx` (title and outside click), `GlobalSearch.test.tsx` (the hint fades; errors do not), `topBarStyle.test.ts` (the hint and panel are laid over the page; a pressed button looks pressed), `ThemeToggle.test.tsx` and `LargeExpansionPrompt.test.tsx` hold the units; `keyboard/keyboard.spec.ts` (small view named; menu named and closed by a click elsewhere) and `keyboard/top-bar.spec.ts` (the bar stays one line with the hint and with Filters open; the hint fades) hold the browser behaviour. The right-click-menu browser case was written after the fix, so it was not shown red; its behaviour was shown red at unit level. How any of it looks has not been judged by the owner.


## ADR-072 — The light and dark choice reaches every page of a deployment, through a cookie

Status: accepted 3 October 2026 (the owner asked for it in a comment on the verification walkthrough, after seeing the launcher's welcome page and the sign-in page stay dark; the cookie approach was put to the owner and confirmed).

Context. ADR-070 made the Glass light or dark and kept the choice in the page's own storage. A deployment is several pages, each on its own port of one host: the Glass, the launcher's welcome page (`make launch`), Keycloak's sign-in page, and the setup harness. All of them take their colours from `tokens.css`, which already has both ramps, but each started dark and none read a choice, and a browser keeps a page's storage per port so the Glass could not hand its choice on.

Decision.

1. The choice is also kept in a cookie, `ospreyflow_theme`, holding only `light` or `dark`, with `Path=/`, a one-year life and `SameSite=Lax`. A cookie is kept per host, not per port, so a choice made on any page reaches the others. No server reads it. `localStorage` stays as the fallback where cookies are refused.
2. The Glass (`theme/theme.ts`) reads the cookie first, since another page may have changed it since, then its own storage; a choice found only in storage is written to the cookie so existing choices carry over. The setup harness uses the same module, applies the choice before it draws, and carries the same `Light` button in its rail.
3. The launcher's pages and Keycloak's sign-in page are not React. They carry one plain script, `harness/theme_cookie.js`: it puts the choice on the page before it is drawn (in the head, so there is no flash of dark) and adds the same `Light` button at the top right (a real button, `aria-pressed` when light, coloured only from tokens). The launcher puts it in its head inline (the main page and its small message pages); the Keycloak theme ships it as `js/osprey-theme.js` and names it in `theme.properties` (`scripts=`). One file, so the pages cannot differ.
4. The button on every page now reads `Light` and is drawn like its neighbours; pressed means light (ADR-071 item 5).

Not decided here. Anything off this host: the pages of a deployment reached by different host names (`localhost` against `127.0.0.1`, or a separate sign-in domain) do not share a cookie and so do not share the choice; making them do so would need a cookie `Domain` and is for a real deployment to decide. The cookie is sent to every port on the host with every request, including other local services (it holds only `light` or `dark`); that is accepted.

Consequences. `theme.test.ts` (cookie written, read first, migrated, ignored when unknown, survives refused cookies), `themeCookieSnippet.test.ts` (runs the shipped file in a page with a cookie jar, against `theme.ts`, so the two cannot disagree about the cookie; every token it uses exists), `SummaryRail.test.tsx` (the harness button), `test_launch.py` and `test_launch_sign_in.py` (the script is in the head of the welcome page and of the message pages) and `test_keycloak_theme.py` (the theme names the script and ships the shared file). **Not proved:** that Keycloak 26's `keycloak.v2` login theme actually loads a script named by `scripts=` in `theme.properties`. That is how Keycloak's own login themes name scripts, but nothing here ran it against a real Keycloak (CLAUDE.md rule 15: a fixture models what the dependency accepts, not what it refuses), so the sign-in page following the choice is to be checked by the owner on a real deployment. Also not run in a browser: the launcher's and Keycloak's own buttons (they are plain buttons and are tested in a page with a cookie jar, not by keyboard in a browser), and the setup harness's button by keyboard (its Playwright suite needs the real harness server).

## ADR-073 — The light and dark button names the theme a press switches to

Status: accepted 3 October 2026 (the owner looked at the launcher's welcome page after switching it to light and said the button should then say `Dark`).

Context. ADR-071 item 5 made the button a worded `Light` button whose brass, pressed look meant "light is on", and ADR-072 item 4 put the same button on every page. The words never changed, so on a light page it still said `Light`: the only cue to what a press would do was the pressed colour, which does not say what the button will do, and a screen reader heard a fixed name with a pressed state.

Decision.

1. On every page the button's words, accessible name and tooltip name the theme a press switches to: `Light` (sun glyph, name `Switch to the light theme`) while the page is dark, and `Dark` (moon glyph, name `Switch to the dark theme`) once it is light.
2. Because the words now change with the state, the button no longer carries `aria-pressed` and no longer takes the brass pressed look. It is drawn like its neighbours in both themes.
