**Tests to write first, named, per stage** (the build is staged in the handover note,
`process/HANDOVER_2026-10-11.md`): the publish step refusing a Build path, an internal demo, a
real-data exception and an absolute path (each planted); `ospreyflow doctor` refusing each missing
prerequisite in words; a non-interactive Lite install from a clean checkout reaching a signed-in Glass
at the single address (over the wire); `start`/`stop`/`status` round trip; a demo pack's checksum
refused when wrong and PaySim's licence and attribution present beside it; the proxy publishing
nothing but its own ports; Keycloak keeping an account across a restart; the Admin area's invite,
disable and reset routes behind `manage_people` with each change audited, refused to anyone else;
`update` rolling back a release that fails verification; the ClickHouse adapter passing the
AnalyticsPort suite unchanged; the Blob adapter passing the MediaStore suite; OpenTofu plans for both
clouds validated in CI without credentials (`tofu validate`); the Helm chart rendering with every
stateful component external.

### ADR-055, Amendment (11 October 2026) — PaySim's licence verified; reclassified `shipped`, as a downloadable pack

ADR-055 §3–4 required PaySim's licence to be verified and recorded "before any change of
classification". **Verified 11 October 2026** from Kaggle's public metadata for `ealaxi/paysim1`
(`/api/v1/datasets/view/ealaxi/paysim1`): title "Synthetic Financial Datasets For Fraud Detection",
owner and creator Edgar Lopez-Rojas, licence **CC BY-SA 4.0**. The data is synthetic (generated by the
PaySim simulator), so no real-data exception applies. The owner ruled it included in the starter demo
packs (ADR-114 decision 5). It is reclassified **`shipped`** on these conditions: it travels as a
downloadable pack, never in a repository; the pack carries the attribution (Lopez-Rojas, Elmir and
Axelsson, *PaySim: A financial mobile money simulator for fraud detection*, EMSS 2016) and the CC
BY-SA 4.0 text; and anything derived from it that is redistributed — a seeded graph, its events —
carries the same licence. The demo registry changes with the pack's build (handover stage B0), not
before: until then `paysim` stays `internal` in `scripts/demo_registry.py`, and the gate is unchanged.

### ADR-114, Amendment 1 (12 October 2026) — stage B0: the demo packs, and where PaySim comes from

**The owner's ruling** (asked 12 October 2026, because decision 5 says PaySim is "a downloadable pack"
but not from where, and Kaggle's own download needs a signed-in account): **both** — by default from
a release asset the owner attaches to each release of the user repository, and from a file the
person downloaded themselves (`--file`) for an offline or air-gapped install. The owner then
redistributes PaySim under CC BY-SA 4.0 and carries its attribution and licence with every copy. No
release exists until stage B5, so until then the pack's release asset is empty and `--file` is the
only route.

What B0 decides, *(mine)* unless said:

1. **A demo is delivered one of two ways.** Each registry manifest gains `delivery`: `seed` (the
   synthetic packs — generated by code in the repository, so "download" means "seed") or
   `download` (PaySim). The comparison is strict, like `distribution`: anything but `seed` is not
   seeded. **A download pack's data never travels inside an artefact**, though it is `shipped`:
   the packaging gate refuses its paths exactly as it refuses an internal demo's, so a pack that is
   not seeded fails closed into "never in a bundle".
2. **Operation Ledger joins the registry** as `operation-ledger`, `shipped`, `seed`
   (`scripts.seed_ledger_fixture`), which ADR-114 found it missing from. **PaySim becomes `shipped`,
   `download`, data licence `CC-BY-SA-4.0`**, per the ADR-055 amendment.
3. **The pack catalogue is derived from the registry.** `scripts/demo_packs.py` in Core describes each
   pack — title, what it shows, delivery, licence, attribution, and for a download its file name,
   size in bytes, SHA-256, source page and release asset — and offers a pack **only** for a registry
   entry that is `shipped`. An id that is not a pack, or is an internal demo, is refused in the same
   words ("There is no demo pack called …"), so the refusal reveals nothing about what is held
   internally. A downloaded file is refused unless its size and SHA-256 are exactly the pack's.
4. **PaySim's pack**: `PS_20174392719_1491204439457_log.csv`, 493,534,783 bytes, SHA-256
   `16910f90577b0d981bf8ff289714510bb89bc71bff7d3f220f024e287e4eea6b` (measured 12 October 2026 from the
   owner's copy, which matches Kaggle's `ealaxi/paysim1`); carried with
   `packages/demo_fixtures/licences/paysim/LICENSE.txt` (the Creative Commons legal code for CC BY-SA
   4.0, verbatim from creativecommons.org, SHA-256 `28a9529c…fd1cf5`) and `ATTRIBUTION.md` (the
   dataset, its creator, the citation and the share-alike note for anything derived).
5. **A share-alike data licence is admitted only by download.** The licence check (ADR-035 §C7) flags
   a demo's data licence not on the code allowlist. CC BY-SA 4.0 is now admitted for a pack whose
   `delivery` is `download` — the data travels on its own with its licence, never mixed into a
   distributed artefact — and still flagged for one that is seeded or bundled; every other
   share-alike licence (CDLA-Sharing, the existing named case) stays flagged.

**Tests**, named before the code: an unregistered pack and an internal demo refused in the same
words; every shipped demo a pack and no internal one; a misspelled distribution offering no pack; a
download with a wrong size or a wrong checksum refused; a seeded pack with nothing to download;
PaySim's licence, attribution, size and checksum; each seeded pack's seed module existing; the
gate refusing PaySim's data inside an artefact although `shipped`, and refusing a manifest whose
`delivery` is misspelled; CC BY-SA admitted for a download pack and flagged for a seeded one; the
real registry with no data-licence offender.

### ADR-114, Amendment 2 (12 October 2026) — stage B1: Core stands alone, and what the publish step refuses

**The owner's rulings** (asked 12 October 2026, after a read-only sweep found 27 Makefile targets, two
`package.json` scripts, `pyproject.toml`, `.dockerignore` and `harness bundle` reaching into
`../OspreyFlow_Build`):

1. **The gates move to a Makefile in Build** ("New Makefile in Build"). `OspreyFlow_Build/Makefile`
   holds every quality gate, test suite and developer check; each recipe runs in the product folder
   (`cd ../OspreyFlow_Core && …`, with this folder on `PYTHONPATH`), so each command behaves as it
   did. `OspreyFlow_Core/Makefile` keeps only what runs without this repository — lint, type check,
   the image scans, the Glass's and the harness's browser suites, the synthetic seeds, `dev-up`,
   `launch`, `refresh` until stage B2 replaces them — and a `check` target of its own gates that
   Build's `ci` calls. The root Makefile forwards a target to Build when Build has it, else to Core.
   `ci.yml` is the owner's: the change it needs is written for the owner, not made.
2. **Code that exists only for an internal demo moves to Build** ("Move Enron code to Build"). The
   Enron reader and its seed (from the product's `packages/demo_fixtures/` and `scripts/`), its
   registry entry and its row in the seed runner's table leave Core for `internal_demos/` here.
   Core's seed runner (`scripts/seed_internal.py`) learns to run a dataset its caller defines, with
   the caller's code folder mounted beside Core's — generic, naming nothing in Build — and keeps
   every real-data check (the local exceptions list, the attested checkout) for any caller.

What B1 decides *(mine)*:

3. **`harness bundle` leaves Core.** The bundle is a release step of this repository
   (`tools/osprey_bundle.py`), run as `make bundle` from Build; the harness's dispatcher no longer
   names it.
4. **The publish step copies a commit, never the working folder.** `tools/publish_user_repo.py
   r2 <out>` takes `OspreyFlow_Core` as it is at that commit (`git archive`), so nothing
   uncommitted — the owner's local `osprey.yaml`, which carries a machine path, or a gitignored data
   folder — can leave. It writes into an empty folder outside this repository and nothing at all if
   any check refuses. It refuses, naming each file: (a) any mention of `OspreyFlow_Build`; (b) an
   internal demo's data or code (every path of an `internal` or not-seeded registry entry, Build's
   internal-demo registry included) and the fixed internal locations (`config/real_data_exceptions.yaml`,
   `demo-data/`, `OspreyFlow_Data/`); (c) an absolute path into a home folder (`/Users/…`, `/home/…`,
   `C:\Users\…`), except the homes of the users the product's own images run as (`arcadedb`,
   `ubuntu`), which are inside containers; (d) the personal authorship identifiers the packaging gate already refuses
   in a bundle. Pushing the result is the owner's.

**Tests**, named before the code: the published copy names no Build path and Core's own `check`
runs from Core alone; the root Makefile forwarding a gate to Build and a product target to Core; the
Enron seed refused without its exceptions entry when run from Build; the publish step refusing a
Build mention, an internal demo's data, an internal demo's code, a home-folder path and an authorship
identifier — each planted in a commit made for the test — and writing nothing when it refuses; the
uncommitted `osprey.yaml` never reaching the copy.

### ADR-114, Amendment 3 (12 October 2026) — stage B2: the `ospreyflow` command, its answers file and its guided page

**The owner's rulings** (asked 12 October 2026):

1. **"Replace my deployment."** B2 is proven by replacing the owner's running deployment with one the
   new command installs: back it up (`harness.backup`, every store and the configuration), uninstall
   it, install fresh, restore, re-seed the synthetic packs, and sign in over the wire. Nothing of the
   running deployment is touched until the backup is verified complete.
2. **"Every mode, designed now."** The guided page covers Lite, Small and Enterprise from the start.
   Lite installs from it; Small and Enterprise collect and save their answers and say, in words, that
   their install arrives with stages B6 and B7 — never a button that silently does nothing.

**What the drift survey found** (a fresh render into a scratch folder against the live deployment):
the hand-edited Superset and report-sync are exactly what the renderer writes when `osprey.yaml`'s
`reporting:` switches them on, and their secrets are minted at install (`harness.reporting`); the
ingest and tiles folders are `storage:` settings; ArcadeDB's loopback port is the renderer's
(ADR-054 Amendment 5) and the live deployment's missing one is the hand edit. So the drift is
configuration, not code: an install that asks for those settings reproduces the deployment.

What B2 decides *(mine)*:

3. **A small command over the harness.** `ospreyflow` is its own package in the product folder
   (`cli/`), depending on nothing but the standard library and PyYAML, installed as a `uv` tool by the
   bootstrap (`install.sh`, `install.ps1`). The heavy work stays where it is — rendering, preflight,
   build, up, verify (`harness.apply`), backup and restore — run inside the checkout's own
   environment (`uv run --project <checkout>`) or as `docker compose` against the rendered
   deployment. The command knows its checkout from `OSPREYFLOW_HOME`, else the folder the bootstrap
   recorded, else the checkout it is run inside.
4. **The verbs.** `doctor` checks each prerequisite of decision 4 for the chosen mode and says each
   failure in words with its fix (Docker installed, running, Compose v2; memory; free disk; Git;
   `uv`; for Lite, the ports the deployment publishes free or already its own). `install --mode
   lite|small|enterprise [--config FILE] [--yes] [--gui]` runs `doctor` first and stops on any
   failure; it writes `osprey.yaml` from the answers (never over an existing one without `--force`),
   then `harness.apply`, then the chosen demo packs (`scripts/demo_packs.py`; PaySim from `--file` or,
   once a release carries it, its release asset), and ends by saying the address and where the
   sign-in details are kept — never a password. `start [--build]` brings the deployment up; `--build`
   first rebuilds from the checkout, which is what `make refresh` did. `stop`, `status` (each service's
   state and health in words), `open`, `logs [SERVICE] [--follow]`, `demo list | add PACK [--file]`,
   `backup`, `restore DIR`, `uninstall [--keep-data]`. `update` is stage B5's. The `--install`-style
   spellings are accepted as aliases.
5. **The answers file** (`install.yaml`) is what every question writes and what `--config` reads, so
   the page, the prompts and CI install the same way: `mode`; the components (dashboards on by
   default — `reporting.sync` and `reporting.superset`); `storage` (the data, ingest and tiles
   folders); the models; governance; the map; the demo packs; and, for Small and Enterprise, the
   cloud, region, domain and sizing B6/B7 consume. Unknown keys are refused, as `osprey.yaml`'s are.
6. **The guided page** is the Set-up console's own screens (`apps/harness`), served by `install
   --gui` on `127.0.0.1` at a free port behind a one-time token, only while the install runs, then
   gone. Its screens: *Mode*; then, for Lite, *Folders*, *Components*, *Map*, *Models*,
   *Governance*, *Demo packs*, *Review*, and *Installing* (each step's progress in words); for Small
   and Enterprise, *Cloud and region*, *Domain*, *Components*, *Models*, *Governance*, *Demo packs*
   and *Review*, whose action saves `install.yaml` and says when that mode's install arrives.
7. **The old ways in are removed** (ADR-114 decision 3): `make refresh` and `make launch`, the launcher
   (`scripts/launch.py`), the welcome service, and `python -m harness` with no subcommand serving the
   Set-up console on 7100 for good. `process/CLAUDE.md`'s "No `osprey` CLI yet" convention is replaced.

**Tests**, named before the code: `doctor` refusing each missing prerequisite in words (each one
faked absent); `install --yes --config` refusing to overwrite `osprey.yaml` without `--force`, and
writing the reporting, storage and demo-pack settings the answers name; the answers file refusing an
unknown key and a mode it does not know; `start`/`stop`/`status` driving Compose against the
rendered deployment, round trip; `demo add paysim --file` refusing a wrong checksum before anything
starts; the guided page refusing a request without its token and closing when the install ends; the
removed targets and the launcher gone; and the over-the-wire proof — the owner's deployment
replaced, signed in at its address, the restored cases present.

**Added 12 October 2026, preparing the replacement (B2e): the backup now carries the whole
deployment.** An inventory of the running deployment found two things no backup held. The dashboards
keep their own Postgres database (`superset`) beside `ospreyflow`, and the backup dumped one; and
Keycloak runs with no persistent store, so no backup held anyone's account — restoring cases without
the people who hold their grants locks everyone out, because every grant, `created_by` and audit row
names a person by the identity provider's subject id. So:

8. **Every Postgres database, and the roles they grant to.** `harness.backup` dumps each database
   (`dump.sql` is the deployment's own, `<name>.sql` each other) and the roles (`roles.sql`); the
   restore replays the roles first, tolerating those the fresh install made, creates a database the
   fresh server lacks, then loads each.
9. **An identity item, with ids** (`harness/identity.py`). The realm's people and each dashboard
   identity (`osprey-dashboard-*`) with its secret and its service account, exported through
   Keycloak's admin API; imported with the same ids after removing what a fresh install made under
   the same names; passwords never travel (the demo accounts' are set again from the new
   deployment's own file). Measured first against a real Keycloak 26.0: an imported user keeps its
   id, attributes and roles; ids are unique across a server (a duplicate is refused 409); a client
   keeps its secret but not its internal id, which nothing names; a service account keeps its id —
   the subject its case grants name — only when imported with its client named. report-sync's
   dashboards setting travels in the same file, which is written readable by its owner only.

### ADR-114, Amendment 4 (12 October 2026) — stage B3: one address per app

Decision 6 asked for `*.localhost` to be checked on Safari, Chrome, Edge and Firefox before it is
relied on. **Measured 12 October 2026 on macOS 26.7.1**, with a loopback-only page that reports
back: Safari 26.6.2, Chrome 155 and Firefox 155 (Playwright's build) each reached
`ospreyflow.localhost`, `id.ospreyflow.localhost` and `bi.ospreyflow.localhost` on this machine, and
each treated them as a **secure context** over plain HTTP (`isSecureContext` true, `crypto.subtle`
present — which the Glass's PKCE sign-in needs). macOS's own resolver also answers every
`*.localhost` name with loopback. **Edge was not installed and is not measured**; it is Chrome's
engine, and it is to be checked on Windows, together with Windows' own resolver, before a Windows
pilot. The fallback decision 6 allowed for is therefore not built.

What B3 decides *(mine)*:

1. **Every address derives from `network.public_origin`.** Its default becomes
   `http://ospreyflow.localhost`. The identity provider is `id.` and the dashboards `bi.` in front of
   the same host, with the same scheme and port; the front proxy publishes that port (80 for a bare
   `http://`, 443 for `https://`), so moving the deployment's address or port is one edit, never two
   that can disagree. The install's answers set it: Lite `http://ospreyflow.localhost`, Small and
   Enterprise `https://<cloud.domain>`.
2. **The front proxy is Caddy 2.11.4** (Apache-2.0; released 3 June 2026), a `proxy` service with a
   rendered `Caddyfile` beside the compose file, routing each name to its service on the internal
   network and nothing else; its admin API is off. On a laptop it serves plain HTTP: the three
   browsers measured treat `*.localhost` as secure, so no local certificate authority has to be
   trusted. An `https://` origin turns on Caddy's automatic HTTPS, which stage B6 proves in the cloud.
3. **Nothing else is published** — the Glass, Keycloak and Superset lose their ports. Two exceptions,
   neither reachable from another machine: ArcadeDB's loopback port stays, because the basemap's
   place-name load runs on the host (the owner's ruling of 29 September 2026); closing it means moving
   that load into a container, for the owner to rule. And `network.expose_conduit` stays an explicit,
   off-by-default opt-in for debugging the Conduit.
4. **Keycloak has a fixed hostname**: `KC_HOSTNAME` is the identity origin, with
   `KC_HOSTNAME_BACKCHANNEL_DYNAMIC` on so the Conduit, report-sync and Superset still reach it inside
   the network at `keycloak:8080`, and `KC_PROXY_HEADERS=xforwarded`. Every token then names the same
   issuer, whichever door it was minted through.
5. **The Glass reads the identity provider's address at run time.** The renderer writes `glass.json`
   (the identity origin and the realm) and mounts it read-only into the workspace image as
   `/deployment.json`; the Glass reads it before it draws anything. The bundle is the same for every
   deployment. Where the file is absent — the Vite development server — the development default
   stands.
6. **Superset's and the Conduit's origins are derived**: Superset's public origin is the dashboards
   origin, its identity provider the identity origin, its permitted framer and the Conduit's CORS
   origin the Glass's; Superset trusts the proxy's forwarded headers (`ENABLE_PROXY_FIX`), which only
   the proxy can send it.
7. **Tools on the host never depend on the operating system resolving `*.localhost`.** Each host
   entry point (apply, the sign-in registration, backup, restore, the seeds, the CLI's checks) answers
   any `*.localhost` name with loopback for its own process (RFC 6761 §6.3), so the same request
   reaches the proxy with its name intact on a machine whose resolver does not answer such names
   (Windows', unmeasured). Each reads the identity and Glass origins from `deployment.env`
   (`OSPREY_IDENTITY_ORIGIN`, `OSPREY_GLASS_ORIGIN`, not secrets).
8. **The light and dark choice is kept for the base name** (added 12 October 2026, the owner's "fix
   the theme cookie first"). ADR-072 shared it as a cookie kept per host, which stopped reaching the
   sign-in page once it moved to `id.`. The Glass (`theme/theme.ts`) and the sign-in page's script
   (`harness/theme_cookie.js`) now write it with `Domain=` the base name — `id.` or `bi.` stripped —
   and clear the old copy kept for one host; `localhost` and an address keep it per host, where a
   browser takes no `Domain`. Measured first in Safari 26.6, Chrome 155 and Firefox 155: a cookie for
   `ospreyflow.localhost` reaches `id.` and `bi.`. Superset's own pages at `bi.` follow the operating
   system's preference (a board in the Glass follows the Glass).
9. **Left for stage B4**, which reworks identity: the launcher's and the old console's loopback
   clients in the realm (`harness/realm.py`) and the Glass's launcher hand-off
   (`auth/launcherHandoff.ts`).

**Tests**, named before the code: only the proxy publishing a port on every interface, and each
exception loopback or opted into (`test_only_the_proxy_is_published`); each name routed to its
service and to nothing else, and `bi.` only when Superset is on (`test_each_name_reaches_its_service`);
the identity and dashboards origins derived from `public_origin`, port and scheme included
(`test_every_address_derives_from_the_public_origin`); Keycloak's fixed hostname
(`test_keycloak_names_one_issuer`); the Glass's run-time file mounted and naming the identity origin,
and the Glass reading it, not a build-time value (`test_the_glass_learns_its_identity_provider_at_run_time`
and `oidcConfig.test.ts`); Superset's origins (`test_superset_origins_are_the_derived_names`); a
`*.localhost` name reached on loopback by a host tool against a resolver that refuses it
(`test_a_localhost_name_reaches_loopback_where_the_resolver_refuses_it`); and over the wire, a port
scan of the deployment showing only the proxy, and sign-in, the Glass, the embedded board and
Superset all working through the names.

### ADR-114, Amendment 5 (12 October 2026) — stage B4: accounts in production

**The owner's rulings** (asked 12 October 2026):

1. **Invitations: "Email if set, else one-time code".** With a mail server in the install answers,
   Keycloak emails a set-your-password link; without one, the Admin area shows a one-time temporary
   password once, for the administrator to pass on in person, and the person must choose their own at
   first sign-in. Resetting someone's sign-in works the same way.
2. **The Demo packs tab: "Show and explain".** It lists each pack — what it shows, its licence and
   attribution, whether it is loaded and into which case — and the exact `ospreyflow demo add` command
   to run on the host. The Conduit is never given control of Docker.

What B4 decides *(mine)*:

3. **Keycloak runs in production mode with its data in the deployment's Postgres** (B4a), in a
   database and role of its own (`keycloak`), made before Keycloak starts by a one-shot step
   (`keycloak-db`, the deployment's own Postgres image) that runs at every `up`, creates them when
   missing and sets the role's password from `deployment.env` each time. Measured first against
   Keycloak 26.0.8 and Postgres 16.4: `start` on plain HTTP behind `KC_HOSTNAME` imports the realm
   once ("already exists. Import skipped" afterwards); a user created later survives a recreated
   container; the bootstrap admin is made only on the first start, and a later start's new bootstrap
   password is refused (401). So the admin password, like Postgres's own, is never minted again while
   the database exists: `ospreyflow uninstall` removes both, and carrying a deployment's data forward
   is `update`'s (stage B5). The step was run against a real Postgres twice, the password changed
   between: each time only the current password signed in over the network.
4. **The backup leaves Keycloak's database out**: the identity item carries the people and dashboard
   identities with their ids (Amendment 3, point 9), and a fresh install's Keycloak makes its own
   realm — dumping both would load every person twice.
5. **The launcher's client is retired.** With the realm kept across restarts, a client nothing uses
   would stay for good; `register_sign_in` removes `osprey-launcher` from a realm that still has it.
   The Glass's hand-off (`auth/launcherHandoff.ts`) is **not** removed, although Amendment 4 listed it:
   it outlived the launcher — switching cases and opening a branched case on its Questions panel
   carry the sign-in on through it — so it stays, under its old name. The console's own client
   (`osprey-harness`) stays while the harness console exists.

6. **The people routes** (B4b): invite, set access (clearance, unit, receivable handling codes),
   disable, enable and reset sign-in, each behind `manage_people` and audited. Measured first on
   Keycloak 26.0.8, and the test fixture made to refuse the same: a name or address already held is
   409; an actions email with no mail server is 500 ("No sender address configured"); a username with
   a space or most punctuation is 400; Keycloak has no password policy of its own (a one-letter
   password was accepted), so the one-time code carries its own strength — sixteen letters from an
   alphabet without 0/O or 1/I, 80 bits; and a PUT naming `attributes` **replaces them whole** (setting
   clearance alone wiped the unit and roles), so every change reads the person and writes them back
   entire. Email or code is decided per person: by email only when the deployment has a mail server
   **and** the person an address. An email that cannot be sent leaves no half-made account. **Nobody is
   given more than the administrator holds** — a clearance above their own or a handling code they
   cannot receive is refused (403) before the identity provider is asked, the dashboard rule (rule 3)
   applied to people. **No administrator disables their own account** (409): they would have no way
   back in. A one-time code is in the answer only — never in the audit record, never stored.

7. **The Demo packs tab** (B4d) reads the pack catalogue (`scripts/demo_packs.py`, in the Conduit's
   image) and says each pack's command; it never runs one. A pack is "loaded" only when the case its
   seed makes is one the administrator can open — naming a case they cannot would disclose that it
   exists. The pack catalogue now carries that case's name, held to the seed runner's by a test.

8. **Email** (B4e): `osprey.yaml` gains an optional `mail:` (server, port, sender, STARTTLS, sign-in
   name) — never a password. The install reads the password from `OSPREY_SMTP_PASSWORD` into
   `deployment.env` and stops, in words, if a server that signs in has none. The render sets
   `OSPREY_SIGN_IN_EMAIL=true` only with a mail server; registration writes the realm's
   `smtpServer` every time (Keycloak never returns the password). Measured with a mail catcher: the
   email arrives from the sender with Keycloak's set-password link; a person with no address is
   refused (400, "User email missing"). **Also measured: a PUT that leaves out the email, or a name,
   erases it** — the fixture now does the same, and every change writes the whole person back.

9. **Start: where a person goes after signing in** (found at B4's live proof; owner's ruling "I should
   be able to go Admin, Glass or Ingest Studio right after logging in"). ADR-107's welcome page, with
   its Glass, Ingest Studio and Admin tiles, was the entry point; decision 3 removed it with the
   launcher, and nothing in the Glass took its place — signed in with no case open, an administrator
   met only *Choose a case*, and could reach the Admin area only by opening a case first (on a fresh
   install, with no case, not at all). So the Glass opens on **Start** whenever no case is open: one
   tile per place the person's rights (`GET /v1/me/rights`, ADR-112) open — *The Glass*
   (`investigate` or `read_reports`), *Ingest Studio* (`edit_pipelines`, the rail's own rule) and
   *Admin* (any administration right, only once known). *The Glass* goes to *Choose a case*; *Ingest
   Studio* to *Choose the case to load into*, then the Studio on that case, because what it loads goes
   into a case; *Admin* opens the Admin area **with no case**. A person with one place only (a Reports
   Viewer) goes straight to it, without Start. The mark at the top left is a button back to Start from
   anywhere, and *Choose a case* and the case-less Admin area both have *Start*. The tiles are a
   convenience, never the gate: every route still checks its own right. A case already open in the
   tab (`?investigation=` or the tab's session) still opens the workspace directly, so a reload keeps
   the analyst where they were.

**Tests**, named before the code: Keycloak in `start` on Postgres, its database made first and kept in
step, every secret the compose file requires minted by `apply`, the backup leaving Keycloak's database
to the identity item (`tests/harness/test_keycloak_persisted.py`); no launcher client in the realm and a
retired one removed (`test_realm.py`, `test_register_sign_in.py`); invitation by code and by email,
an unsendable email leaving no account, a held name refused, a role outside the set refused before
any account is made, access kept whole, disable ending sessions, reset handing over a new code, a
service account no person (`test_identity_admin.py`); each people route refused without
`manage_people`, the code never in the audit, the ceiling, no self-disable, a held name a 409
(`test_admin_routes.py`, `test_route_rights.py`); Start's places per rights, one place going
straight there, and Admin without a case (`visibility.test.ts`, `StartPage.test.tsx`), and each tile
and the mark's way back by keyboard (`keyboard/start.spec.ts`, `START_ACTIONS`); and live, an account
kept across a restart.

### ADR-113, Amendment 1 (11 October 2026) — report packs built: what an item rests on, and the gaps the decisions left

Stage 3 (handover A3). Decisions 3 to 5 and 7 are built as decided. Building them found places where
the decisions were silent; each was filled as below, all *(mine)*, none loosening a decision, each
open to the owner's overruling.

1. **An item rests on handling, not on a classification alone.** Decision 4 marks a snapshot at the
   highest classification it counted. That decides the *banner*, not who may read it: an event under
   a recipient-restricted handling code (`R` in the UK scheme) is limited to its owning and
   originating units whatever the reader's clearance (`01_DOMAIN_MODEL.md` §2.2), and a snapshot
   counted by its author would otherwise carry that event's figures to a case Viewer of another
   unit — rule 3, broken by an aggregate. So every item keeps each distinct handling it rests on (a
   trend's counted events; an assessment's supporting entities; a chosen entity's own; a note's
   own), and a reader gets the item only if they may view each one. `AnalyticsPort.trend` returns
   the distinct handlings it counted (`TrendResult.handlings`), its conformance case first: a hidden
   event adds none. The banner is still the highest classification.
2. **An entity or an assessment is checked again as the reader, now.** A frozen item could outlive
   a reclassification of what it names. On every read, a chosen entity must still be visible to the
   reader in the graph, and an assessment's supporting entities must pass ADR-046's hide-in-full
   rule for them (R7's narrowing kept: a superseded citation resolves forward). A trend or a note has
   nothing to re-read and rests on its frozen handlings.
3. **A note is marked by its author.** The words are the author's, so the marking is too: a
   classification is required (never assumed), the handling code defaults to the scheme's least
   restrictive, owning and originating unit are the author's, and a note cannot be marked above
   what its author may read.
4. **"Never which" includes the place.** Items are served in order without positions, so a
   withheld item leaves no gap; its id appears nowhere in the reader's response. Reordering moves
   only the reader's own items, in the places they held; each withheld item keeps its place.
5. **Nobody publishes what they cannot read.** Publishing is refused (409, with the count) while the
   draft holds an item withheld from the publisher; an empty pack is refused (422).
6. **Drafts are for assemblers.** Reading a draft or its history needs `record_assessment` with
   Viewer, so a Reports Viewer sees only published versions. *Published* shows each pack's newest
   version not withdrawn; a withdrawn version is no longer served to readers but is kept, with who
   withdrew it, when and why, in the pack's version list and the audit stream.
7. **A refresh is counted as the refresher.** It replaces the snapshot in its place; the earlier one
   is kept in the pack's history (`replaced_by`, `replaced_at`), withheld there by the same rule.

**Limitation, stated.** The analytics store keeps an event's classification, handling code and
units but not its action or sanitisation code, so the export gate (decision 6) cannot ask whether a
trend's counted events need the originator consulted; it can for an entity or an assessment.

**Tests.** `tests/conformance/analytics_port/test_suite.py::test_trend_says_the_handling_it_counted_and_only_what_the_reader_sees`;
`tests/services/api/test_packs.py` (13) and `test_pack_store.py` (4); the route-rights table's twelve
rows.

### ADR-113, Amendment 2 (11 October 2026) — a pack's export through the gate, and how its PDF is drawn

Stage 4 (handover A4). Decision 6 is built as decided: `POST …/packs/{pack}/export` (`export`, at
Editor like every export) takes the pack's newest publication not withdrawn — never a draft, never a
withdrawn version — and runs it through the gate. What the decision left open, filled *(mine)*:

1. **Item by item, as the exporter, now.** The exporter's access is checked again at export time
   with the same rule a reader gets (Amendment 1: every handling an item rests on, and an entity or
   assessment re-read in the graph). An item they may not see is **withheld and counted**, never
   named — the manifest names only what they may see, and ADR-045's policy decides whether the count
   is printed (`disclose`) or absent (`omit`). An exporter who may see **no** item is refused (403
   `export_refused`, naming nothing) and nothing is written to the ledger: there is nothing to
   export, and the refusal is what "refused above the exporter's handling" means for a pack.
2. **The originator, as for any export.** An item resting on a handling whose originator must be
   consulted (ADR-045/047) needs both a justification and an originator reference, or the export is
   refused naming the item — the exporter can see it, or it would have been withheld. A trend's
   events carry no sanitisation code (Amendment 1's limitation), so this can bite only an entity or
   an assessment.
3. **The mark** (ADR-047 Gap 1) carries the pack, its version, the exporter, the time, the highest
   marking exported, and whether an entity or assessment rests on a record since superseded. A pack
   is frozen snapshots, not a view of the graph, so it carries no resolution threshold.
4. **The ledger** (ADR-047 Gap 2) gets one entry per allowed export, `artefact_kind = report_pack`,
   with the items exported, the count withheld, the handling level, and whether an override was
   given (never its words — those are in the audit stream).
5. **The PDF is the browser's own.** The Glass draws the approved manifest as a print view — a
   cover with the mark, then each item on its own page under a banner and footer giving that item's
   marking — and opens the browser's print dialogue, from which the analyst saves the PDF. Nothing
   but the manifest is drawn, no PDF library enters the licence register, and no page can carry a
   marking lower than its item's.

**Tests.** `tests/services/api/test_pack_export.py` (6, against the real export ledger); the
route-rights row `export_pack_route`.

### ADR-113, Amendment 3 (11 October 2026) — what the live walk found

Stage 6 (handover A6), walked as `osprey-demo-analyst` on the deployment. Four findings; three
fixed, one recorded (finding 4 added 12 October 2026, from the same walk's screens).

1. **People are named (ADR-106), fixed.** The walk showed a version "published … by" a Keycloak
   subject UUID: the pack routes served `published_by`, `withdrawn_by` and the export mark's
   `exported_by` with no name, which ADR-106 decision 3 forbids for any id served for display. Each
   now carries its `<field>_name`, resolved at read time and never stored: `PackVersionSummary`'s
   `published_by_name` and `withdrawn_by_name` (on every route that serves a pack's versions — the
   list, the draft, a reorder, the history, a withdrawal), `PublishedPack` and
   `PublishedPackSummary`'s `published_by_name`, and `PackExport`'s `published_by_name` with its
   mark's `exported_by_name`. The directory is asked only for the people the response shows —
   never an item's adder, whose id the Glass does not display. The Glass and the printed cover show
   the name, or the id when there is none. An item's `added_by` and a pack's `created_by` are not
   displayed, so they carry no name.
2. **A case that reads another's dataset has no events of its own — recorded, not changed.**
   *Operation Ledger — AML review* reads the ledger dataset (ADR-099 Amendment 8) and its trend
   counted nothing: its 44 transactions belong to *Operation Ledger (synthetic demo)*, the case
   they were loaded into, because the analytics store keys events to their case, not a dataset
   (ADR-099 decision 7). Its Timeline is empty for the same reason. The walk was made in the case
   the events belong to. Whether a case that reads a dataset should also count that dataset's
   events is a decision about ADR-099, for the owner; nothing here changes it. **Ruled 12 October
   2026: say so, change nothing** — ADR-099 Amendment 9.

3. **The printed cover is marked, and periods are days, fixed.** Amendment 2 gave each item's page
   its own banner but left the cover — a printed page carrying the title, the publisher and the
   mark — with none. The cover now carries the highest marking exported (the mark's handling
   level), top and bottom. And the trend table in the PDF, with the chart's span sentence, its
   accessible description and each bar's title on screen, printed each period as a timestamp
   ("2026-08-03T00:00:00Z"); each is now said as a day ("3 August 2026"), in the words the rest of
   the pack uses.

4. **Every period of a trend's window is drawn, the empty ones too, fixed.** The published pack
   said "over 44 events in 12 weeks" above nine bars: `AnalyticsPort.trend` returns a point only
   for a period with events (unchanged — a zero is not a fact the store holds), and the Glass drew
   a bar only for a period it had a point for, so an empty week closed up the time axis without
   saying so. The periods are now every period the snapshot's own window touches — from the
   Monday week or calendar month holding `window_start` to the one holding `as_of`, in UTC, the
   periods the AnalyticsPort suite pins (`test_trend_counts_events_per_week`,
   `test_trend_counts_per_month`) — with any point outside them kept, never dropped. An empty
   period is an empty bar on screen and a "No events" row of 0 in the PDF. The first and last
   periods may be partial; their bars say "Week of" the period's own start. Computed in the Glass
   from what every snapshot already carries, so a pack published before this is drawn correctly
   with nothing stored changed, and no adapter changes.

**Tests.** `test_who_published_and_withdrew_is_named_and_no_one_else_is_looked_up`
(`tests/services/api/test_packs.py`, its directory fake recording every id asked for) and the names
in `test_the_manifest_names_only_what_the_exporter_may_see_and_the_ledger_records_it`; the Glass's
version line, Published line and printed cover (`PacksTab`, `PublishedTab`, `packExport` tests).
Six planted faults, each red: a published read asking for every item's adder; the withdrawer, the
exporter, the published list, the history's versions and the publish response each left unnamed. For
finding 3: the cover's two banners (`packExport.test.ts`) and the days in the table and on the chart
(`packExport.test.ts`, `TrendChart.test.tsx`), each red before the change. For finding 4:
`packText.test.ts` (every Monday week and calendar month of the window; a point outside it kept),
the empty bar in its place with each bar's stack (`TrendChart.test.tsx`) and the "No events" row
(`packExport.test.ts`), the chart and print cases fed timestamps as the server sends them; eight
planted faults, each red: no window fill, Sunday weeks, months bucketed as weeks, a point outside
the window dropped, the empty row omitted from the print, and the chart's stacks, the chart's
totals and the print's rows each matched on the raw timestamp.

### ADR-113, Amendment 4 (24 October 2026) — trend options are the case's domain packs (ADR-126)

ADR-126 decision 6 amends decision 1's "the deployment ontology's temporal link types".
- **What a case is offered.** The core types, plus those of the packs among the case's domain packs,
  narrowed by `OntologySchema.type_packs`.
- **Where the narrowing applies.** It is checked when a trend is saved or previewed, never when a
  saved trend runs or a pack holding it is refreshed. So a trend saved before a change of packs keeps
  running, marked as outside the case's domain models.

### ADR-114, Amendment 6 (13 October 2026) — owner rulings for stages B5–B8

The owner's answers to the questions the overnight run of 12–13 October recorded (`process/
07_BUILD_PLAN.md`, the 13 October rows), each the recommended option:

1. **Releases (B5, decision 13).** A Lite install from a release **pulls the signed images by digest**
   and checks their signatures; a developer checkout keeps building from source. Images are signed
   **keyless** — through GitHub's OIDC in `release.yml`, verified against that workflow's identity — so no
   private key is held. `ospreyflow update` looks at **the user repository's GitHub releases** at the
   address `install.sh` cloned from, and `update --from <bundle>` serves a deployment that cannot reach
   GitHub. A failed update **restores both** the previous release's images and the backup taken just
   before it. Admin → System learns of an update from a file **`ospreyflow update --check` writes**,
   which the Conduit reads: the deployment itself never calls out. Versions are **`vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`**
   tags; until the first, the short commit is shown.
2. **Small on Azure (B6, decision 8).** One plain VM: **Azure's service healing plus Docker's restart
   policy** are its recovery — a single VM has no automatic repair, only a scale set does, and
   decision 8's "VM auto-repair" is read as this. The database takes a password, so **the OpenTofu state
   is kept as a secret**, in the client's own encrypted, access-restricted storage, which the install
   says; the password is also in Key Vault for the server.
3. **The three background workers (B7, decision 9)** are the processes that already run apart from
   the Conduit: **the job worker** (`services/api/worker_main.py`), **report-sync** and **the ingest
   service**. Extraction, resolution and compute stay libraries the job worker calls.
4. **A client's own model provider (B8, decision 11)** **replaces the local model for the roles named**,
   subject to the sendable handling codes; a request above them **runs on the local model where the
   deployment has one, and is refused in words where it does not** — never sent. Admin → System shows
   each role's model, where it runs, and that case content leaves the deployment. The codes are enforced
   in the model path with B8 (they are enforced nowhere today), with a test that a request above them is
   not sent.

### ADR-114, Amendment 7 (13 October 2026) — nothing reaches outside unless a configured feature needs it

**Owner-directed** ("add the fix for the outbound traffic from the containers since that will breach
the security promise of the product"). Found: every container of a rendered deployment could reach the
internet, against 04 §4's "egress is default-denied".

**Measured on Docker Desktop first:** a container on an `internal` network cannot reach the internet
and cannot publish a port; a bridge with masquerading turned off still reaches the internet there. So:

1. **Every service is on the internal `osprey` network.** Only a service whose configured feature needs
   the outside world also joins `egress`: the **front proxy** (the one door in — a published port
   cannot be had without a route out — and, in the cloud, its certificates); the **model gateway** only
   when a client provider is named (Amendment 6); **Keycloak** only when mail or an organisation's
   sign-in is configured; the **Conduit** only when a map provider proxies remote tiles.
2. **Model weights are fetched by one-shot steps that exit** (`ollama-models`, `whisper-models`), into
   the volumes the model servers read; Ollama and the speech server, which read case content, never
   have a route out (speech reads its cache with `HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1`).
3. **Only the proxy publishes a port.** The graph store's loopback door (Amendment 4 decision 3, the
   owner's ruling of 29 September that seeds run on the host) and the Conduit's opt-in door
   (`network.expose_conduit`) are served through the proxy (`harness/site.py`'s `loopback_doors`),
   so neither service needs a route out.

**Proved live** on a rendered slice (the proxy, ArcadeDB, the speech download and server): no route out
from the internal network, and the speech server unable even to resolve a name; ArcadeDB answering on
`127.0.0.1` through the proxy; the speech model downloaded once, then listed and used for a
transcription with no route out; the `egress` network reaching out. **Not measured live:** the Ollama
download step (some 2 GB) — the same pull script, now run as its own step. **Applying it to a running
deployment needs it rendered again**; `ospreyflow start --build` does not re-render.

**Tests:** `tests/harness/test_render_egress.py` (8), with the front-proxy and render tests moved to the
new layout; plants red: the internal network made ordinary, the model server given a route out, the
gateway always reaching out, speech allowed to fetch, the graph store's door lost, a door published
but not routed.

**Applied to the owner's deployment, 13 October 2026 (the owner: "Re-render now").** Two defects found
doing it, both fixed with a test shown red first:

1. **A refresh gave a deployment half of the layout.** `ospreyflow start --build`'s refresh brings in
   any service the checkout renders and the deployment lacks; it copied `ollama-models` and
   `whisper-models`, with their `networks`, into a deployment that defines none, and the build step
   refused the file (nothing had restarted; the two services were taken out again by hand). Now a
   deployment without the internal network is never given those steps, and says so; any other new
   service joins its default network; and the model pull is written to whichever service pulls.
   (`tests/test_refresh.py`, two cases on a deployment of the old shape.) Contrary to the line above,
   refresh does write the compose file — it never renders it whole.
2. **`up --wait` read the finished weights step as a failure:** a container that has exited fails it
   unless a service waits on it, and the model server must not wait on a first pull of gigabytes. So
   `ollama-models` now stops and reaps the server it ran for its pulls and idles (`sleep infinity`); a
   failed pull still exits non-zero and is reported. It reads no case content and serves nothing.

The re-render took only `compose.yaml` and the Caddyfile from a fresh render of the deployment's own
`osprey.yaml` (`deployment.env`, which holds the secrets, untouched; a fresh `apply` would have minted
new ones); apart from the layout the render matched the deployment's file exactly. **Proved on the
owner's deployment:** every service but the proxy and the idle weights step is on the `osprey` network
alone, which is `internal`; the Conduit has no route out; the proxy does; ArcadeDB answers 204 on
`127.0.0.1:2480` through the proxy; the Glass answers 200; the Conduit reaches the model server; both
weights steps completed (the Ollama one, unmeasured before, verified every model's digest).

### ADR-114, Amendment 8 (13 October 2026) — how B5 is built: versions, the update notice, `update`

Amendment 6 point 1 settled the policy; these are the mechanics it leaves open, taken in building
*(mine)* and recorded before the code (rule 11).

1. **A deployment's version** is the release tag its images came from. A deployment built from a
   checkout reports the checkout's exact `vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` tag if it sits on one, else
   `dev-<short commit>`. `harness.render` writes it as `OSPREY_RELEASE_VERSION` in
   `deployment.env` (refresh keeps it current); the Conduit reports it on Admin → System.
2. **The update notice is a file.** `ospreyflow update --check` (run by a person, or their own
   scheduler — the deployment never calls out) asks the user repository's GitHub releases and writes
   `state/update.json` in the deployment's directory: the version checked against, the newest
   release, its notes (the release's changelog section), its address and when it was checked; or
   why the check failed, in words. The Conduit reads `state/` read-only (a mount) on each System
   request, so a check needs no restart. No file: "Never checked", and how to check.
3. **The repository is the checkout's own `origin`**, read from its git configuration — the
   address `install.sh` cloned from. Only `https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>(.git)` is accepted;
   anything else is refused in words (a mirror is served by `update --from`).
4. **A release is its `versions.lock`**, published as a release asset beside the bundle: every
   image by digest. `update` reads it from the release (or the bundle), never computes it.
5. **Signatures.** Every owned image in the target lock is checked with cosign (Apache-2.0, run from
   its pinned image, as OpenTofu is) before anything changes: keyless, against the certificate
   identity `https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/.github/workflows/release.yml@refs/tags/v…` and the
   issuer `https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com`. Any image unsigned or signed by anything
   else refuses the whole update, naming the image; nothing is changed. Third-party images are
   pinned by digest and not signature-checked (their publishers do not sign to one identity).
6. **`update` in order:** refuse a deployment that builds from a checkout (it moves with `git pull`
   and `ospreyflow start --build`); find the target (newest, or `--to vX.Y.Z`); refuse one not newer;
   verify signatures; back up every store (`harness.backup`); keep the rollback point (the
   deployment's compose file and lock, beside the backup's name); write the target's digests into the
   compose file and lock (owned and third-party images; nothing else changes); pull (or `docker load`
   from `--from`); `up -d --wait`; **verify** — every service running and healthy, and each owned
   container running the target's digest. A failure at any step after the backup **rolls back**: the
   kept compose file and lock put back, `up -d --wait`, then the backup restored (`harness.restore`),
   then the same verification against the old version. The result is said in words: updated, or
   which step failed, why, and that it was rolled back (or, if the rollback failed too, exactly what
   state the deployment is in and the backup to restore by hand).
7. **The changelog** is `CHANGELOG.md` in Core, one `## vX.Y.Z — DATE` section per release. A tag
   with no section is refused by `scripts/changelog_check.py`, which `release.yml` runs first; the
   release's notes are that section.
8. **`release.yml` is the owner's file.** The signing steps (`id-token: write`, cosign-installer,
   `cosign sign --yes` per pushed digest), the changelog check, the notes and the `versions.lock`
   asset are written as a change for the owner to apply (`process/B5_release_workflow.md`).
6a. **A release moves the checkout, not only the images** (added in building B5c): a release can
   change configuration as well as images — a new service, a new launch option, a third-party
   version — so swapping images alone would leave a deployment half on each. A release install is
   a checkout of the user repository at a tag, so `update` checks out the target tag (refused, before
   anything is backed up, if the checkout has changes of its own), brings the deployment's files up
   to date with refresh's existing steps (which never touch a secret), and then pins every image by
   the digest in the target's lock (`repository@digest`, stronger than a tag). The rollback point
   therefore includes the commit the checkout was on and every file in the deployment's folder that
   `update` may write. **`--from` (a bundle for a deployment without GitHub) is stage B5d**, after
   the online path is proved: the bundle must then carry the tag's source, the images and their
   signatures.
10. **B5d and B5e, the owner's rulings of 13 October 2026, from options.** *Offline updates carry full
    signatures* ("Full signatures carried"): `ospreyflow update --make-bundle <file> [--to vX.Y.Z]`, on
    a machine that reaches GitHub, verifies the release online first, then writes one file holding the
    release's notes and lock, the tag's source (`git bundle`), and each image twice — as `cosign save`
    keeps it (the image with its signatures and their transparency-log proofs) and as `docker save`
    writes it. `ospreyflow update --from <file>`, on the machine that cannot reach anything, verifies
    each image itself with cosign `--offline` against the same identity, then loads the images and
    checks the chain: the signature covers the manifest, the manifest names the image's configuration
    digest, and the loaded image's ID must be that digest — so a bundle altered anywhere is refused.
    The release is then applied as online, with nothing pulled. *An install from a release pulls the
    signed images* ("Now, after B5d"): when the checkout sits on a release tag, `ospreyflow install`
    verifies the release's images before starting them; a developer checkout keeps building.
    *(Amendment 34, 3 November 2026: the bundle also carries the cosign image, pinned by digest, and
    the release's lock names every image any option can run; 4 November 2026, build order step 29:
    `--platform`, the images of a named platform, `linux/amd64` by default.)*
11. **The lock is signed too** (found designing B5d): third-party images are trusted only through the
    lock's digests, and a lock in a bundle — or a release asset replaced on GitHub — could be altered
    to name another image. So `release.yml` also signs `versions.lock` itself (`cosign sign-blob`,
    keyless, published beside it as `versions.lock.sigstore.json`), and `update` verifies the lock's
    signature against the same identity before anything else, online and offline; a release without
    a signed lock is refused. Probed first with the real cosign: a lock altered by one character is
    refused offline.
9. **What can be proved before a real release, and how:** everything but the keyless identity is
   proved against real tools — a throwaway local registry, images signed with a throwaway cosign
   key (the verifier's key/identity is the one seam a test sets), a real `update` and a real rollback
   of a throwaway deployment. **The throwaway key's signatures are never uploaded** to Sigstore's
   public transparency log (`--tlog-upload=false`; verified with the log check off for that key
   only): a test must publish nothing. The keyless check itself is proved only by the first real
   release; until then it is a disclosed gap, not a claim.

### ADR-114, Amendment 9 (13 October 2026) — CI that runs, and an object store that can be installed

Found reading the developer repository's own CI runs for the first time (the owner: "can you help step
me through this"; `aykr/OspreyFlow_Dev` runs every push — an older note that Actions had never run was
about the previous repository and wrong for this one):

1. **`ci.yml` had drifted from the layout** (ADR-054's two folders, ADR-114 Amendment 2's Build
   Makefile): every `tools.*` gate ran with `PYTHONPATH=OspreyFlow_Build` from inside Core (no such
   folder there); the model jobs mounted LiteLLM's configuration from the repository root; and **the
   `test` job, and `make test`, collected no tests at all** — pytest ignores `testpaths` when it is not
   run from the ini file's own folder, so the unit suite has not run in CI since the folders split.
   Each is fixed, and the tests folder is now named on the command line.
2. **The whole-deployment exit tests run on demand** (the owner's ruling, from options: "Run them on
   demand"): they need 16 GiB and GitHub's runners for a private repository have 7.8 GiB, so in
   `ci.yml` they could never pass. They move to `.github/workflows/exit-tests.yml`, started by hand
   (with a runner label, for a larger runner if one is ever added), and `test-file-coverage-check`
   reads both workflows.
3. **MinIO's public images are withdrawn** — Quay answers "no such manifest" and Docker Hub "access
   denied" for every tag, `latest` included — so a new install fails at the object store, and only a
   machine with the image cached still runs. **The object store becomes SeaweedFS** (the owner's
   ruling, from options: "Switch to SeaweedFS"; Apache-2.0, actively published, S3-compatible): the S3
   adapter stays, the MediaStore conformance suite proves the change, and a running deployment's
   objects move across by backup and restore. Recorded here; built as its own stage.
3a. **SeaweedFS, as built** (probed first against the real image, `chrislusf/seaweedfs:4.48`, signed by
   its publisher): one process (`server -s3`), credentials from `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID`/
   `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` (a wrong secret and an anonymous request are each refused, reading and
   writing); `-volume.max=1000`, 1 GiB volumes, no preallocation and volumes grown one at a time
   (`WEED_MASTER_VOLUME_GROWTH_COPY_1=1`) — its defaults ran out of volumes by the third bucket. The
   MediaStore suite and every object-store test pass against it unchanged. The service is
   `objectstore`; the settings keep their `MINIO_*` names, so nothing that reads them changes. **Its
   data is on a named volume** — MinIO's was on an anonymous one (found reading the owner's
   deployment), which a `down` and `up` would have replaced with an empty one. **Backup and restore
   move to the S3 level** — every object as a plain file with its size and SHA-256, exported and
   imported through the Conduit's image inside the deployment's network — instead of copying one
   store's private data folder, which no other store can read; a MinIO-format backup is refused by
   name if restored into SeaweedFS.
4. **The owner's rulings of the same day, from options, on what follows:** the owner's own deployment
   moves to SeaweedFS **once SeaweedFS is proven** (conformance and a throwaway rehearsal), by backup,
   switch and restore with every store compared, the backup kept; the steps that need a signed-in
   browser (B10's screenshots, E7) are **left to one sitting at the end**; B7's Helm chart is
   **published beside the images**, as an OCI artefact in the user repository's own registry, signed
   like them, by its release workflow.
5. **The owner's deployment moved, 13 October 2026, and the move found a defect older than it.** The
   application's two buckets had been out of its sight since 12 October: **the MinIO backup wrote
   every archive one level too deep** (it copied `minio:/data` into a staging folder that already
   existed, making `staging/data`, then tarred that folder as `data`), so each restore put the
   buckets one level further down, where MinIO served them as objects of a bucket named `data`. The
   owner's store was three restores deep (B2e, B3, B4). Its 71 objects were read out at the right
   level by a throwaway MinIO on a copy of the data folder, and imported into SeaweedFS; all 71
   compare equal by size and SHA-256. A full backup was taken first and is kept, as is the old
   MinIO volume. S3-level backups cannot nest (they name each object by bucket and key); restoring
   an old MinIO-format archive into MinIO now takes it from the level it was taken at.

### ADR-114, Amendment 10 (13 October 2026) — how Small is installed, and Enterprise's shape

The owner's rulings, from options, each the recommended one, on what decisions 8 and 9 left open:

1. **Small installs itself on first boot.** OpenTofu writes the install answers — the managed database's
   host, the buckets, the names of the secrets — into the server's first-boot file; the server reads its
   passwords with its own cloud identity (instance role, managed identity), never from the file, and runs
   `ospreyflow install --yes`. `ospreyflow install --mode small --cloud aws|azure` on the operator's
   machine runs plan, then apply on confirmation, then waits until the address answers.
2. **On Azure, the S3-protocol stores run on the server:** staged Parquet, site images, the tile cache
   and the backup transfer use SeaweedFS (Amendment 9 point 3a) on the server's own data disk, covered by
   Azure Backup's daily VM backup. Media stays on Blob (decision 8). On AWS they use S3.
3. **DNS:** when the answers name a Route 53 or Azure DNS zone, OpenTofu makes the record; otherwise the
   install prints the record to create and waits until the name resolves to the server before Caddy asks
   for the certificate.
4. **The first administrator's sign-in is a one-time code** (as B4's invites): made on the server, put
   in the cloud's secret store, shown once by the operator's command and then deleted from the store.
5. **Enterprise runs ArcadeDB and ClickHouse in the cluster**, as StatefulSets on persistent volumes —
   ArcadeDB as three Raft replicas, ClickHouse as a replicated pair with ClickHouse Keeper. Postgres,
   Valkey, object storage and (on AWS) OpenSearch are the cloud's managed services. The Helm chart's
   test reads "every stateful component external" as **every one the cloud manages**.
6. **The three workers are one image each** — the job worker, report-sync and the ingest service, each
   its own Dockerfile over the Conduit's code with only its own entrypoint, signed and locked with the
   rest by `release.yml`.
7. **Enterprise's front door is Caddy**, the same routing as Lite and Small (the base name, `id.`,
   `bi.`), as a Deployment behind the cloud's load balancer, getting its own certificates.

## ADR-115 — The design handoff: the welcome page, Home and the Glass to `DESIGN.md` v0.2 — ACCEPTED (design)

Status: **accepted on the owner's rulings of 12 October 2026; design only, nothing built.** The
owner asked Claude Design for a review of the sign-in page, the page after sign-in and the Glass; its
handoff (`design/handoff/` at the repository root, never committed — the workspace reference draws
real Enron identifiers, `CLAUDE.md` rule 9) has a `README.md`, `DESIGN.md`, `Workspace Design
Review.md`, three `.dc.html` references (rebuilt in the product's own components, never shipped, nor
their `support.js` and `image-slot.js`) and seven screenshots of synthetic cases. Each decision below
was put to the owner as options and ruled. The build is staged as Phase E (E0–E7) in the handover note.

**What was true when decided:** the handoff's `DESIGN.md` equals `spec/design/DESIGN.md` but for one
note on two band steps no token uses, which it drops; `tokens.css` already carries its ramps, brass,
channels, scale and both typefaces; the Glass already has a marking strip (ADR-097 Amendment 1), the
solid-cut mark, a legend, zoom and a brass-use test; the signed-out Glass shows a sign-in screen whose
button starts the OIDC code flow with PKCE, and the password is typed only on Keycloak's own page,
which `harness/keycloak_theme.py` restyles; the realm has no brute-force protection; most Lite
installs have no mail server (Amendment 5 point 8); Start (Amendment 5 point 9) hides a place the
person cannot open and goes straight to a person's only place.

### Decisions

1. **`DESIGN.md`.** `spec/design/DESIGN.md` stays the source, with the handoff's one change applied
   (the stale note dropped). Core's root carries a copy for the design detector, held equal to the
   source by a test. A value the product needs that is not in it is asked for, never invented.
2. **The marking strip: the deployment's marking as a floor, the data above it** (ruling "Deployment
   floor + data"). A surface with no case data — the welcome page, Home, the Admin area, the Ingest
   Studio — shows the deployment's configured marking; inside a case the strip shows the higher of that
   and the highest marking on screen (ADR-097 Amendment 1, kept). The strip is always shown: no "none".
3. **Organisation sign-in only when one is configured** (ruling "Only when configured"). Until the
   install answers name a brokered identity provider, the welcome page's card has one *Sign in*,
   leading to the restyled Keycloak form. With one, *Continue with organisation sign-in* appears and
   goes straight to it (`kc_idp_hint`). Configuring a broker is not built in this phase.
   *Since ADR-114 Amendment 33 (drop 2), it is: `sign_in.organisation` registers the
   organisation's OpenID Connect provider in the realm (its "Drop 2 as built").*
4. **The credential form lives in Keycloak's login theme.** The Glass never takes a password and
   direct grants stay off; the email-or-username form, its validation copy exactly as the handoff's
   README writes it, *Reset your password* and *Check your email* are Keycloak's own pages, restyled
   to the card.
5. **Lock-out: five failed attempts, fifteen minutes** (ruling "Turn it on, 5 / 15 min"). The realm's
   brute-force protection is set so, measured on a throwaway Keycloak before the copy relies on it.
6. **Without a mail server, no reset by email** (ruling "Say ask your administrator"). *Forgot
   password?* then says "Ask your OspreyFlow administrator to reset your sign-in. They'll give you a
   one-time code." With a mail server, the designed reset and *Check your email*.
7. **Home shows all three places to everyone** (ruling "Home design, always shown"), replacing Start's
   hiding and skipping (Amendment 5 point 9): a place the person cannot open is dimmed with "You need
   the {role} role for this. Ask an administrator to add it." Every signed-in person lands on Home when
   no case is open; the tiles stay a convenience, never the gate.
8. **About and the footer** (ruling "Build it; links from config"). About is built as designed, on by
   default and switchable off in the install answers; each footer link (account help, accessibility
   statement, privacy notice, service status) appears only when the deployment gives its address —
   they are the deploying organisation's documents.
9. **The handoff's conflicting values go back to Claude Design** (ruling "Ask Claude Design first"):
   provenance dashes (README `4 3`/`1 3`, `DESIGN.md` §3.8 `4 2`/`1 2`), the canvas grid (README
   16 px, `DESIGN.md` §9 8 px), the regions (README top bar 44, rail 48, right panel 340; the review
   40, 44, 360) and node size (README radius 7; the review 20 px). **Settled the same day:** Claude
   Design's `DESIGN.md` v0.3 adopts the prototypes' values — dashes `4 3`/`1 3`, a 16 px grid in
   `--border-subtle` mixed to 40%, and a new §5a of layout dimensions (top bar 44, or 48 on the welcome
   page and Home; rail 48; right panel 340, resizable 300–480; control heights 24–36; breakpoints at
   1200 and 1100; person node radius 7 with a 24×24 hit area). v0.3 replaced `spec/design/DESIGN.md`
   whole after a diff showed only those hunks and the stale note.
10. **Order** (ruling "Phase E before B5"): Phase E runs next, then B5–B10, then Phase D.

**Tests to write first** are named per stage in the handover note's Phase E table.

**As built (12–13 October 2026).** *E1:* `governance.marking` (default the scheme's lowest), carried in
`/deployment.json`, which `refresh` now keeps up to date. *E2:* `governance.organisation_sign_in` (a
brokered provider's alias) and `welcome:` (`about`, `account_help`, `accessibility`, `privacy`,
`service_status`, each an http(s) address) in `osprey.yaml`, also carried in `/deployment.json`; the
welcome page in the Glass; the email form, its validation, *Reset your password* and *Check your
email* as the `osprey` login theme on Keycloak's own `keycloak.v2` pages (messages, a script and
rules — no copied templates, so a Keycloak upgrade keeps working), proven in a real Keycloak
26.0.8 with a mail catcher. **Not matched, and why:** the welcome page's off-scale sizes (a 15/23
lead, a 17px wordmark, gaps of 3/5/7/9/10/18/28/48px, 1px bar radii) take the nearest `DESIGN.md`
step; "Check your email" says "what you entered" because Keycloak does not hand the typed value to
its message; the Keycloak page's submit is the region's one brass action, since organisation sign-in
lives on the welcome page; with no organisation provider the card's one button is *Sign in* and its
note says the password is entered "only on the OspreyFlow sign-in page, never here" (the handoff's
note names an organisation's page, which would then be untrue).

### ADR-115, Amendment 1 (13 October 2026) — owner rulings on the seven E4 questions

The design reference conflicted with accepted decisions in seven places (`process/HANDOVER_2026-10-11.md`,
Phase E row E4). The owner ruled:

1. **The right panel stays a stack** (ADR-097 conflict 1 stands): no Inspector / Query / Case tabs.
2. **No Timeline view tab, and the Match strictness row stays visible** (ADR-097 Amendment 1 stands).
3. **`Enter` keeps spec 02's meaning**: it expands the focused node, or opens a Document in the reader.
4. **The theme switch moves to an icon in the top bar**, as the reference has it — amending ADR-097
   step 3 and the review's item 15, which kept it in the account menu.
5. **A case shows a mono scope badge** beside its name, as the reference has it. **Its scope is the
   datasets the case reads** (ADR-099; the owner's ruling of 13 October, from options): the first by
   name in capitals, then how many more ("ENRON +1"), all named in its title; "NO DATA" for a case
   that reads none. Nothing new is stored: the case listing already carries them. Built
   (`scopeBadge`, `CaseSwitcher.test.tsx`; plants red: others not counted, a no-data case unmarked,
   the badge not in mono).
6. **Nodes are drawn at radius 7 (14px) with a 24×24 hit area** (`DESIGN.md` v0.3 §5a), amending ADR-097
   step 2's 20px node. **Refined by the owner the same day ("small, icons on zoom-in"):** the icon or
   picture is not dropped but drawn only from the neighbourhood zoom band in (a camera ratio of 0.4 or
   closer, `zoomBands.ts`), where the node is drawn large enough to read it; below that the node is
   drawn plain and the type is carried by colour, the legend and the label. The canvas redraws when
   the zoom crosses a band (`cameraMoves.ts` `redrawOnBandChange`), since the renderer reruns its
   reducers only when asked and a wheel zoom does not ask. Tests that fail if this is violated:
   `keyboard/canvas-look.spec.ts` ("a node is 14 pixels across at 100%"; "a click just beside a node
   selects it, and one well clear of it does not") and `keyboard/keyboard.spec.ts` ("a picture given
   from a file is drawn in the shape…", which checks it is drawn when closed in and not at 100%).
   Found building the hit area: the renderer's display cache can hold unframed positions at the first
   click after loading, so the hit area reads node positions from the graph itself.

Found capturing E7's screens (`process/07_BUILD_PLAN.md`, 14 October), put as options and ruled, each

### ADR-115, Amendment 3 (29 October 2026) — the top bar wraps whenever its items do not fit

Found preparing the Prison Intelligence demo, and fixed on the owner's instruction of 29 October.
- **The finding.** Amendment 2 kept the bar to one line of §5a's height from 1,100 pixels up, on the
  measurement that everything fitted there. The case menu and its scope badge carry the case's own
  names, and "Prison Intelligence Dataset (synthetic demo)" with "PRISON INTELLIGENCE DATASET
  (SYNTHETIC)" make the bar 1,466 pixels wide at 1,440 (1,476 for the data engineer). The account

  its dataset). It was red before (the account menu ended at 1,506 pixels) and green after, with
  the one-line case at 1,440 and Amendment 2's 924 case still passing. `shellSizes.test.ts` now
