### ADR-115, Amendment 4 (1 November 2026) — intelligence mapping first

Status: accepted, the owner's ruling: "update the welcome page to emphasize the Intelligence Mapping
with crime analysis, AML and Fraud detection as follow up … I want this theme reflected across the
board", with "event monitoring and alerting needs to be highlighted as key features".

Decision. The product says what it is in one order everywhere it describes itself: **intelligence
mapping, for crime analysis, anti-money-laundering, fraud detection, and event monitoring and
alerting.** It replaces "intelligence analysis and network discovery" and the welcome page's "Crime
analysis on one graph", which decision 8 had taken from the handoff.

1. **The welcome page.** The heading is "Intelligence mapping"; the lead opens "For crime analysis,
   anti-money-laundering, fraud detection, and event monitoring and alerting." The capabilities are
   five: network analysis, geospatial, timeline trends, **monitoring and alerts**, reporting.
2. **About** is "One intelligence map", in four parts: crime analysis and anti-money-laundering as
   before, then **fraud detection** and **event monitoring and alerting**, each three points in words
   about what the product does today (shared identifiers, typology rules, match-on-read resolution;
   hotlists with review dates, rules on every load, alerts that explain themselves). No new screens.
3. **The README, the three guides' openings and the documentation site** say the same sentence. The
   marketing site and the decks already did.

Tests: `SignInScreen.test.tsx`'s "says what the product is, with its five capabilities" and "shows
About unless the deployment switches it off" (the four parts, in order), and `App.test.tsx`'s heading
case, each shown red first. The guides' new versions and PDFs are held by `test_docs_pdf.py`.

### ADR-114, Amendment 11 (14 October 2026) — the guided install page ships built

Found capturing B10's screens: the guided page's front end (`apps/harness/dist`) is gitignored and
built by nothing in the install, so `ospreyflow install --gui` had no page on a fresh checkout and an
old one on the owner's. **The owner's ruling, from options: the release builds it.** `release.yml`
builds `apps/harness` and ships the built page with each release (an asset unpacked into the checkout
by `install.sh` and by `update`); a developer checkout builds it with `npm run build`, and
`install --gui` refuses in words — naming that command — when the page is missing or older than its
sources.

### ADR-114, Amendment 12 (14 October 2026) — B7: the replicated stores, before the chart

Status: accepted 14 October 2026 (mine, within the owner's "carry on with B7"; recorded so it can be
overruled). Decision 9 names three ArcadeDB replicas and a replicated ClickHouse; this is what each
needs of the Conduit, proved in containers before the chart is written.

1. **ArcadeDB:** written through its leader, saying `eventual` — ADR-101 Amendment 2, which has the
   defect that forces it and the measurements.
2. **ClickHouse:** one shard, two replicas, three Keepers. With `CLICKHOUSE_CLUSTER` set (the chart
   sets `osprey`) the Conduit makes its database `ON CLUSTER` with the `Replicated` engine, so every
   table definition reaches both servers through Keeper, and its two tables `ReplicatedMergeTree` with
   no arguments (the server's default Keeper path and `{replica}` macro). Not set, nothing changes.
   Measured on `clickhouse-server:25.8.33.6`: a plain `MergeTree` in a `Replicated` database kept its
   rows on the server that took them (1 and 0), so the chart's server profile sets
   `database_replicated_allow_only_replicated_engine`, which refused one; `ReplicatedMergeTree`
   carried an insert across within 50 ms, and a mutation with `mutations_sync = 2` was on both servers
   when it returned. Replication of an insert is asynchronous: a read on the other replica in the
   first milliseconds after a load can miss it. A quorum insert would close that window at the cost of
   refusing every write while one replica is down; not taken.
3. **The conformance fixture makes its database the way the Conduit does** (`create_database` and
   `drop_database` in `adapters/analytics_clickhouse/schema.py`, dropped `ON CLUSTER`), so the suite
   runs unchanged on a pair: 80 of 80 on the pair, 80 of 80 on one server.
4. **Tests:** `tests/services/api/test_analytics_store.py`, three cases (the cluster's statements, one
   server's unchanged, a cluster name that is not a plain name refused); red first, and each branch
   shown red by a planted fault.

### ADR-114, Amendment 13 (14 October 2026) — B7: the chart, translated from the compose services

Status: accepted 14 October 2026 (mine, within the owner's "carry on to the next stage"; recorded so
it can be overruled). `05_DEPLOYMENT.md` §3b has the shape; this is why.

1. **The chart is generic and the renderer fills it.** Writing each service again as a template would
   be a second description of the deployment, free to drift from the first; so `harness/cluster.py`
   translates the compose stanzas `harness.render` already writes (`compose_services`) into the
   chart's `workloads`, and changes only what a cluster changes. The chart creates nothing from its
   own defaults.
2. **The configuration files are inside `values.yaml`**, not beside it as §3b first said: Helm reads no
   file outside the chart, and one file to install from cannot be half-forgotten. They fit a
   ConfigMap with room to spare (43 KB of the 1 MiB limit, measured; the test holds it under).
3. **A one-shot step that reaches out is a Job**, never an init container of the server it feeds: a
   NetworkPolicy applies to a whole pod, so a download inside Ollama's pod would give Ollama a route
   out (Amendment 7). A service compose starts only after such a step waits for the Job's mark on
   their shared volume. Keycloak's database step reaches only the managed Postgres Keycloak itself
   reaches, so it runs in Keycloak's pod first, at every start.
4. **The stores' peers start together** (`podManagementPolicy: Parallel`) and are named before they
   are ready (`publishNotReadyAddresses`): a Raft member becomes ready only once it has peers, so
   starting them one at a time would wait for ever.
5. **Superset is a release image** (`release.yml` builds `deploy/superset`): pull mode named
   `osprey/superset:local`, which exists only where it was built — a release install of Small could not
   start Superset either. `tests/harness/test_release_matrix.py` holds every pulled owned image to the
   release's matrix; nothing compared the two before.
6. **A managed Valkey takes a password and TLS** (`ValkeyConfig.client_kwargs`, used by the Conduit and
   the worker alike), proved against a password-and-TLS Valkey 8.0: answered with both, refused with a
   wrong password, refused in plain text.
7. **Tests:** `test_cluster_render.py` (21), `test_helm_chart.py` (19, both clouds, Helm and
   kubeconform as pinned images), `test_release_matrix.py` (2), `test_valkey_config.py` (3),
   `test_reporting.py` +1; `make chart-check` in `make ci`. Red: 26 planted faults across the
   templates and the renderer, each turning its own test red, and a 27th that survived — the
   translator's order, which the cluster's changes rebuild for the only value it applied to — replaced
   by two plants where the real output is ordered and a direct case for the translator; 4 more in
   the Valkey settings and 3 in the release matrix.
8. **Not yet:** resource requests, a GPU pool, the on-demand loader, the update notice, guarding two
   Conduits publishing recipes at once (§3b says so); the Secret's creation, which is the install's
   (B7's install stage); and the chart in a running cluster, which is the next stage.

### ADR-114, Amendment 14 (14 October 2026) — B7: the chart in a running cluster, and what it found

Status: accepted 14 October 2026 (mine, within the owner's "proceed to the next stage"; recorded so it
can be overruled).

1. **The proof.** k3s 1.31 in a container capped at 9 GiB (so nothing it does can take memory from
   the owner's deployment on the same machine), the chart installed from this checkout with values
   `harness.render` wrote for an HTTPS Azure-shaped cluster, and the cloud's services stood in for
   in a namespace of their own: Postgres over TLS, Valkey, Azurite for Blob. The Secret was built
   from the same functions `apply` writes Lite's secrets with, and held every key the values name.
   Images built from this checkout, imported (no registry). Proof-only changes, so it fitted the
   machine: ArcadeDB's heap 768 MiB (the cluster's 8 GiB is per replica), no model downloads, and the
   six workloads whose images were not imported at no replicas (Superset, OpenSearch, the recogniser,
   Ollama, LiteLLM, whisper) — the disk had room for one copy of the rest, not two.
2. **What held.** All 22 pods ready. ArcadeDB's three formed one Raft group and kept it through a
   rolling restart (leadership moved; nothing lost); ClickHouse's database was made `Replicated` and its
   tables `ReplicatedMergeTree` on both replicas by the Conduit itself; the Keepers elected a leader;
   Keycloak's two pods formed one cache cluster. Through the load balancer by name: the workspace,
   Keycloak's realm, the Conduit's `/healthz` through the workspace, `/v1` answering the Conduit's own
   401; plain HTTP redirected; an unknown name refused. The policies held: the Conduit reached the
   managed Postgres, Valkey and the internet; ArcadeDB and the workspace reached neither the managed
   services nor the internet, and still reached their peers. The adapter's own client in a Conduit pod
   wrote through the leader, followed a new one after the leader's pod was deleted, and stored each
   write once.
3. **Found and fixed:**
   - The proxy's Service named 80 and 443 whatever the address; on plain HTTP Caddy listens,
     unprivileged, on 8080. Its ports now follow the address.
   - **On HTTPS the proxy never became healthy, on Lite and Small too:** its check asked
     `http://127.0.0.1:80/healthz`, Caddy redirected it to HTTPS, and a bare address has no
     certificate. The catch-all that answers `/healthz` is plain HTTP on 80 on HTTPS addresses; a name's
     own HTTP request still redirects (`tests/harness/test_proxy_health.py`, against the real Caddy).
   - **The workspace's nginx named Docker's DNS** (`resolver 127.0.0.11`), which a pod does not have:
     every `/v1` request answered 502. Its configuration is now a template filled at start — the
     container's own resolver (`NGINX_ENTRYPOINT_LOCAL_RESOLVERS`) and `OSPREY_CONDUIT_HOST` (`api`; on
     a cluster the Service's full name, since nginx's resolver applies no search domain)
     (`tests/harness/test_workspace_proxy.py`, against the image built from this checkout).
4. **Found, not fixed (for B9):** the Conduit refuses to start without a `map:` section in
   `osprey.yaml` (`load_map_config`), while the schema says a deployment with no basemap is a real
   state. An install writes one; a hand-written configuration without one crashes the Conduit on
   every profile.
5. **Still owed:** a signed-in round trip on the cluster (Keycloak's grants and a first account are
   the install stage's, as on Small); the six workloads not run here; the cluster on EKS and AKS.

### ADR-114, Amendment 15 (14 October 2026) — the install package's documentation

Status: accepted 14 October 2026 — the owner's request ("a /docs folder that includes a developers
guide (for data engineers), a users guide (for analysts) and an administration & installation guide
for admins, with sufficient details around the architecture design … all the interfaces that would
be relevant for the target user group", "both as PDFs (with screenshots) and .md"), and their three
choices between presented options, each the recommended one.

1. **Three guides in the install package**, `OspreyFlow_Core/docs/`: a developer guide for data
   engineers, a user guide for analysts, and an administration and installation guide for
   administrators — each with the architecture its reader needs and every interface that reader uses
   (screens, commands, files, endpoints).
2. **Markdown is the source; PDFs are built from it** into `docs/pdf/`, screenshots in
   `docs/images/`, and a test holds each PDF in step with its Markdown.
3. **After B7** ("Finish B7 first"): the administration guide's Enterprise chapter describes the
   finished, proven install.
4. **Screenshots from a signed-in sitting:** a browser window is opened, the owner signs in, and only
   the synthetic cases are captured — never real data (rule 9).
5. `spec/10_ADMINISTRATION_GUIDE.md` (B10) is the specification's copy; the shipped administration
   guide is written for the reader who has only the package, and is checked against the same schema
   reference so the two cannot drift.
6. **Core's README is kept current with them** (the owner: "update the readme in the core as needed
   as well"): updated on 14 October for what B6 and B7 changed (Small builds its server with
   OpenTofu; Enterprise's chart, proven, its install still to come; `deploy/`), and again when the
   guides land, to point at them.

### ADR-114, Amendment 16 (14 October 2026) — B7: the Enterprise install

Status: accepted 14 October 2026 (mine, within the owner's "proceed to the next stage"; recorded so
it can be overruled). Built in parts; each part's own point says what it proved.

1. **A cluster names its namespace and storage classes** (`cluster.namespace`, default
   `ospreyflow`, a Kubernetes name; `cluster.storage_class`, each store's own volumes, the cluster's
   default when unset; `cluster.shared_storage_class`, **required**: the one volume every Conduit
   mounts needs a class several pods can share, which neither EKS nor AKS has by default). Declared at
   any other profile, they are refused, as `hosts` already was. The chart's values take the classes.
2. **The answers file carries them** (`cluster:`, Enterprise only), and Enterprise sets
   `analytics_engine: clickhouse` — before this an Enterprise answers file made a configuration the
   cluster renderer refuses.
3. **One identity step for every deployment** (`register_sign_in.ensure_identity`): the sign-in rules,
   mail, the Conduit's service-account roles, Superset's sign-in, the retired clients, the realm's look.
   Lite's registration runs it and adds the harness client and the demo accounts; a Small server now
   runs it too (`register_sign_in --no-demo-accounts`), **which it never did: Superset's sign-in was
   registered only beside the demo accounts, so a Small deployment's Superset had no client to sign
   in through**. Not proved on a running Small server (no cloud here): the same function the cluster
   install runs live is what it runs.
4. **`ospreyflow install --mode enterprise`** (`harness/cluster_install.py`), from the operator's
   machine with `kubectl` and `helm` pointed at the cluster; the doctor checks those two and that the
   cluster answers (OpenTofu and the cloud's command line arrive with the stage that builds the
   cluster). Answers without their managed services are refused in words. In order, each step safe
   to run again: render; the namespace; **the Secret** — minted where missing, **every value it
   already holds kept** (Keycloak's administrator and database passwords cannot change under a running
   deployment), what the configuration decides written each time, a managed service's password from
   the environment or kept, all of it on `kubectl`'s stdin, never on disk or a command line; `helm
   upgrade --install … --wait`; **the identity provider through a port-forward** (the names may not
   point at the cluster yet) — the Conduit's client secrets and roles, then `ensure_identity`; **the
   first administrator** in Keycloak's pod (`kubectl exec`, the account on stdin), never replaced;
   the load balancer's address and the names to point at it. `--chart-values` takes a site's own
   Helm values over the rendered ones.
5. **Proved in k3s** (capped as in Amendment 14, the cloud's services stood in for, proof-only site
   values as there): the install ran clean first time; a second run kept all 38 Secret values (same
   hash), the namespace and the account, minted nothing and printed no code; through the load balancer
   by name, the first administrator signed in with the code — Keycloak asked them to choose a password
   and complete their profile (name and email: the realm requires them, and only the email comes from
   the answers) — invited an analyst through the Conduit (whose service account the install had
   granted), and the analyst signed in with their own code and opened a case, listed back to them and
   to no one else. Three throwaway administrators were deleted and remade on the way, each time by
   the install. **Proof-only, in addition:** the report sync and two workers scaled down once the
   9 GiB cap was reached.
6. **Tests:** `test_cluster_install.py` (9, against a fake `kubectl`/`helm` refusing what the real
   ones refuse), `test_doctor.py`, `test_install.py` (Enterprise installs; refused without its
   managed services; a Small server configures the sign-in), `test_answers.py`,
   `test_deployment_schema.py`, `test_register_sign_in.py`, `test_cluster_render.py`; red first,
   and plants red: 9 in the schema, answers and identity, 8 in the install.

### ADR-114, Amendment 17 (14 October 2026) — B7: each release publishes the chart

Status: accepted 14 October 2026 (mine, within the owner's "proceed to the next stage"; recorded so
it can be overruled).

1. **Packaged at the tag's version** (`helm package … --version X.Y.Z --app-version vX.Y.Z`) in the
   release job, after the install page.
2. **Signed twice, keyless, as the rest of the release is:** the packaged file by a `cosign
   sign-blob` bundle, attached to the release beside it; and, pushed to the registry as an OCI
   artifact (`oci://ghcr.io/<owner>/charts/ospreyflow`), by its digest, as each owned image is. The
   job takes `packages: write` for the push.
3. **Verified before the release is published:** `harness.signatures` now takes any number of
   `--blob`/`--blob-signature` pairs (the install page and the chart) and `--artifact` references
   (the chart in the registry), each checked against the release workflow's identity at the tag;
   an unsigned one refuses the release.
4. **Proved with a throwaway key against a throwaway registry** (`--tlog-upload=false`, never
   uploaded): the workflow's own commands at `v9.9.9` packaged the chart, signed it, pushed it, read
   the digest from `helm push`'s answer, signed the artifact by digest; both signatures verified, a
   tampered file was refused, and the chart pulled back from the registry was 9.9.9 (app v9.9.9),
   carried no `Icon` file, and rendered. **Not provable before the first real release:** the keyless
   identity on GitHub, and `helm push` to `ghcr.io` with the workflow's token.
5. **An Enterprise install uses the chart in its checkout**, as Lite and Small use their checkout's
   code: on a release tag it is byte for byte the published one. Installing from the registry alone,
   with no checkout, is not built.
6. **Tests:** `tests/harness/test_release_chart.py` (4, read from the workflow), `test_signatures.py`
   (+3); red first; plants red: 3; actionlint clean (`rhysd/actionlint:1.7.3`).

### ADR-114, Amendment 18 (14 October 2026) — B7: the Enterprise cluster on each cloud, in OpenTofu

Status: accepted 14 October 2026 (mine, within the owner's "proceed to the next stage"; recorded so
it can be overruled).

1. **Two modules, one shape** (decision 10): `deploy/opentofu/cluster/aws` and `cluster/azure` make
   the cluster the chart is installed on and the managed services under it, take the same inputs
   (`name`, `region`, `domain`, `size`, `kubernetes_version`, `api_cidrs`, `backup_days`,
   `namespace`, `admin_email`; AWS adds `search`), and give the same outputs where the two mean the
   same thing — above all `install_answers`, the answers `ospreyflow install --mode enterprise`
   installs from, which hold no secret.
2. **On AWS:** EKS (secrets encrypted with a key of their own; a node group in three private subnets
   behind one NAT gateway), RDS for PostgreSQL 16 (two zones, password kept by Secrets Manager,
   deletion protection), ElastiCache for Valkey 8 (two nodes, TLS, a token), the S3 buckets Small
   makes, Amazon OpenSearch Service (decision 9; `search = false` leaves it out and the chart's own
   runs), and EFS for the shared volume. **On Azure:** AKS (no local accounts: every sign-in is an
   Entra ID one; a system pool for Kubernetes' add-ons and the deployment's own pool, three zones),
   PostgreSQL flexible server 16 (zone-redundant, a delete lock), Azure Cache for Redis (TLS only,
   port 6380), Blob for media; search and the S3-protocol stores run in the cluster (decision 9;
   Amendment 10 point 2).
3. **The cluster's API answers only `api_cidrs`**, and `0.0.0.0/0` is refused; on Azure, Key Vault
   answers the same addresses. Every managed store is reached only from inside the network — the
   cluster's security group on AWS; a delegated subnet or a private endpoint, each with its private
   DNS zone, on Azure — and no node has a public address.
4. **The chart's NetworkPolicies are enforced:** the VPC CNI's policy engine on AWS, Azure network
   policy on AKS. Without one, Kubernetes accepts the policies and nothing enforces them.
5. **The two storage classes the answers name are made by the module**, through the cluster's own
   API: `ospreyflow-volumes` (encrypted gp3 on AWS; zone-redundant premium disks on Azure, so a
   store's volume follows its pod to another zone) and `ospreyflow-shared` (EFS access points on
   AWS; premium Azure Files behind a private endpoint on Azure), both owned by 1000:1000.
6. **Pods reach S3 as the node does** (`credentials: instance`, as Small's server does): the node's
   role, with the instance metadata hop limit raised to 2 and tokens required.
7. **Secrets:** no secret is in the answers or an output. The AWS database password is RDS's own;
   the Valkey token is made in the state and copied to Secrets Manager. On Azure the database
   password and the cache's and Blob account's keys are in the state and copied to Key Vault. The
   state is therefore a secret, as Small's is.
8. **The database is guarded against deletion** by RDS's deletion protection and, on Azure, a
   `CanNotDelete` lock, which Azure enforces against `tofu destroy` too. Small's Azure module uses
   `prevent_destroy` instead; a lock replaces it here because it is checked by a test, and because a
   module test that applies cannot tear down a `prevent_destroy` resource.
9. **Kubernetes 1.34 by default**, on both modules: by October 2026 1.31 is in paid extended support
   on EKS and out of support on AKS.
10. **The operator needs, besides `kubectl` and `helm`:** the `aws` command line on AWS (the
    Kubernetes provider and kubeconfig sign in through `aws eks get-token`), and `az` with
    `kubelogin` on Azure. The doctor does not yet check for `kubelogin`.
11. **Not proved:** neither module has been applied to a real account; no cloud is reachable from
    this build. Microsoft has announced the retirement of Azure Cache for Redis in favour of Azure
    Managed Redis; moving to it is a later change. Feeding `install_answers` and the named secrets
    to `ospreyflow install` is the next stage.
12. **Tests:** `cluster/aws/tests/cluster.tftest.hcl` (12) and `cluster/azure/tests/cluster.tftest.hcl`
    (11), against mock providers, run by `make opentofu-check` with the Small modules'. Every promise
    above that a plan can see has a run; plants red: 15 on AWS, 18 on Azure, each failing the run
    that holds its promise, against a baseline that passes. One plant (the AWS nodes moved to the
    public subnets) first passed unnoticed, because the mock provider gives `public[i]` and
    `private[i]` the same identifier; the run now pins each set to an identifier of its own.

### ADR-114, Amendment 19 (14 October 2026) — B7: the Enterprise install builds its own cluster

Status: accepted 14 October 2026 (mine, within the owner's "proceed to the next stage"; recorded so
it can be overruled).

1. **`ospreyflow install --mode enterprise --cloud aws|azure`** does for a cluster what `--cloud`
   does for Small (Amendment 10 point 1): OpenTofu plans the module of Amendment 18, builds on the
   operator's yes (or `--yes`), and keeps its state in `.cloud/enterprise-<cloud>/`, readable only by
   its owner. Without `--cloud`, the install of Amendment 16 is unchanged: onto a cluster kubectl
   already reaches, with the managed services named by hand.
2. **`cloud.api_cidrs`** is a new answer: the addresses the cluster's API (and on Azure the Key
   Vault) answers, given to OpenTofu as `api_cidrs`. It is for Enterprise only, a list of address
   ranges, at least one, never a `/0`; it goes no further than the build — not into `osprey.yaml`.
3. **The module's answers join the operator's**: the cluster's storage classes and `external:`
   come from OpenTofu's `install_answers`; with `--cloud`, answers that give their own `external:`
   or storage classes are refused, as are answers whose `cloud.provider` disagrees with `--cloud`.
4. **A kubeconfig of the install's own**, `.cloud/enterprise-<cloud>/kubeconfig`, made by `aws eks
   update-kubeconfig --kubeconfig` or by `az aks get-credentials --file` and `kubelogin
   convert-kubeconfig -l azurecli`; the operator's `~/.kube/config` is not touched. The cluster
   install runs with `KUBECONFIG` set to it.
5. **The secrets travel by environment only.** Each secret OpenTofu named is read with the
   operator's own identity (`aws secretsmanager get-secret-value`, the RDS one's JSON taking its
   `password`; `az keyvault secret show --id`) into `OSPREY_POSTGRES_PASSWORD`, `VALKEY_PASSWORD`
   and on Azure `AZURE_STORAGE_KEY`, given to the cluster install's environment and to no other
   step; none is on a command line, in `osprey.yaml` or printed. A secret that cannot be read stops
   the install, naming the secret and not its value.
6. **The doctor**, with `--cloud`, checks OpenTofu, the cloud's command line, kubectl and Helm, and
   on Azure kubelogin — and not that a cluster answers, since none exists yet.
7. **The administration guide gains its Enterprise chapter** (section 6; the later sections
   renumbered), and the README its Enterprise build. **Found writing it: nothing backs up the graph
   store or the analytics database on Enterprise** — `ospreyflow backup` drives a Compose
   deployment, and both stores run in the cluster. The guide says so and points to the cloud's
   volume snapshots; a cluster backup is an open gap for the owner to schedule. **Also found:**
   `--chart-values` (Amendment 16) was never in the guide, so `test_admin_guide.py` had been red
   since that commit; the Enterprise chapter now names it.
8. **Not proved:** no real cloud. The commands each step runs are taken from the clouds' own
   command lines as documented; the fake runner models a refused secret read and an RDS secret
   without a password.
9. **Tests:** `tests/cli/test_cluster_cloud_install.py` (11), `test_answers.py` (+3),
   `test_doctor.py` (+1); red first; plants red: 18, each failing the case that names its fault.

### ADR-114, Amendment 20 (14 October 2026) — the install package's guides, landed

Status: accepted 14 October 2026 (mine, carrying out Amendment 15; recorded so it can be
overruled).

1. **The three guides are in `OspreyFlow_Core/docs/`:** `administration-guide.md` (installers and
   administrators: how it is built, the three modes, every command and setting — section numbers
   kept equal to `spec/10_ADMINISTRATION_GUIDE.md`'s, with an unnumbered architecture section
   ahead of them), `user-guide.md` (analysts) and `developer-guide.md` (data engineers), with the
   39 screenshots of Amendment 15 point 4, every one shown by a guide. Each was written from the
   code and the specification, read for the purpose by two read-only research passes; nothing a
   reader is told was assumed.
2. **The PDFs** are printed by `tools/docs_pdf.py` (`make docs-pdf`): each guide rendered by
   `tools/simple_markdown.py` into a page styled only from `tokens.css`'s light theme, printed by a
   headless Chromium (`--chrome`, `OSPREY_CHROME`, or Playwright's cache) to `docs/pdf/`, and
   recorded in `docs/pdf/manifest.json` with the SHA-256 of its Markdown, of each image and of the
   PDF. **The check, not a rebuild, is the gate:** `tests/test_docs_pdf.py` fails when a guide or an
   image changed since its PDF was made, a PDF was replaced or is missing, a guide shows an image
   that is not there, or a screenshot is shown by no guide. Printing needs a browser and stays a
   person's step; a PDF's bytes differ per printing (the browser stamps the time), which is why the
   manifest records the PDF's hash rather than expecting a reproducible one.
3. **The renderer gained four constructs**, each tested and shown red: an image alone on its line as
   a captioned figure; inline links (relative, `#`, `http(s):`, `mailto:` only — any other scheme
   stays text); an indented line continuing a list item; and `\|` as a pipe inside a table cell.
4. **Both copies of the administration guide are held to the product** (point 5): the settings
   appendix is written into both by `tools.admin_guide_options --write`, and
   `tests/test_admin_guide.py` runs every case — the appendix, each command and flag, each answers
   setting — against each copy.
5. **The documentation site renders the guides** (`tools/doc_site.py`): each a page with its images
   beside it; a link to a guide's Markdown or PDF leads to its page; the Analyst guide page, which
   said the guide was not yet written, now leads to the User Guide.
6. **Core's README starts with them** (point 6, and the owner's "make sure that the readme is
   updated to point to these documents for any one starting the journey"): a *Start here* section
   under the title names the guide for each reader, with its PDF.
7. **Found writing the guides — recorded, not fixed here** (each is for the owner to schedule):
   - an expansion past the working set's limit shows the canvas's generic "Expand failed (409)";
     the three options the server returns (branch, filter, promote to a batch job) are not shown,
     and Home's tip says they are;
   - there is no control in the Inspector to confirm an inferred node, though the route exists and
     `02_GLASS_FRONTEND.md` §3.1f says it is confirmed there; an alert closed as a true positive, a
     same-as link's *Confirm as the same*, are the confirmations the Glass offers;
   - the subgraph export takes everything on the canvas, not the selection;
   - the Studio's Files tab is shown to a Data Engineer, whose role lacks `extract_files`, which
     adding files there needs;
   - `revert_loads` is granted to Data Engineers but no screen or command reverts a load —
     the administration guide said Data Engineers could; corrected in both copies and the deck;
   - the administration guide's first draft of its architecture named the media store as one of
     the four ports; `00_ARCHITECTURE.md` names ComputePort, with the media store a narrower port
     beside them — corrected before it shipped, and in the owner's deck;
   - the demo screenshots show the Ingest Studio to the demo analyst, which the Analyst role does
     not grant — the guide does not tell analysts they will see it;
   - `tests/test_osprey_bundle.py` (8 cases) fails on a developer machine whose rendered
     deployment carries the home folder's user name — the packaging gate refusing correctly; for B9.
8. **Tests:** `test_docs_pdf.py` (10), `test_simple_markdown.py` (+7), `test_admin_guide.py` (both
   copies), `test_doc_site.py` (+2, one replaced); plants red: 12 (renderer and PDF check), 4 (site),
   1 (a flag missing from the package copy only).

### ADR-114, Amendment 21 (14 October 2026) — the user repository is aykr/OspreyFlow, private

Status: accepted 14 October 2026 — the owner: "the user repo should be aykr/ospreyflow, private".

1. **The user repository** (decision 1; `make publish-user-repo`) is `aykr/OspreyFlow` on GitHub,
   **private** — created by the owner on 14 October 2026, empty. Pushing to it is the owner's (the
   agent's push authority is `git push origin main` of the development repository only).
2. **A trial publish refused, as it should, and the causes are fixed:** the guides' PDFs printed each
   link between guides as an absolute `file:///Users/<owner>/…` address (now printed as the guide's
   name, and `tools/docs_pdf.check` refuses a PDF carrying any `file://` address — shown red on the
   real PDFs before they were made again); a harness test's synthetic home was shaped like a real
   one (`/home/ada` → `/u/ada`); a recipe's comment named the developer repository's folder.
3. **The packages are public; the source is private** (the owner, 14 October 2026: "make the images
   and chart public"). Every machine pulls the seven images (`workspace`, `api`, `ingest`, `ner`,
   `worker`, `report-sync`, `superset`) and the chart (`charts/ospreyflow`) from GitHub's registry
   without signing in, so Lite, Small's first boot and Enterprise's chart need no registry token and
   no image-pull secret, and the signature check (cosign, in its own container) reads them as it does
   today. Only the source needs a token: cloning the repository, and `update --check` and fetching a
   release's install page or bundle (`GITHUB_TOKEN`, Amendment 8).
4. **One step GitHub keeps for a person:** a package published from a private repository starts
   private, and no workflow can change that. After the first release the owner sets each of the eight
   packages to *Public* once (the package's settings, *Change visibility*); later versions stay public.
   Until then an install from that release cannot pull its images and says so.

### ADR-114, Amendment 22 (14 October 2026) — an operator runs `ospreyflow`; `make` is the developer's

Status: accepted 14 October 2026 — the owner asked whether any `make` commands were still active and
to move them to `ospreyflow`; of the line drawn below, "go ahead with all the steps".

1. **The line.** What an operator runs is an `ospreyflow` verb (decision 13; `make refresh` and
   `make launch` went with Amendment 3). The developer's gates and suites stay `make` — Core's
   `check`, `lint`, the scans and the browser suites, and all of `OspreyFlow_Build/Makefile` — since
   the command ships with the product and those check the product while it is built; moving them in
   would carry the developer repository's tooling out with it.
2. **Removed:** `make seed-hmp`, `seed-fixture-corp`, `seed-ledger`, `seed-paysim` — exact duplicates
   of `ospreyflow demo add <pack>`, which runs the same `scripts.seed_internal <pack> --stop-api`.
   `make register-sign-in` goes too, replaced by point 3's verb. (`make docker-clean` stays: it
   removes every OspreyFlow container on the machine, test copies included — the developer's
   clean-up, not an operator's.)
3. **New verb, `ospreyflow repair-sign-in`:** registers the deployment's sign-in again (the identity
   provider's clients, roles and the demo accounts — `harness.register_sign_in` for the deployment's
   own profile), safe to run again; `--no-demo-accounts` for an install made without them. It
   replaces `make register-sign-in` in every message that named it.
4. **No message tells an operator to run `make`:** a test reads every string a person sees in the
   product's Python (comments and docstrings aside) and fails on a backticked `make` command.
   Messages that named one now name the verb: `repair-sign-in`, `ospreyflow start --build`, and,
   for ports in use, `ospreyflow stop` for another deployment on the machine. The basemap builder's
   message also said a running deployment does not publish ArcadeDB — Lite does, on 127.0.0.1:2480
   — and now says so.
5. **Left for B9:** `DEMO_GUIDE.md` still walks through `make dev-up`; it needs a rewrite around
   `ospreyflow install` and `demo add`, which is B9's sweep.

### ADR-114, Amendment 23 (14 October 2026) — the Enron corpus offered as an optional download, with safeguards

Status: accepted 14 October 2026 — the owner: "while enron dataset does not go into the git repo I
would like the user to have the option to download the dataset from
https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~enron/enron_mail_20150507.tar.gz and include it into their demo set"; put to
them that this conflicts with decision 5 ("Never offered: Enron (real data)"), ADR-053 ("never
shipped") and rule 9, with the safeguards below, they chose to "offer it as optional download with
safeguards". **This amends decision 5 and ADR-053; rule 9 in `process/CLAUDE.md` is the owner's to
amend (its proposed text is in the build plan's row).**

What CMU's page says (read 14 October 2026): **no licence or terms of use are stated**; "I am
distributing this dataset as a resource for researchers who are interested in improving current
email tools"; "please be sensitive to the privacy of the people involved"; some messages were deleted
at affected employees' request, and earlier versions are no longer distributed and should be replaced
by this one. No checksum is published. The file is 443,254,787 bytes (CMU's "about 1.7Gb" is its
unpacked size).

1. **OspreyFlow never carries the corpus.** Not in either repository, a release, a bundle, an image
   or CI. Each user downloads it from CMU themselves and gives the file to
   `ospreyflow demo add enron --file <path>`, as PaySim. Nothing in the product fetches it.
2. **The file is checked before anything else**: its size and a SHA-256 pinned from the
   2015-05-07 file, refused in words otherwise (a different or tampered copy, or an older,
   unredacted version).
3. **An explicit acknowledgement, every time it is added**: the command shows that the corpus is
   real people's email and personal data, quotes CMU's request to be sensitive to their privacy,
   says that the user's organisation needs its own lawful basis to process it and that no licence is
   stated, and proceeds only on the typed answer `yes` (or `--accept-real-data`, for a scripted run,
   which says the same). A record of the acceptance (when, which file) is kept beside the unpacked
   corpus on that machine; the seed refuses without it — or, on the owner's machine, without the
   local real-data exceptions entry, which keeps working as before.
4. **It is marked as real wherever it appears**: the pack is listed as "real personal data,
   downloaded by you"; its case is named "Enron corpus (real data, this machine only)"; it is never chosen by default,
   never in an install's suggested packs, and never shared with the demo engineer or report viewer
   (as today).
5. **Its code moves into the product** (from `internal_demos/` to Core), since a user now runs it;
   its data folder stays refused by every packaging and publish check, and CI never adds it.
6. **Licence register:** the corpus is recorded as a data source with no stated licence, obtained by
   each user from its source, for research and demonstration — not redistributed.
7. **The licence gate (added 15 October 2026, found when CI first ran it):** `make licence-check`'s
   data leg refused the pack, since "none stated" is not a licence on the allowlist and the only
   exception (decision 5's share-alike download) did not reach it. The gate now names this one
   entry: the `enron` manifest passes only while it is a download and its declared licence reads
   exactly as recorded, so a change to either fails the gate again and asks for a decision. It is
   not a rule for unlicensed data in general — any other entry with no stated licence still fails.
   Tests: `tests/licence_check/test_data_licence_offenders.py`.

### ADR-114, Amendment 24 (15 October 2026) — CI green: the exit tests on demand, the scans' exceptions in Core

**Owner rulings**, 15 October 2026: "CI green" is the next stage; the deployment-level exit tests
run **on demand only** (Amendment 9 point 2, which this builds); the harness image's Compose
findings take an exception until fixed.

1. **On demand.** `deployment-exit-tests`, `sustained-load-exit-test` and `over-the-wire-exit-test`
   move from `ci.yml` to `.github/workflows/exit-tests.yml` (`workflow_dispatch`, a runner label
   as input), with a new `apply-env-exit-test`. Each needs a whole deployment: a 16 GiB container
   runtime and 20 GiB of disk, where a hosted runner has 7.8 GiB and about 12. Over-the-wire is
   moved for the same reason, though the ruling named two: its apply stops at Preflight on a hosted
   runner, and with no `pipefail` the `tee` hid that until the test step.
2. **The scans' exceptions live in `OspreyFlow_Core/.trivyignore`** (ADR-054's place for it; it had
   stayed at the root), so the user repository's release scan reads the same file; each scan in
   `ci.yml` names it. Every entry carries its reasoning and, from now on, an expiry.
3. **The harness image's Go CVEs** (CVE-2026-78669, CVE-2026-78667, CVE-2026-97031): denial of
   service against a server, in the `docker` CLI and Compose plugin the image copies from
   `docker:29-cli`, which it runs only as clients of the local socket. No Compose release carries
   the fixed libraries (v5.6.0 has x/net 0.58.0). Excepted until 14 December 2026; then rebuild on
   a newer `docker:*-cli`.
4. **What CI found that was wrong, not merely red:** the harness image never copied
   `packages/ontology`, so every render failed on import since E1; the install page said
   Enterprise "arrives with stage B7" after B7 was built, and told a Small or Enterprise user their
   answers were saved before they had saved them; PaySim's refusal promised a release-asset fetch
   "with stage B5" that B5 did not build; the render's refusal sent a reader to a repository that
   does not exist. Each corrected; the tests that pinned the old words now pin the new.
5. **The `test` job collected nothing** since the gates moved to the Build folder: its command named
   no test path, and pytest only falls back to `testpaths` from the ini file's own folder. It now
   names `../OspreyFlow_Build/tests`, as `make test` does.

### ADR-114, Amendment 25 (15 October 2026) — the model server never prunes a download in progress

**Found by a user's install**, which stopped with `Error: rename /root/.ollama/models/blobs/sha256-
c5396e06…-partial …: no such file or directory`. Amendment 7 split model serving in two: `ollama`
serves with no route out, and `ollama-models` (a Job on a cluster) runs its own Ollama server to
pull the weights into the same volume. An Ollama server prunes blobs no manifest names when it
starts, and a download's `-partial` file is one; so `ollama` starting or restarting while
`ollama-models` was pulling took the file from under the pull. **Reproduced** with the pinned
image on a throwaway volume: a second server started mid-pull gives that exact error, on the same
blob (`qwen2.5:0.5b-instruct`'s); with `OLLAMA_NOPRUNE=1` on the second server the pull completes.

**Decided:** the serving `ollama` carries `OLLAMA_NOPRUNE=1`, in compose and in the chart's values
alike; it never pulls, so it never needs to prune. The download step keeps the default. The
administration guide's §16 says how an install made before this recovers: `ospreyflow start`
while the deployment is up starts the download again with the server left running. Test:
`tests/harness/test_deployment_models.py::test_the_model_server_never_prunes_a_download_in_progress`.

### ADR-114, Amendment 26 (15 October 2026) — each guide carries its version, and its PDF a cover, contents and figures

**The owner**, 15 October 2026: "add a cover page and table of contents and table of figures for
all the guides … make sure that there is version record and version history maintained in these
guides", then "extend the version history recording to the .md files (all the contents in the
/docs folder)".

1. **Each guide in `docs/` carries a *Document control* section** (between
   `<!-- document-control:begin -->` and `<!-- document-control:end -->`): its version, date, the
   OspreyFlow release it describes and its status, above its version history, newest first. The
   histories were written from each guide's own commits: the administration guide from its first
   form as spec 10 (0.1, 13 October) to 1.5; the user guide to 1.2; the developer guide to 1.1.
2. **Maintained, not merely present:** `docs/pdf/manifest.json` records each guide's version and
   the hash of everything outside its version record. A guide changed while its version stays the
   same is out of step (`tests/test_docs_pdf.py`), and `python -m tools.docs_pdf --write` refuses to
   print it until the change has its own history row. A record whose version is not its newest row,
   or whose history is not newest first, is named too.
3. **Each PDF opens with** a cover (product, guide, who it is for, version, date, release,
   status), the document control, the contents and the list of figures, both with page numbers;
   every figure is numbered, every page carries the guide, its version and its number, and the PDF
   has bookmarks. Printing is Playwright's Chromium (`tools/print_pdf.mjs`), since the plain shell
   cannot number pages; the page each heading and figure lands on is read back from a first
   printing with `pypdf` (BSD-3-Clause, a development dependency only) and the guide printed again
   with the numbers, until they hold.
4. **Found on the way:** the Markdown renderer printed a comment line as visible text, so the
   administration guide's `<!-- options:begin -->` marker showed in its PDF and on the docs site. A
   comment on its own line is no longer printed. And the first version of the page search started at
   the first page containing the words "list of figures", which the version history also contains,
   so every heading was numbered as the contents page; it now starts after the page the list
   begins on, with a test in the shape of that mistake.
5. **Not in scope:** the specification's own copy of the administration guide (`spec/10`), which
   is the specification's text and versioned by its history in git.

### ADR-114, Amendment 27 (15 October 2026) — the user repository is public

**The owner**, 15 October 2026, after the second run of the v0.1.0 release was not started by
GitHub ("recent account payments have failed or your spending limit needs to be increased" — a
private repository's Actions minutes are paid, and the first release's seven images for two
platforms used many): asked whether making the repository public would help, was told it would (the
standard hosted runners are free for a public repository) and what it means, and made
`aykr/OspreyFlow` public. This replaces Amendment 21's "source private"; its images and chart were to
be public already.

What makes publishing the source safe is unchanged: every publication is an export checked for local
paths, real names and data files (`tools/publish_user_repo.py` and the owner's publish scripts), and
it carries the Apache-2.0 `LICENSE` and `NOTICE`; the Enron pack's code ships and its data never
does (Amendment 23). `ospreyflow update --check` no longer needs `GITHUB_TOKEN` for it — the token
remains for a private fork, which the guides already describe as conditional. The development
repository (`aykr/OspreyFlow_Dev`) stays private: it holds the build record and the history, which
are not exported, and its CI minutes stay paid.

## ADR-116 — Find connections: two people by search, explored by degrees of separation — ACCEPTED (design)

Status: **ACCEPTED by the owner, 13 October 2026**, from options: "search or canvas" for the two ends;
"grouped by degree, widened step by step". Built the same day (Amendment 1).

**Context.** The Pathfinder (spec 02 §3.1, ADR-033) finds up to ten shortest paths between two nodes
already on the canvas and shows them one at a time in a popover. The owner asked to search for the
connections between two nodes and explore them by degrees of separation.

**Decisions.**

1. **A *Find connections* panel** in the Glass's side-panel stack: *From* and *To*, each a search box
   over the case's datasets (the existing entity search), each also fillable from the selected canvas
   node (*Use selected*). Neither end need be on the canvas.
2. **Shortest first, then widened one degree at a time.** The panel first finds the fewest degrees
   that connect the two ("3 degrees apart") and lists the routes at exactly that degree; *Show routes
   at N+1 degrees* widens one step, up to six degrees (the domain model's default, §6.3) and never past
   ADR-033's ceiling of eight. Each degree is its own group, so a longer route never hides a shorter.
3. **Never cut silently (rule 2).** A degree with more routes than are shown (ten) says so — "10 of
   more than 10 routes at 4 degrees" — rather than presenting ten as all of them.
4. **Explored on the canvas.** Any route can be added to the canvas; a route added marks each node
   with its degree from *From*. Several routes may be added; the panel shows which are on the canvas.
5. **Access in the traversal (rule 3).** Routes are found in the graph store, filtered as they are
   walked: a route through a node the reader cannot see does not exist for them, and neither the
   shortest degree nor any count can reveal that such a route exists. A new `GraphPort` method,
   `paths_at_length(source, target, length, limit, principal)`, gives the simple paths of exactly
   `length` hops; its conformance cases are written before the adapter (rule 1).
6. **A Conduit route** under the case — `POST /v1/investigations/{id}/connections` with `source`,
   `target`, an optional `degree` (absent: the shortest) and optional link types — answering the
   degree, its routes, and whether more exist; Viewer level and the `investigate` right; audited.

**Tests to write first, named.** The conformance suite: routes of exactly the asked length and no
other; none through a hidden node, and the shortest degree unchanged by a hidden shorter route (rule
3's path-length leak); `limit` honoured with "more exist" said. The route: the shortest found when no
degree is asked; refused past eight; refused to a principal without `investigate`; a hidden end
answers as an unknown one. The Glass: the two ends by search and by *Use selected*; the shortest
degree said in words; widening by one; "of more than"; a route added to the canvas with its nodes
marked by degree; every action by keyboard (rule 13).

### ADR-116, Amendment 1 (13 October 2026) — built, and two things the decision did not say

**Built.** `GraphPort.paths_at_length(source, target, length, limit, principal, *, edge_types)`
returns `RoutesAtLength` (the routes and `more`); the ArcadeDB adapter holds `PathBuilder`'s
traversal to exactly `length` links (`times()` in place of `until()`), with the access step at the
source, every link and every node walked onto, and asks for one more than `limit` to say whether
more exist. `services/api/connections.py` asks one length at a time from one link up and stops at
the first with a route, so the fewest degrees are the fewest the reader can see. The route answers
`Connections` (`degree`, `paths`, `more`, `searched_to`); with no route up to six, `degree` is
empty. A hidden end and an unknown one answer alike, since neither has a route. The Glass's *Find
connections* panel sits in the side-panel stack; marks are drawn by the canvas's badge overlay,
below and to the left of a node, clear of a judgement count.

**Decided in building, then confirmed by the owner the same day, from options:**

1. **A `NOT_SAME_AS` link is never a step on a route — in Find connections and in the Pathfinder
   ("Never, in both").** It records an analyst's judgement that two records are *different* people,
   so it is not a connection between them. Both builders share one step filter; asked for by name,
   it is still not walked (`test_paths_never_walk_a_not_same_as_judgement`).
2. **Degrees are counted in stored links, a `SAME_AS` link counting as one, as the Pathfinder
   counts them ("Count it as 1 for now").** 01 §4 collapses `SAME_AS` components at query time for
   display, so two records of one person drawn as one node are "1 degree apart" here. Counting a
   match as no degree would need the resolution threshold in the traversal; not built.

**Tests that fail if this is violated.** The conformance suite (`test_routes_at_a_length_are_
exactly_that_long_and_every_such_route_is_found`, `test_no_route_passes_through_a_hidden_node_or_
link_and_the_fewest_degrees_do_not_move`, `…_honour_the_limit_and_say_when_more_exist`,
`test_a_not_same_as_judgement_is_never_a_step_on_a_route`, the link-type and dataset cases);
`test_connections_route.py` (11); `FindConnectionsPanel.test.tsx`, `connectionsApi.test.ts`,
`DegreeMarkOverlay.test.tsx`; `keyboard/connections.spec.ts` (`CONNECTIONS_ACTIONS`, six actions)
and the canvas walkthrough "a route's nodes are marked on the canvas with their degree from From".
**Unmeasured:** a search that finds nothing walks every simple route up to six links; on a dense
store (Enron's hubs) that may be slow, as the Pathfinder's six-hop search already may be.

## ADR-117 — Custody links in the NIEM pack, and the HMP pack drawn as a prison intelligence network — ACCEPTED (design)

Status: **ACCEPTED by the owner, 18 October 2026** ("yes, go ahead with the new link types"), for
a demonstration to analysts who work a prison network in i2 and in a purpose-built network viewer.

**Context.** A prison intelligence analyst's network is drawn from custody records as much as from
communications: who shared a cell, who stood trial together, who is kept apart, who was involved in
an incident, who visits whom (in person or by video call), whose phone numbers and bank accounts
overlap. The core ontology has `ASSOCIATE_OF` but no way to say *which* of these a link is, so the
"links to include" filter such an analyst works with could not be offered. The HMP demo pack
(Scenario A) carried yards, incidents, families, groups, associates and reports, but none of the
phones, calls, visits or payments its own pack description names.

**Decisions.**

1. **The NIEM pack gains them (pack version 2), not the core.** NIEM is the pack already named
   "Crime case analysis", and its corrections and justice domains own these ideas; ADR-108's packs
   only add, so the core stays at version 16 and no published recipe is flagged. Added:
   - `Incident` — an entity of `pole_class: event` (plum hexagon, shield icon) with `name`,
     `category` (assault, disorder, find, other), `item`, `occurred_at` and the identifier
     `incident_ref`. The core `Event` declares no properties, so an incident written as one would
     have no name, kind or date to show; a pack may add an entity type but not a core property.
   - `ROLE_IN` reaches `Incident` as well as `Event`; the person's part is its required `role`.
   - `SHARED_CELL_WITH` (undirected, temporal, `cell`), `CO_DEFENDANT_OF` (undirected,
     `case_ref`), `IN_CONFLICT_WITH` (undirected, temporal, `reason`), and `VISITED` (person to
     person, directed visitor to visited, temporal, `channel`: in person or video).
   Each new link type carries a channel colour (ADR-081), so the network reads by link type as the
   analyst's own tools do. Phones and bank links need nothing new: `USES` and `COMMUNICATED_WITH`
   (core), `HOLDS_ACCOUNT` and `TRANSACTED` (FIBO).
2. **The HMP pack is seeded against the deployment ontology** (core and every pack,
   ADR-108 Amendment 4), as the Ledger pack already is, and gains a synthetic custody network
   around its principal subject and relay group: cell histories, co-defendants, conflicts, incident
   involvement, visitors in person and by video, prison-phone and outside numbers with calls, and
   accounts with payments. The calls, visits and payments are also analytics events, dated and
   with a place, so the timeline, the map and the dashboards show them. Every name, number, account
   and place is invented (rule 9); the prison is the fixture's own HMP Hollywood.

**Cost.** Five more link types and one entity type in the pack. `pack_version` is recorded but no
code reads it yet — ADR-108's "a pack bump flags recipes exactly as a core bump does" is not
enforced by anything (logged in `07_BUILD_PLAN.md`'s gaps, rule 12); with only additions here,
nothing a recipe wrote before can be refused after.

**Tests that fail if this is violated.** `tests/ontology/test_packs.py`
(`test_niem_brings_the_custody_links_and_incidents`), and the HMP network's shape tests
(`tests/scenarios/test_hmp_network.py`).

## ADR-119 — Large working sets zoomed out: grouped by community, links between communities, nodes as dots — ACCEPTED (design)

Status: **ACCEPTED by the owner, 20 October 2026**, from options put in chat: "Links between
communities" with "10,000", then "Overview and structure", then "Group large cases by community",
then node dots "Yes, overview and structure". (ADR-118 is the parked Sigma 4 record, on its branch.)

**Context.** Spec 02 §5 requires level-of-detail drawing for large working sets, and §1.1's
overview row draws "only above the strength filter; aggregated between hulls". Neither was built:
the strength filter (ADR-088) is the analyst's own slider, off by default, and the perf fixture's
links all weigh 1, so a weight floor thins nothing. A large case also opens at the fitted view,
which is the structure band, so the overview row alone never touched what an analyst sees first.
Measured on the 50k-node / 250k-link fixture (software rendering, as CI draws): drawing the
50,000 nodes with their pictures was most of the first frame; the links were a small part.

**Decisions.**

1. **More than 10,000 links: links between communities, zoomed out.** In the overview and structure
   bands one link is drawn between each pair of communities, its width growing with the number of
   links it stands for (`canvas/communityLinks.ts`), on a canvas over the nodes and under the labels
   (`communityLinkLayer.ts`); individual links are not drawn, and from the neighbourhood band in
   every link is. A selected link, and a link on a found path, are always drawn.
2. **More than 10,000 nodes: ordinary nodes as dots, zoomed out.** In the same bands a node is drawn
   by Sigma's plain circle program, in its type's channel colour (dimming kept), without its shape,
   icon or provenance outline; a node that is selected, under the pointer, on a found path, carries
   a resolution-cluster ring, or is a folded group keeps its full drawing. From the neighbourhood
   band in, every node is drawn in full.
3. **A large case opens grouped by community.** Once communities are known, a working set of more
   than 10,000 links is arranged as Clustered bubbles by community (`layoutModes.packBubbles`,
   without the 6,000-node limit of the other arrangements; nodes in no community share one bubble),
   unless the analyst has chosen a layout; links between communities mean little on a scattered
   layout, which is what the force layout leaves above 1,000 nodes.
4. **Communities come from a Web Worker** (Louvain, seeded, via Comlink; `communityWorker.ts`), as
   §5 requires of metrics: the first frame draws nodes at once and the community links follow when
   the worker answers; a newer question supersedes an older answer (`communityAssigner.ts`).
5. **Zoom still never changes what exists** (§1.1): the links and nodes drawn less are still in the
   working set, counted, searchable and selectable; the pointer's own hit test skips only links
   not drawn.

**Cost.** A change of band on a large case changes what is drawn at once rather than fading (§1.1's
"nothing appears abruptly" is not met at these two thresholds). Shapes and provenance outlines are
not seen zoomed out on a large case. The opening view of a large case is rearranged a second or
two after it first appears, when the worker answers.

**Measured (owner's machine, the perf gate's first frame).** `main` 8.2–8.7 s; with decisions 1 and 4
alone 7.6 s; with decision 2 as well 5.3–5.6 s. Not yet measured on CI.

**Tests that fail if this is violated.** `perf/community-links.spec.ts` on the 50k/250k fixture (the
case opens grouped; community links drawn and individual links not; a node is a dot and a selected
one is not; a selected link is drawn; zoomed in, every link and node is drawn in full) — red with
community links never drawn, with the selected link not excepted, and with a selected node drawn as
a dot. `canvas/communityLinks.test.ts`, `communityAssigner.test.ts`.
