### ADR-135, Amendment 1 (1 November 2026) — Ask to search carries the case's handling

Status: built on 1 November 2026 from the owner's answer to open question 2 ("Ask to search carries
the case's handling, so the engine choice applies"). Open to the owner's review.

**Before:** Ask to search sent no handling code, so the routing always kept it on the local engine,
whatever the analyst chose (this ADR's "Found while building").

**Now:** the question is sent under the case's handling and from the case's datasets, through the same
two gates as Ask the case (decision 4; ADR-136 decision 3):
1. **The case's handling** is the one its material shares *as the analyst sees it*: the handlings of
   the visible working set (`WorkingSetService.visible_membership`, the projection every read
   applies), passed through `questions.shared_handling` — one handling code, or none. A case of
   mixed codes, or one the analyst sees nothing of, has none and stays local. A node the analyst may
   not see plays no part, so where the question goes reveals nothing about it (rule 3).
2. **The datasets** are every dataset of the case (`DatasetStore.ids_of_case`), as Ask the case sends
   them — never only those of the visible nodes, since the question may be about anything in the case.
3. A hosted engine is asked only when the code is sendable **and** every dataset allows that engine;
   otherwise the local engine answers and the proposal says `engine: "local"`, which the Glass shows
   ("Answered by …"). The engine picker already used the case's route
   (`/v1/investigations/{id}/models/engines`), so an engine the case's data may not reach is shown
   unavailable with the reason.
4. What is sent is unchanged: the case's vocabulary and the analyst's question, never an id (rule 7).

**Tests** (rule 12): `tests/services/api/test_ask_to_search_egress.py`, against the stand-in gateway
(rule 15): sent to the engine chosen when both gates allow (the positive control, red before: only the
local model was ever asked); **never sent** with a dataset set to `none`; not sent when a kept-in
dataset is one the visible nodes do not come from (shown red with that mistake planted — the visible
nodes' datasets in place of the case's); mixed codes and an empty view stay local; a hidden node
changes nothing.

### ADR-127, Amendment 41 (1 November 2026) — monitoring in the storyline: use cases P1 to P4 (build-order step 8a)

Status: recorded during the owner's autonomous-build instruction of 1 November 2026, on the owner's
choice of the same day (`process/ALERTING_MONITORING_PLAN.md`): all of P1 to P4, "built into the
story line", part of the prison demo's narrative and not an appendix. It rests on ADR-133 stages (a)
to (d) and ADR-134, as built (their Amendments 1 to 5 and 1). Each point the spec left open is read
conservatively and listed at the end for the owner's review (`BUILD_ORDER_2026-11.md`, open
questions).

**Where the cases sit.** Chapters 9, 10 and 11 of Act 2 carry them, in the order the investigation
meets them; chapters 1 to 8 and Act 1 are unchanged, and so is every figure they quote (no new link
touches the principal).

| Chapter | What happens | Case |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 9. Watch: a hotlist, a rule and three alerts | The analyst hotlists the coordinator's number; the second seized-phone batch loads and raises **H1** (as before). The week's visit bookings load and the same hotlist raises **H2**, five days before the visit it names. The analyst writes a rule as a sentence; the data engineer attaches it to the new PIN pipeline's *Checks on load*; the week's PIN first contacts load and the rule raises **S1** | P2, P1 |
| 10. Assess and report | H2 closed by its owner with a reason; S1's close proposed and approved by a second person; a weekly alert trend beside the throw-over trend; the monitoring figures | P4, P3 |
| 11. Pack and gaps | H1, still open, is an `alert` item in the pack beside the two trends; the gaps now include what S1 and H2 found about the third group member | P3 |

**The data** (`packages/demo_fixtures/pid_monitoring.py`; rule 9: synthetic, in the repository only).
Two files, derived from `pid_plan.build_plan("demo")` and drawn from `random.Random` seeded by the
plan's seed, the same on every run, written by `pid_files.write_files` under `incoming/` beside batch
2, so the listing does not show them until chapter 9. They cover the week after the plan's cut-off,
Monday 4 to Sunday 10 May 2026. Each is loaded by a recipe of its own, published by the seed:

- **R18, `pid-visit-bookings`** (`pid_visit_bookings_recipe.yaml`, `generic-csv`) reads
  `pid_visit_bookings.csv`: eight bookings. A booking is a record, not a visit: a `Document` found or
  made on its booking reference (`message_id`), titled with the visit's day and time, dated when it
  was booked (`sent_at`), with the visitor (by National Insurance number), the prisoner (by prison
  number) and the contact number (through `msisdn`) each `MENTIONED_IN` it. No `VISITED` is written,
  since the visit has not happened. The storyline's row, `VB-2605-001`: Marcus Ellery books a social
  visit to Darren Ashcombe (`Z2558ZZ`, the third group member, named in no report) for Saturday 9 May
  2026 at 14:00, on Monday 4 May at 10:17, giving 07700 900640. The other seven are background
  visitors booking a Fenwick Moor prisoner they have visited before, each giving the number they own.
- **R19, `pid-pin-new-contacts`** (`pid_pin_new_contacts_recipe.yaml`, `pin-calls-csv`) reads
  `pid_pin_new_contacts.csv`: fourteen calls, the PIN supplier's weekly first-contact extract (calls
  to numbers the account had not called before), in the call log's own columns. Each call is a
  `COMMUNICATED_WITH` from the PIN account, found by reference, to the number. It writes no `USES`:
  R5 tied every account to its prisoner, and writing it again would merge into R5's link. The
  storyline's rows: Darren Ashcombe's account `PIN-Z2558ZZ` calls 07700 900718 on 5 May at 18:42
  (312 s) and 7 May at 19:05 (95 s): the number nobody owns, which Jamie Pryce's seized handset called
  30 times (batch 1). The other twelve are ten background Fenwick Moor prisoners' first contacts with
  numbers no seized SIM ever called.
- **Every link either load writes is new** (a booking is a new `Document`; each first contact is a
  pair the plan holds no call for), so the rehearsal reset can revert both loads, which decision 6
  requires.

**The rule (P1).** Written by the analyst in the sentence builder (ADR-133 decision 1), named "Calls
to a number on a seized handset" (`pid_monitoring.P1_SENTENCE`): *"When an Endpoint whose endpoint kind
is msisdn, is within 2 step(s) of a Device, raise a high-severity alert for the case team, after each
load commits."* A number is within two steps of a handset in this case only through a seized SIM
that called it (`PAIRED_WITH`, then `COMMUNICATED_WITH`); the batches test that no other path does.
A sentence has one subject, so the alert names the number, not the caller: opening it and expanding
the number shows the new link from Darren Ashcombe's PIN account.

**The four cases, exactly.** Every alert is raised in the case "Prison Intelligence Dataset
(synthetic demo)", dataset `prison-intelligence`.

- **P2, the bookings (chapter 9).**
  - *Data:* R18 over `pid_visit_bookings.csv`, after batch 2.
  - *Raises exactly one alert,* **H2**: a hotlist alert (`hotlist:<the chapter-9 hotlist>`), high
    severity, the owner's alone ("only me", the default), naming the `Endpoint` +447700900640. The
    booking's load touches the number by reference (decision 7(a)), so the alert is raised as the
    file loads, before the visit of 9 May.
  - *Stops firing:* `test_the_bookings_raise_one_hotlist_alert_before_the_visit`.
  - *Fires when it should not:* `test_a_hotlist_added_after_the_bookings_load_raises_nothing`;
    `test_a_hotlist_made_in_another_dataset_raises_nothing`;
    `test_another_analyst_does_not_see_the_owners_hotlist_alerts` (rules 4 and 7: another analyst of
    the case, and a reader without the dataset, find no H1 or H2 in their queue).
- **P1, the new contacts (chapter 9).**
  - *Data:* R19 over `pid_pin_new_contacts.csv`, after the rule is deployed and attached.
  - *Raises exactly one alert,* **S1**: a sentence alert (`typology:<rule>`, typology `sentence`),
    high severity, for the case team, naming the `Endpoint` +447700900718, its words beginning
    "+447700900718 (Endpoint): within 2 step(s) of Device …" (the handset seized from Pryce, named
    as below) and then the rule's sentence, with an `Alert` node (inferred) and its `ALERTED_ON`
    link recorded in the load's record (decision 6). The load writes 11 new links for its 14 calls.
  - *Stops firing:* `test_the_new_contacts_raise_one_alert_on_the_number_from_pryces_handset`.
  - *Fires when it should not:* `test_a_rule_deployed_after_the_new_contacts_load_raises_nothing_for_it`;
    `test_a_rule_author_without_the_dataset_raises_nothing` (the rule is judged as its author,
    rule 3); `test_a_second_run_of_the_new_contacts_raises_nothing`;
    `test_a_reader_without_the_dataset_sees_no_chapter_nine_alert`.
- **The order (P1 and P2 together):** `test_chapter_nine_raises_exactly_these_alerts_in_this_order`
  loads batch 2, the bookings and the new contacts through the committed recipes and asserts the
  alerts are exactly H1, H2, S1, in that order (`pid_monitoring.EXPECTED_ALERTS`). The rule is
  deployed *after* the bookings load: deployed before it, it would also flag the coordinator's
  number (on the batch-2 handset since chapter 9) as the bookings touch it. That is the rule
  working, not a fault, so the script fixes the order rather than the rule narrowing.
- **P3, the trend and the pack item (chapters 10 and 11).**
  - *The trend:* Reports → Trends, source *Alerts*, by week, split by rule, over the case (ADR-134
    decision 3). Counted as the analyst, the week of the demo holds **hotlists 2 and the rule 1**.
    It goes into chapter 11's pack beside the throw-over trend.
  - *The pack item:* **H1**, chapter 9's alert, as an `alert` item (ADR-134 decision 1): status
    *open*, match *inferred* (no person has confirmed it; rule 5), the number it matched, resting
    on that number's handling.
  - *Stops firing:* `test_the_weekly_alert_trend_counts_chapter_nines_alerts_by_rule`;
    `test_chapter_nines_alert_goes_into_the_pack_open_and_inferred`.
  - *Fires when it should not:* `test_the_alert_trend_counts_nothing_for_a_reader_without_the_dataset`;
    `test_a_colleague_counts_only_the_case_alert_in_the_trend` (the hotlist is "only me");
    `test_the_alert_item_is_withheld_from_a_reader_who_may_not_see_the_number` (a yes or no).
- **P4, the monitoring figures (chapter 10).**
  - *The closes:* **H2** closed by its owner, *Referred* ("to the visits team: the visit goes
    ahead under closed conditions"), alone, since only its owner can see it (Amendment 4 item 5).
    **S1**'s close proposed by the analyst, *Referred* ("to the regional intelligence unit for a
    subscriber check on 07700 900718"), and approved by a second analyst of the case (stage (d)).
    **H1** stays open.
  - *The figures* (`reports.alert_report`'s monitoring section and the feed's four sections, one
    computation; ADR-134 decision 2), counted as the analyst for the demo's week: raised by rule
    **hotlists 2, typology `sentence` 1**; closed by outcome **referred 2**; time to close **under
    a day 2**; hotlist matches **2**; the open queue **H1 alone**.
  - *Stops firing:* `test_the_monitoring_figures_count_raised_closed_and_the_open_queue`.
  - *Fires when it should not:* `test_the_proposer_cannot_approve_their_own_close`;
    `test_the_board_never_counts_the_owners_only_me_hotlist` (a case viewer's figures hold S1 alone);
    `test_a_reader_without_the_dataset_counts_nothing_on_the_board`.

All of these are in `tests/scenarios/test_pid_monitoring_storyline.py`: the PID files the cases rest
on are loaded through the committed recipes (`load_with_rules`, the engine's own), the hotlist is
evaluated by `evaluation.evaluate_hotlists_for_entry` over the run's touched nodes as the run route
does, the rule by `RuleGate.post_commit` as `run_published_recipe` does, against real Postgres for
the alert, hotlist, pack-free queue and close paths and real DuckDB for the alert facts. The graph is
the golden tests' `MergingGraph` behind the real `DatasetStampingGraph`, answering every read through
the scheme's own predicate and the reader's datasets, so a node the reader may not see is absent
from the answer, as the adapter's access step makes it (rule 15). The batches' own properties are in
`tests/scenarios/test_pid_monitoring_batches.py`, and R18 and R19 have golden tests of their own
(`tests/ingest/test_pid_monitoring_recipes.py`). The order case is run again against a throwaway
ArcadeDB, with the adapter's own access step (`tests/ingest/test_pid_monitoring_storyline_live.py`,
CI's live job).

**The reset and rehearsals.** `--release-batch-2` now lists all three chapter-9 files (batch 2, then
the bookings, then the new contacts) at once; the presenter loads them in that order. `--reset-live`
reverts every unreverted R18 and R19 load in the case besides what it reverted before, and removes
the two files from the listed folder. Reverting the new-contacts load reverts S1's `Alert` node and
link and closes S1 (decision 6's step 6); H1, H2 and their closes stay, as alerts always have. Two
things the reset says it cannot undo, added to its list: **a rule deployed in a rehearsal, and what
it has raised** (a rule raises a finding once, so the next rehearsal's rule must be written afresh
and the old one retired), and the hotlist alerts' closes.

**Found while building, for the owner:**
- **S1 must not be closed as *True match* in a rehearsal.** A true match confirms the alert's own
  `Alert` node, which supersedes it (`confirm_node`), and the reset then refuses to revert the
  new-contacts load (decision 6 refuses a load whose node an analyst's correction superseded). So
  the script closes it as *Referred*. A true match is still right in real work, where no reset runs.
- **The Glass shows no monitoring figure.** The Reports view's figures count typology alerts only;
  the monitoring sections are in the feed, which Superset's board reads (administration guide
  §12). And a board never counts an "only me" hotlist. So on screen, P4's board holds S1 alone
  unless the hotlist is shared with a team the board's account belongs to. P4 is built and tested
  as figures here; how it is shown is step 9's to settle (open question).
- **No demo account can be the second person.** Only the analyst role triages alerts, and the demo
  has one analyst account. Approving S1's close on screen needs a second analyst account (a demo
  persona, a realm change); not built here (open question).
- **A seized handset has no name in an alert.** A `Device` declares no name property, so the alert's
  words and the queue name the handset "Device" and the last six characters of its id
  (`alert_queue.node_name`), not its IMEI. Whether `imei` should name a device is for the owner
  (open question); the test reads the name as the code gives it.
- **Administration guide §12's `closed` row** still lists `true_positive`, `false_positive` or
  `closed`; since Amendment 5 of ADR-133 a label is any of the five reasons as stored. Left for the
  guides' next version (open question).

**Read conservatively where the spec is silent:**
1. *"For Wing F"* (P3): an alert trend splits and filters by rule, typology, severity and outcome
   only (ADR-134 decision 3), never by place. The case is the Wing F investigation and every
   alert of chapter 9 is about Wing F's network (the coordinator's number, a Wing F prisoner's
   booking and calls), so the trend is the case's alerts. A place filter would be a decision of its
   own.
2. *"Before the visit"* (P2): the alert is raised when the bookings load, and the booked visit
   (9 May) is after every booking in the file. The demo's clock is the presenter's, so "before" is
   in the data's own time; the test asserts the alert exists and no `VISITED` for the booking does.
3. *A booking is a record* (`Document`), not a `VISITED` link and not an `Event` (which declares no
   identifying property), so the load writes only new links and can be reverted.
4. *The first-contact extract* (P1) is how a weekly call log reaches the case: a log that repeated a
   known pair would merge into the seed's link and could not be reverted (decision 6).
5. *A trend's weeks are the demo's own.* Alerts carry the time they were raised, no run time is
   faked, and the owner ruled out a backfill, so the trend shows the demo's week (and any earlier
   rehearsal's weeks).
6. *The hotlist stays "only me"* (the default), so H2 is closed by its owner alone and only S1 needs
   the second person.

**Tests that would fail (rule 12):** each named above; plus `test_every_link_the_batches_write_is_new`,
`test_only_the_story_number_is_within_two_steps_of_a_handset`, `test_the_batches_are_the_same_every_time`
and `test_the_bookings_touch_no_number_the_rule_would_flag` (`test_pid_monitoring_batches.py`); the
reset choosing every R18 and R19 load and the release listing all three files (`test_seed_pid.py`).
Each was shown red, in the code's own shape: a violation planted in the generator's rows, a recipe,
the evaluation, the rule gate, the queue's SQL, the trend's SQL, the pack's reader, the figures or
the seed's reset, and the named test failing for it. One plant stayed green and is recorded so: the
queue's dataset clause removed alone, since the graph's own dataset step still hides the alert (two
layers, rule 3); removing both turns `test_a_reader_without_the_dataset_sees_no_chapter_nine_alert`
red.

### ADR-133, Amendment 6 (1 November 2026) — the UK Sanctions List (FCDO) connector; OFSI marked as reading a closed list

Status: built on 1 November 2026 from the owner's answer to open question 10 ("Build a UK Sanctions
List (FCDO) connector in step 8"), within build-order step 8b. Open to the owner's review; the points
read conservatively are listed at the end.

**Why.** Amendment 3 found that HM Treasury's OFSI Consolidated List closed on 28 January 2026 and that
the FCDO's UK Sanctions List is now "the only source for all UK sanctions designations" (gov.uk). The
OFSI connector reads a list nobody updates. Decision 4 names OFSI's list because it was written before
the closure; the successor list is the same publisher's (HM Government's), under the same licence, and
this amendment adds it as a sixth connector. It does not reopen decision 4.

**Built.**
1. **A sixth connector, `uk_sanctions_list`** (`packages/knowledge_adapters/screening_lists.py`), a
   Knowledge Adapter with a synthetic golden file (rule 8), reading the FCDO's XML file
   (`UK-Sanctions-List.xml`). The XML is chosen over the CSV because the FCDO publishes the XML's
   schema (`SanctionsListSchema-4.33.3.xsd`, linked from the list's page), so its element names are
   confirmed; the CSV's column order is not documented anywhere found (the format guide lists the field
   headings and says all seven formats hold the same data).
   - **Read from the publisher's own documents:** the schema for the elements (root `Designations` with
     `DateGenerated`; each `Designation` with `UniqueID`, `OFSIGroupID`, `Names`/`Name` holding
     `Name1` to `Name6` and `NameType`, `IndividualEntityShip`, `RegimeName`, `Addresses`/`Address`/
     `AddressCountry`, `IndividualDetails`/`Individual` with `DOBs`/`DOB` and
     `Nationalities`/`Nationality`; no target namespace); the *Format guide for the UK Sanctions List*
     for their meaning (`Name 6` a surname or an entity's or ship's whole name; Primary Name, Primary
     Name Variation or Alias; a date of birth dd/mm/yyyy, possibly partial; "Individual, Entity, Ship").
   - **As the other connectors:** each designation is one entry, keyed by its `UniqueID`, every entry a
     sanction; a ship is counted in `skipped`, never dropped silently (rule 2); a date of birth only
     when the designation gives exactly one exact date; anything that is not the format (another
     list's XML, the closed OFSI CSV, XML with entity expansion) is refused in words and nothing is
     kept.
   - **Marked unverified in the code** (the schema types every value as a plain string): the spelling
     of the `IndividualEntityShip` values (read as Individual, Entity or Ship in any case; anything
     else refused); the text of `DateGenerated` (taken as the version as written); one `UniqueID` on two
     designations (read as one entry, the second's names its aliases, since the guide says a person
     designated under several regimes may carry several Unique IDs but not the reverse); and a
     designation with no `UniqueID` (allowed by the schema; read as `OFSI-<group id>`, since the change
     notice says older records keep their OFSI Group ID, and refused when it has neither).
2. **The licence** (spec 00 §7): Open Government Licence v3.0, from the list's publication page
   (gov.uk/government/publications/the-uk-sanctions-list, last updated 30 October 2026, read 1 November
   2026). The Lists tab says it ("Open Government Licence v3.0 (Crown copyright; the FCDO's UK Sanctions
   List, gov.uk)"); the connector's licence is confirmed, so a real file is admitted by a device's
   exceptions entry like OFAC's or the EU's (rule 9 unchanged).
3. **The OFSI connector reads a closed list, in words.** Its code is kept (Amendment 3). The Conduit's
   `CLOSED_LISTS` and the Glass's, held in step by a drift test, say: "this connector reads a closed
   list: the OFSI Consolidated List closed on 28 January 2026 and is no longer updated, and the FCDO's
   UK Sanctions List is now the only source of UK designations". The Lists tab shows it on an OFSI
   list's row (`ScreeningListStatus.closed_note`), and the subscribe form names the connector "…: reads
   a closed list" and points to the UK Sanctions List.
4. **Synthetic lists for the demo** (`packages/demo_fixtures/screening_lists/`,
   `synthetic_uk_sanctions_list_v1.xml` and `_v2.xml`, their SHA-256 in `synthetic.sha256`): version 1
   holds four invented people and organisations and one ship, none of them an Operation Ledger
   customer; version 2 adds one designation (Sofia RUIZ, born 14 June 2001), changes one (a spelling
   variation) and removes one. Operation Ledger's A3 uses them (ADR-108 Amendment 5).

**Tests that would fail (rule 12), each shown red in the code's own shape:**
`test_uk_sanctions_list_reads_its_golden_file` (planted: a ship screened as an organisation; one
UniqueID read as two entries; a partial date of birth kept);
`test_uk_sanctions_list_refuses_a_designation_it_cannot_name_or_place` (planted: an unknown
`IndividualEntityShip` read as an organisation instead of refused — first planted so that it failed by
a `KeyError` rather than the missing refusal, which proved nothing, and planted again; rule 15);
`test_uk_sanctions_list_refuses_the_other_lists_files`, `…_with_no_date_generated`,
`…_refuses_entity_expansion`; `test_every_synthetic_list_file_is_in_the_manifest_by_its_digest` (now
over the XML files too; planted: version 2's digest left out);
`test_the_closed_ofsi_list_says_so_and_its_successor_does_not` (planted: the route not sending the
words); `test_the_glass_says_the_same_closed_list_words_as_the_conduit`; and the Lists tab's vitest case
(planted: the row and the form not saying it).

**Read conservatively, for the owner:**
- **The XML, not the CSV.** A customer whose bank publishes the CSV only would need a second connector
  once the CSV's columns are documented.
- **The schema's own notice.** The XSD file carries a notice that is not the OGL: use "for the purpose
  of developing, testing, or implementing compatible systems", not "for commercial resale or as part of
  a paid service without prior consent". OspreyFlow does not ship the schema; the connector was written
  from its element names. Whether a paid deployment's use is "part of a paid service" is for the owner
  to confirm with the FCDO (spec 00 §7).
- **No HTTP fetch**, as for every list (Amendment 3 item 3): the file is placed in the ingest folder.
  The FCDO's static URL (`sanctionslist.fcdo.gov.uk/docs/UK-Sanctions-List.xml`) is named in the
  administration guide, not fetched.

### ADR-108, Amendment 5 (1 November 2026) — Operation Ledger's monitoring week: use cases A1 to A4 (build-order step 8b)

Status: recorded during the owner's autonomous-build instruction of 1 November 2026, on the owner's
choice of the same day (`process/ALERTING_MONITORING_PLAN.md`): all of A1 to A4, woven into Operation
Ledger's walkthrough. It rests on ADR-133 stages (a) to (d) and ADR-134, as built (their Amendments 1 to
6 and 1), as ADR-127 Amendment 41 did for the prison demo. Operation Ledger is this ADR's synthetic case
(Amendment 4); its money-laundering rules are ADR-109's. Each point the spec left open is read
conservatively and listed at the end for the owner's review.

**Where the cases sit.** A new act at the end of the Ledger walkthrough (`DEMO_GUIDE.md` §8b, "the
monitoring week"), after the structuring ring, the onboarding gate and the ownership trace, which are
unchanged, as is every figure they quote: nothing of the week touches September's flows.

| Step | What happens | Case |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. After the SAR | The analyst hotlists Jamal Carter's Lloyds account ("only me"), and deploys two rules from the typology templates, each after each load commits: "Money straight through an account" (rapid movement, the template's 48 hours and 80%) and "Money back where it started within a week" (circular flow, 4 movements, tuned from 30 days to 7) | A1, A2 |
| 2. The next weekly export | The data engineer loads `ledger_transactions_week2.csv` through a Studio pipeline mapped as `ledger_transactions_recipe.yaml`; *Checks on load* applies the case's rules (the default). The load raises **R1**, **C1** and **H1** | A1, A2 |
| 3. A list update | The administrator refreshes the UK Sanctions List (synthetic) at version 1 (nothing found); the presenter releases version 2; *Refresh now* re-screens every customer and raises **K1** | A3 |
| 4. Close and report | The analyst closes R1 as *Referred*; it goes into the case's pack as an `alert` item, closed; the monitoring figures count the week | A4 |

**The data** (`packages/demo_fixtures/ledger_monitoring.py`; rule 9: synthetic, in the repository only).
One file, the bank's next weekly export for Monday 5 to Sunday 11 October 2026 (the seed's own export
ends with the week of 28 September), in the seed's own columns, so the committed transactions recipe
loads it unchanged. Its background is drawn from `random.Random` seeded by a fixed digest, the same on
every run. Thirteen rows:
- **A1:** Crescent Imports pays £18,000 into Sofia Ruiz's Monzo account (Monday 10:05); £17,400 leaves
  it for Tomas Zelinsky's Starling account at 16:20; Zelinsky pays £16,900 back to Crescent on Thursday
  at 11:30, more than 48 hours after his account was paid.
- **A2:** on Friday at 11:40, £9,700 is paid in, in cash (`CASH_IN`), from Zelinsky's account into
  Carter's Lloyds account (a cash deposit as the seed writes its own: the depositor's account paying the
  account credited).
- **Background:** nine payments between the three trading counterparties, always buyer to supplier
  (Kesterton Freight to Midland Pallets and Arden Fuel Cards; Midland Pallets to Arden), each onward
  payment under £450 against at least £1,200 paid in, and no three of one pair summing past £10,000.
  None touches Hale Logistics, whose September trading would close a circle with any new payment to or
  from it.
- **A3:** the synthetic UK Sanctions List, version 1 and version 2 (ADR-133 Amendment 6). Version 2 adds
  Sofia RUIZ, born 14 June 2001, who is the case's customer (the KYC export's Ruiz, same date of birth).

**The seed, the release and the reset** (`scripts/seed_ledger_fixture.py`). The seed writes the week's
file under `<ingest root>/uploaded/ledger/incoming/` (which the Studio's listing does not show), the
list's version 1 at `uploaded/ledger/lists/uk_sanctions_list.xml` and version 2 under `incoming/`, and
subscribes "UK Sanctions List (synthetic)" to that file through the `uk_sanctions_list` connector (it
does not refresh it: a refresh re-screens, which is the administrator's step on screen). Three mid-demo
commands, file copies only, so the Conduit stays up, run as `python -m scripts.seed_internal ledger
<flag>`: `--release-week-2` (the week's file into the dataset's listed folder), `--release-list-update`
(version 2 over the subscribed file) and `--reset-week-2` (the released file removed and version 1 put
back). The reset says what it cannot undo: the week's load (reverted with `python -m
scripts.revert_load <load id>`, the Conduit stopped), the rules, the hotlist, the alerts and their
closes, and the list's applied versions (a refresh after the reset applies version 1 again, which
delists Ruiz and raises nothing).

**The four cases, exactly.** Every alert is raised in the case "Operation Ledger (synthetic demo)",
dataset `ledger`, as the analyst may see it.

- **A1, rapid movement and a circle (step 2).**
  - *Raises exactly two alerts,* both typology alerts (medium severity, the case's team, an `Alert` node
    written `inferred`): **R1**, `rapid_movement`, naming Ruiz's Monzo account and citing the two
    transfers through it ("18,000 arrived … and 17,400 left within 6.2 hour(s) — the account is a
    pass-through"); then **C1**, `circular_flow`, naming Crescent Imports' account and citing the three
    transfers of the circle ("value left … and returned to it over 3 movements").
  - *Stops firing:* `test_the_week_raises_one_pass_through_and_one_circle`.
  - *Fires when it should not:* `test_a_rule_deployed_after_the_week_two_load_raises_nothing_for_it`;
    `test_a_second_run_of_the_week_two_file_raises_nothing`; `test_the_background_raises_nothing`
    (the background alone, with both rules and the structuring template live);
    `test_the_structuring_template_raises_nothing_for_the_week` (one cash deposit is no ring);
    `test_a_rule_author_without_the_dataset_raises_nothing` (rule 3);
    `test_a_reader_without_the_dataset_sees_no_week_two_alert` (rules 4 and 7).
- **A2, the hotlisted account (step 2).**
  - *Raises exactly one alert,* **H1**: a hotlist alert (`hotlist:<id>`), high severity, the owner's
    alone ("only me"), naming Carter's account, as the load touches it by reference.
  - **A product gap found and closed here.** A hotlist matched a node's `value_normalised` alone, and an
    `Account` (FIBO) carries none: a hotlist on an account number could never fire, in the evaluation
    or in a sentence's "on a hotlist". Read as ADR-038's "one exact identifier", which the FIBO pack
    already declares an account has (`identifiers: [iban, card]`): a hotlist identifier in the IBAN's
    shape (two letters, two digits, eleven to thirty letters and digits, spaces allowed) is stored in the
    `account_ref` adapter's form (spaces removed, upper case; its checksum not asked for, since an account
    is matched on what the bank's file says and the Ledger's own numbers are invented), and a node is
    watched by its `account_number` in that form beside its `value_normalised`
    (`evaluation.watched_values`, used by the evaluation and by the sentence's `_identifiers`). Nothing
    about who is told changes: the match is disclosed by `record_match` as before.
  - *Stops firing:* `test_the_cash_deposit_raises_one_hotlist_alert_on_carters_account`; with the
    adapter's form, `test_an_account_number_is_stored_compact_and_upper_case` and
    `test_a_node_is_watched_by_its_account_number_as_well_as_its_value`.
  - *Fires when it should not:* `test_a_hotlist_added_after_the_week_two_load_raises_nothing`;
    `test_a_hotlist_made_in_another_dataset_raises_nothing`;
    `test_a_hotlist_on_an_account_the_week_does_not_touch_raises_nothing` (Hale Logistics');
    `test_another_analyst_does_not_see_the_owners_hotlist_alert` (rules 4 and 7).
- **The order (A1 and A2 together):** `test_the_week_raises_exactly_these_alerts_in_this_order` loads
  the week through the committed recipe as the run route runs it (the rules after commit, then the
  hotlists over the load's touched nodes) and asserts R1, C1, H1, in that order
  (`ledger_monitoring.EXPECTED_ALERTS`), and nothing else in the store.
- **A3, the list update (step 3).**
  - *Raises exactly one alert,* **K1**: a `kyc_screening` alert, high severity, the case's team,
    naming Sofia Ruiz, with the listed party and a scored `SAME_AS` written `inferred` (rule 5), raised
    by version 2's refresh re-screening every customer of each case with an active screening rule,
    against the one added and one changed entry only. The refresh says "1 added, 1 changed, 1 removed …
    1 alert raised".
  - *Stops firing:* `test_the_list_update_raises_one_screening_alert_on_ruiz`.
  - *Fires when it should not:* `test_the_first_version_raises_nothing`;
    `test_the_same_version_again_rescreens_no_one`; `test_a_case_without_a_screening_rule_raises_nothing`;
    `test_a_screening_rule_whose_deployer_lacks_the_dataset_raises_nothing` (rule 3);
    `test_a_reader_without_the_dataset_sees_no_screening_alert` (rules 4 and 7).
- **A4, closed and reported (step 4).**
  - *The close:* R1 closed by the analyst as **Referred** ("To the MLRO: a further SAR on the Monzo
    account, citing the circle through Crescent."), alone: a medium-severity alert needs no second person
    (ADR-133 Amendment 4 item 5 is about high severity).
  - *The pack item:* R1 as an `alert` item (ADR-134 decision 1): status *closed*, outcome *referred*,
    match *inferred* (only True match confirms; ADR-133 Amendment 5 item 3), resting on the handlings of
    the accounts and links it cites.
  - *The figures* (`reports.alert_report`'s monitoring section, the feed's four sections), counted as the
    analyst for the week of the demo: raised by rule **hotlists 1; typology `rapid_movement` 1,
    `circular_flow` 1, `kyc_screening` 1**; closed by outcome **referred 1**; time to close **under a
    day 1**; hotlist matches **1**; the open queue **C1, H1, K1**.
  - *Stops firing:* `test_the_referred_alert_goes_into_the_pack_closed_and_inferred`;
    `test_the_monitoring_figures_count_the_week`.
  - *Fires when it should not:* `test_a_reason_outside_the_five_is_refused`;
    `test_the_alert_item_is_withheld_from_a_reader_without_the_dataset` (a yes or no);
    `test_the_board_never_counts_the_owners_only_me_hotlist` (a colleague's figures hold the three case
    alerts and no hotlist); `test_a_reader_without_the_dataset_counts_nothing_on_the_board`.

All of these are in `tests/scenarios/test_ledger_monitoring_storyline.py`: the Ledger's September is
built by the seed's own `build_ledger_graph` (its recipes through the engine, behind the real
`DatasetStampingGraph`), its events in a real DuckDB; the week is loaded by `load_with_rules` through the
committed recipe; the rules run by `RuleGate.post_commit` and the hotlists by
`evaluation.evaluate_hotlists_for_entry`, as `run_published_recipe` runs them; the list is refreshed by
`screening_refresh.refresh` with the real `Rescreener`; the alert, hotlist, screening and close paths run
against real Postgres. The graph is ADR-127 Amendment 41's `AccessGraph` (every read through the scheme's
own predicate and the reader's datasets), with `list_nodes` paged as the adapter pages it. The batch's
own properties are in `tests/scenarios/test_ledger_monitoring_batches.py`; the seed's files, release and
reset in `tests/test_seed_ledger_monitoring.py`.

**Read conservatively where the spec is silent:**
1. *A cash deposit "into" an account* is written as the seed writes its own: `CASH_IN` from the
   depositor's account to the account credited, since the fixture has no account for cash itself.
2. *The circle's window is tuned to 7 days.* With the template's 30 days, the circle also finds the
   ring's September deposits going round through Brightpath and Crescent, and Hale Logistics' ordinary
   trading going round its suppliers: the rule working, but several alerts for one week's story
   (`test_the_story_makes_one_pass_through_and_one_circle` shows it). The walkthrough says why, and
   deploys at 7. A typology template has no preview: ADR-133 decision 3's preview is built for a
   rule written as a sentence only (Amendment 2 item 6), so the tuning cannot be shown against
   evidence on screen — for the owner.
3. *Checks on load, not a schedule.* A1 runs as the week loads (after commit), which is when a weekly
   export is judged; a schedule (stage (d)) would judge the same rows a day later and adds nothing.
4. *The week is loaded through a pipeline the engineer builds in the Studio*, mapped as the committed
   recipe, as the onboarding chapter is: the Ledger's seed writes from code and publishes no Studio
   recipe, so there is nothing for its reset to revert by recipe, and the reset names the revert command.
5. *The list is subscribed by the seed and refreshed by the administrator*, so the first refresh, and
   the re-screening it starts, are on screen and as the person, never the seed's.
6. *A hotlist on an account number* (A2 above) is a product change, built here because without it A2
   cannot be shown; it is the smallest reading of ADR-038 that makes the case fire.

**Tests that would fail (rule 12):** each named above; plus `test_the_week_is_the_same_every_time`,
`test_only_the_story_rows_touch_the_storys_accounts`, `test_the_background_never_comes_back_round`
and `test_the_list_versions_differ_by_one_designation_matching_one_customer`
(`test_ledger_monitoring_batches.py`); the seed placing the files, each release and the reset
(`test_seed_ledger_monitoring.py`); and `seed_internal` running the three steps for `ledger` alone,
leaving the Conduit up. Each was shown red in the code's own shape; the evidence is in the step's report.

## ADR-138 — Starter packs: a theme and a domain chosen at install, several deployments side by side, and a public dataset of the administrator's choosing — ACCEPTED (design)

Status: accepted from the owner's request of 2 November 2026 ("in the installation guides … clear
options for installing starter packs … multiple deployments covering themes like vanilla, i.e. the
base OspreyFlow branded installs, and any available design system based ones like gov.uk, along with
the domain models like AML, crime etc."; and, answering the scope questions: an install option and the
guides; crime, AML, fraud and cyber; "provide an ability to the user to specify a public dataset like
Vast to be included in the install pack"; a blank starter as well). Built in build-order step 9c.

**Context.** Every piece exists but is scattered: `appearance.brand` (`ospreyflow`, `govuk`), the
domain packs every deployment composes (FIBO, NIEM, STIX; a case's `domains`, ADR-126), the demo
packs (section 11 of the administration guide), and `deployment.name` with `network.public_origin`
(ADR-132 Amendment 1), which let a second deployment share nothing with the first. But `osprey.yaml`
sits in the checkout, so a second deployment today needs its own checkout (the owner's GOV.UK demo runs
from a git worktree, switched by a script outside the product). An administrator has no single choice
that says "a GOV.UK service for crime analysis" or "the OspreyFlow look for AML".

**Decision.**
1. **A starter is a theme and a domain**, named `<theme>-<domain>`, chosen with
   `ospreyflow install --starter <name>` and on the guided install page's first screen. It only
   pre-fills answers the install already asks; every one can still be changed, and the rendered
   `osprey.yaml` records the starter as a comment, not a setting (nothing at run time depends on it).
   - **Themes:** `ospreyflow` (the base brand, "vanilla") and `govuk` (the GOV.UK Design System; for a
     service on a gov.uk domain only, as appendix A already says: the install asks for the service
     name, organisation and phase). A theme is an `appearance.brand` value, so a later design system
     is a new brand value plus its tokens, and becomes a starter theme without changing this ADR.
   - **Domains:**
     | Domain | Case domains | Demo data it loads | Notes |
     | --- | --- | --- | --- |
     | `crime` | `niem` | `prison-intelligence` (and `hmp`) | Intelligence analysis, prison intelligence |
     | `aml` | `fibo` | `operation-ledger`; the synthetic screening lists | Typology and AML templates deployed in its case |
     | `fraud` | `fibo` | `fixture-corp` at install; `paysim` offered as the administrator's download | PaySim is never fetched by the install |
     | `cyber` | `stix` | a new synthetic STIX 2.1 pack, `cyber-intrusion` (to build) | Until it exists, the cyber starter loads no demo case and says so |
     | `blank` | none chosen | none, and no demo accounts | A real service starting from nothing; every domain pack remains available |
   - Every starter keeps every domain pack in the ontology (ADR-126 is unchanged): the domain sets the
     demo case's `domains`, the demo data and the starter's templates, never what the ontology offers.
2. **Several deployments side by side, supported.** `ospreyflow install --name <name>` gives a deployment
   its own folder (`~/.ospreyflow/deployments/<name>/`, holding its `osprey.yaml`, rendered files and
   `deployment.env`, mode 600), its own Compose project and volumes, and its own address
   (`--address`, default `http://<name>.localhost:<next free port>`). The checkout is shared; no
   worktree is needed. `ospreyflow deployments` lists them (name, starter, address, running or
   stopped), and every verb takes `--name` (default: the only deployment, or the one last used).
   `ospreyflow switch <name>` stops the running Lite deployment and starts the named one, since a Lite
   machine runs one at a time by default. An existing checkout-rooted deployment keeps working
   unchanged and is listed as `default`.
3. **A public dataset of the administrator's choosing** may be added to a starter at install or later:
   `ospreyflow demo add public --file <path> --manifest <dataset.yaml>`. The manifest names the
   dataset, its source page, its licence text, its checksum and the Ingest Studio recipe (or one of
   the shipped recipes) that loads it.
   - **The VAST Challenge datasets are the first catalogue entries.** These are the IEEE VAST Challenge
     scenarios: fictional, published for visual-analytics research. Each is shipped as a manifest
     and a recipe only. The data itself is downloaded by the administrator and never carried by
     OspreyFlow, as with PaySim. Which challenges are catalogued, and their licence terms, are
     confirmed in step 9c and recorded in spec 00's licence register.
   - **Rule 9 holds.** A dataset that is fictional or synthetic loads like PaySim. A dataset holding
     real people's data is accepted only through the Enron path: the administrator types `yes`,
     acknowledging the real data and their organisation's own lawful basis. It never enters CI or the
     repository, and the owner's device additionally needs its real-data exceptions entry (ADR-035
     §C3).
4. **The guides.** The administration guide gains a new section, "Choosing a starter", near the front:
   the theme × domain table, one command per starter, the guided-page equivalent, running several
   deployments side by side, and adding a public dataset. Section 11 (demo packs) points to it. The
   user guide says which demo case each starter brings.

**Tests that would fail if this were violated (rule 12):**
- each starter's rendered `osprey.yaml` carries its brand and its demo packs, and nothing else differs
  from the defaults;
- two named deployments share no volume, folder, Compose project or port;
- `--name` on every verb reaches only that deployment (planted: a verb that ignores it);
- `blank` makes no demo case and no demo account;
- a `govuk` starter without a service name is refused in words;
- a public-dataset manifest whose checksum differs is refused before anything loads;
- a manifest declaring real personal data is refused without the acceptance;
- `deployment.env` under `~/.ospreyflow/deployments/` is mode 600.

**Consequences.** The owner's `ospreyflow-switch` script becomes unnecessary once `ospreyflow switch`
exists. The owner's two existing deployments (everyday in the checkout, GOV.UK in a worktree) keep
working, and can be moved under `~/.ospreyflow/deployments/` later, which the guide describes and
which needs the owner's go-ahead. A cyber demo pack is new synthetic data work, and is built with
fixtures before it is offered.

### ADR-138, Amendment 1 (2 November 2026) — what step 9c built, and how it read the decision

Built on branch `starter-packs` (build-order step 9c). Where the ADR was silent, the reading taken is
the conservative one, recorded here for the owner, who may overturn any of it.

**Starters (decision 1).**
1. *A starter is an answer.* `ospreyflow install --starter <theme>-<domain>`, and `starter:` in the
   answers file, which is how the guided page passes it (its Mode screen writes it). The answers file
   gains `appearance` (`brand`, `service_name`, `organisation`, `phase`) and `demo_accounts`; the
   command gains `--service-name`, `--organisation` and `--phase`. A starter pre-fills the brand, the
   demo packs and `demo_accounts`; any of them given outright wins. `ospreyflow starters` (and
   `install --list-starters`) list them. The rendered `osprey.yaml` begins with two comment lines
   naming the starter, its theme and domain and its demo packs; nothing reads them but
   `ospreyflow deployments`.
2. *The GOV.UK theme.* The service name is required: offered at the prompt and on the guided page,
   and refused in words with `--yes` or an answers file that gives none — before anything is
   changed. The organisation is asked and optional (the schema allows none); the phase offered first
   is `beta`, since a service just installed is not live.
3. *The name offered names the service, not a case* (step 9d finding 3): crime "Analyse crime
   intelligence", AML "Investigate money laundering", fraud "Investigate fraud", cyber "Investigate
   cyber incidents"; blank offers none. This settles finding 3 for an install from a starter only:
   the two existing deployments keep the `service_name` their `osprey.yaml` sets until it is
   changed there and applied (`ospreyflow apply`).
4. *The domain sets the demo cases' domains.* Each pack a starter loads is seeded with the
   starter's case domains (`--case-domains`, through `scripts.seed_internal` to every seed's
   `scripts/case_seed.py`), set only while nobody has chosen (ADR-126 decision 2 is unchanged). So
   the crime starter's HMP case is NIEM, not the seed's own FIBO and NIEM, and the fraud starter's
   Fixture Corp case is FIBO, not the POLE core. A pack added later with `ospreyflow demo add` takes
   its seed's own.
5. *The table's notes.* AML: Operation Ledger brings its synthetic screening lists; its typology
   templates are deployed in the case as its walkthrough says, not by the install (the "Screen
   customers against the lists" template is step 9d finding 4). Fraud: PaySim is named at the end of
   the install, with its download page and command, and never fetched. Cyber: on a checkout without
   `cyber-intrusion` the starter loads nothing and says so. Blank: no demo pack, no `--demo-analyst`,
   no sign-in registration of demo accounts, and the install says so.

**Several deployments side by side (decision 2).**
6. *Where it is.* `~/.ospreyflow/deployments/<name>/` (mode 700) holds the deployment's
   `osprey.yaml` and everything `harness.apply` renders from it (`--config <folder>/osprey.yaml
   --out-root ~/.ospreyflow/deployments`), `deployment.env` 600 as everywhere. Its `osprey.yaml`
   starts from the checkout's less `deployment` and `appearance` (which name the checkout's own
   deployment and look), with the answers over it, then `deployment.name: <name>`, its address and
   its graph-store port.
7. *Building from the checkout.* Compose reads `build.context` from the compose file's folder, and
   `../../..` from a home-folder deployment is the home folder. `harness.render.build_context_for`
   names the checkout by its own path for a deployment rendered outside it, and keeps `../../..`
   for one in `deploy/generated/`, whose files are byte for byte as before; `scripts.refresh` reads
   the context a deployment already has.
8. *No port shared.* A new setting, `deployment.graph_port` (Appendix A): the loopback port the
   graph store's door is published at, 2480 when unset (every existing deployment). A named
   deployment is given the first free from 2500, and an address port, the first free from 8090;
   neither is ever 80, 443, 2480, 5432, 8000, 8080 or 8081, one another deployment this command
   knows has, or one something on the computer is listening on. `--address` is checked the same way.
9. *Its Compose project.* `deployment.name` is the project and names the volumes. A name that
   Docker already lists as another folder's project is refused before anything is written: Compose
   would otherwise recreate that project's containers from the new file — worse than a refusal. The
   test stand-in refuses a duplicate project and a bound port, as Docker would leave them broken
   (rule 15). A name already installed is refused (use `apply` or `start`), never reinstalled over.
10. *Which deployment a verb acts on.* `--name` (every verb; it may follow a demo pack's or a key's
    own words); else the one last used, recorded in `~/.ospreyflow/current` by `install --name`,
    `switch` and any verb given `--name`; else the only one; else `default`. `current` is never
    written on a computer with no named deployment, so the owner's two deployments behave exactly as
    before. `--name default` is the checkout's. Scripts that find the deployment themselves
    (`scripts.refresh` for `start --build`, every seed) take `OSPREYFLOW_DEPLOYMENT_DIR`; `backup`,
    `restore` and `repair-sign-in` are given its `--config` and folder; a named deployment's backups
    go to its own `backups/`.
11. *Lite only, and the terminal only.* `--name` with Small or Enterprise is refused (each is a
    deployment of its own); the guided page installs the checkout's deployment and refuses `--name`.
12. *The owner's deployments.* Nothing was moved, started, stopped or touched. The worktree
    deployment (`osprey-govuk`) stays reachable as before, with `OSPREYFLOW_HOME`; `switch --list`
    still finds it. Moving either under `~/.ospreyflow/deployments/` is described in the guide (§1a.1:
    a named install, a restore of a backup into it, a check, then the checkout's removed with
    `--keep-data`) and needs the owner's go-ahead.

**Public datasets (decision 3).**
13. *The manifest* is `schemas.public_dataset.PublicDatasetManifest` (no TypeScript: the Glass does
    not read it): id, name, source page, licence text and address, citation, `redistribution` and
    `commercial_use` (`allowed`, `forbidden`, `not_stated`), `fictional`, `real_personal_data` (a
    dataset cannot be both), the file (name, SHA-256, size, delimiter, encoding), the recipe (beside
    the manifest, or the catalogue's) and the case's `domains`.
14. *The order.* The command asks the checkout (`scripts.public_dataset verify`) to check the
    manifest, the recipe and the file's size and SHA-256; a refusal stops it before anything else
    runs. Then any acceptance (below), then `stage` copies the file, manifest and recipe to
    `<demo data>/public/<id>/`, then `scripts.seed_internal public --public-id <id>` runs
    `scripts.seed_public` in the deployment's network, which checks the checksum again and loads the
    rows through `load_with_rules` into the dataset `public-<id>` and a case named "<name> (public
    dataset)"; the load's events go to DuckDB (Lite's analytics store).
15. *A catalogue entry has no checksum.* OspreyFlow never downloads VAST data, so nobody has hashed
    the real files and `file.sha256` is null in the catalogue. `verify` refuses such an entry, in
    words, until the administrator `pin`s the file they downloaded, which writes a manifest of their
    own with its checksum (and the recipe beside it). That is trust on first use, and the guide says
    so: check the file came from the source page before pinning it.
16. *Real personal data* is placed only with `--accepted` (passed once the person typed `yes`, or
    gave `--accept-real-data`), with an acceptance record beside it, and the seed refuses a real
    dataset whose record is missing — Enron's path. As for Enron, the record admits it on a user's
    computer; on the owner's device the real-data exceptions entry (ADR-035 §C3) is the owner's
    own control and is not checked by this path.
17. *The VAST catalogue* (spec 00 §7 has the citations): `vast-2012-mc2`, the 2012 MC2 firewall log
    (the cyber starter's, case STIX), and `vast-2008-mc3`, the 2008 MC3 call records (crime, NIEM).
    No terms are stated for either, so nothing permits redistribution: each manifest records
    `not_stated`, and the guide says to use the data on one's own machine only and not rely on it
    commercially without permission. The rule that the published VAST files never enter this
    repository or CI is unchanged. The 2012 header comes from a secondary catalogue (COMIDDS) and the 2008 file's own header is
    not published, so each recipe says to check the header against the download.

**The cyber-intrusion pack.**
18. A deterministic STIX 2.1 bundle (UUIDv5 ids, fixed times, RFC 5737 addresses, `.example`
    domains): a threat actor, a campaign, a backdoor, the victim's identity, two
    command-and-control servers, five indicators, four observed-data objects and the relationships.
    In the graph, SDOs are the STIX pack's types and the identity an `Organisation`; an indicator is
    a `Document` (its pattern its title) that `INDICATES` what it detects; each watched address or
    domain is an `Endpoint` (`ip`, or `handle` for a domain, which the core's `endpoint_kind` has no
    value for) that `INDICATES` its server; each observation is a `Document` the two addresses are
    `MENTIONED_IN`, with a timed `COMMUNICATED_WITH` link between them. The seed writes the graph
    only; the timeline reads the links' times.

**Not verified here.** No deployment was installed, started or seeded: the named install,
`switch` and `deployments` were driven against stand-ins for Docker and the render; `seed_public`
and `seed_cyber_intrusion` were not run against a real ArcadeDB (their writes are checked against
the deployment ontology by the stand-in graph that validates as the adapter does). The guided
page's starter was walked by keyboard against the real install page.

**Tests that would fail (rule 12)**, each shown red first in the code's own shape (evidence in the
step's report): `tests/cli/test_starters.py` (each starter's `osprey.yaml` and packs, the case
domains, blank, the GOV.UK refusal, the guided page's draft), `tests/cli/test_named_deployments.py`
(no folder, project, volume or port shared; `--name` on every verb, planted with `logs` reading the
checkout's; a taken project name; the checkout's deployment unchanged; `switch`, `deployments`),
`tests/harness/test_named_render.py` (`deployment.env` 600 under the home folder; the build context;
the graph port), `tests/test_named_deployment_scripts.py`, `tests/cli/test_demo_public.py` and
`tests/demo_fixtures/test_public_dataset.py` (a checksum that differs refused before anything is
placed; real data refused without the acceptance; an unpinned entry refused),
`tests/demo_fixtures/test_public_dataset_recipes.py`, `tests/demo_fixtures/test_cyber_intrusion.py`,
`tests/harness/test_install_page.py`, the harness unit tests and the keyboard step
`submit-save-starter`.

## ADR-139 — Connection strength: link-strength influencers, direct links and rarity, as graph filters and monitoring conditions — ACCEPTED (design)

Status: accepted from the owner's instructions of 2 November 2026, after a client described its own
"connection strength" calculation. The owner recorded the client's answers, and the owner's own
rulings, interactively the same day. Built in build-order step 9f. It is to be explained in the user
guide, the developer guide and the decks, and demonstrated in the Prison Intelligence demo with
captures.

**Context: the client's method.** For each dataset, the client applies three steps:
1. **A rarity score, inverse-frequency (IDF-like).** A link resting on a value few others share
   scores higher. Their measure is the log of N divided by how many share the value, summed over the
   shared values.
2. **A flat source boost** for links from assaults, disorders and finds.
3. **A flat direct boost** for direct connections: phone calls and contacts, money transfers, visits
   and cell shares.

Further answers:
- The boosts are **added and stack**. Their size relative to rarity is **not yet known**.
- Strength is used for display, filtering, prioritisation, and alerts and referrals.
- All of the client's analysts see the whole of each dataset.

**Context: OspreyFlow today** (spec 01 §6.1). A link's stored weight comes from that link alone: its
own count against its type's heavy count, and its recency, through a logistic. Structural types have
fixed weights, and the parameters are a versioned, append-only weights file. ADR-123 removed the
corpus-wide rarity term, because a score built from counts across the corpus moves with links the
viewer cannot see (rules 3 and 7).

**Decision.**
1. **Link-strength influencers, a configurable feature.** An influencer has five parts:
   - **What triggers it:** an evidencing record's kind and value. For example, an `Incident` whose
     `incident_type` is `assault`, `disorder` or `find`, or any event or entity type and property the
     ontology defines.
   - **Which link types it influences:** for example `ROLE_IN`, or a person-to-person link that the
     record evidences.
   - **The kind of change:**
     - **add** a boost before the logistic (the default, as the client does);
     - **multiply** the pre-logistic score;
     - **set a floor** (the link is at least this strong);
     - **exclude** (the link is drawn no stronger than the base).
   - **Its size.**
   - **A label for the legend.**

   **Direct links are an influencer too.** "These link types are direct connections" is a rule with no
   trigger, applied to the named link types. It ships as calls (`COMMUNICATED_WITH`), money
   (`TRANSACTED`), visits (`VISITED`) and cell shares (`SHARED_CELL_WITH`), and like every influencer
   it can be changed.

   **Starting sizes** are calibrated as `midpoint` and `scale` were: a boost moves an ordinary link
   about as far as doubling its count would. They are marked "to be confirmed with the client".
2. **Influencers apply at read time, under the viewer's access.**
   - The stored weight stays as weights version 3 computes it. An influencer's effect is applied when
     a link is read, inside the adapter's access predicate (rule 3).
   - **It applies only if the viewer may see the evidencing record.** Otherwise an assault record
     hidden from an analyst would still thicken a line they can see, and reveal that the record exists.
   - **Consequences:** a change takes effect at once, with no recompute. Every viewer who sees the
     same evidence sees the same strength.
3. **Who sets influencers.**
   - **Installation-wide influencers** are proposed by an analyst holding a new right,
     `manage_strength_influencers`, and take effect only when a second person with that right
     approves. This is maker–checker, as for whole-deployment rules (ADR-133 stage (d)); the proposer
     cannot approve their own.
   - **Developers** can also ship influencers in the weights file.
   - **Every version is kept**, with who proposed and who approved it, and is audited.
   - **A case's Author** may add influencers for that case, or switch off installation-wide ones
     there. A case override needs no second person, because it changes only that case; it is shown in
     the legend and audited.
   - **Resolution order:** a case override, then the installation set, then the weights file's
     defaults.
4. **Rarity is computed at query time, over what the viewer may see.**
   - **The measure:** for two entities, `Σ over shared attribute nodes a of ln(N_visible / df_visible(a))`,
     where:
     - `N_visible` is the number of entities of the pair's kind the viewer may see in scope;
     - `df_visible(a)` is how many of them the viewer may see linked to `a`.

     This is the client's IDF score, computed per dataset by default (as the client does), or across
     the case's datasets the viewer may read.
   - **Where it is computed:** in the graph adapter, under the access predicate. It is never stored
     and never computed over the corpus.
   - **What the Glass gets:** the score and the shared attributes the viewer may see, never a count
     from beyond the filter (rule 7).
   - **For this client,** whose analysts all see each whole dataset, the numbers equal theirs. Where
     access varies, two analysts may see different rarity for the same pair, and the user guide says
     so.
   - **A count-based rarity** (the client's "a higher number of incidents") is the same measure over a
     link's occurrence count against the visible distribution for its type.
5. **The connection strength used everywhere** is the stored weight with the influencers that apply
   to it. Rarity is its own measure beside it, not folded into the weight, so each can be filtered and
   explained on its own.
6. **Graph filters, as the social-network metrics are** (ADR-088's Metrics panel; closeness, clique
   and others):
   - "Connection strength" and "Shared-attribute rarity" join the metrics an analyst can choose,
     threshold and dim by, in the same way.
   - The Matrix view can sort by both.
   - Each is keyboard reachable (rule 13) and has its access-control test (rule 4).
7. **The legend box** shows:
   - the active influencers, installation and case, each with its trigger, the link types it changes,
     the kind of change and its size;
   - which link types count as direct;
   - that rarity is computed over what you may see;
   - any case override, marked as such.
8. **A monitoring rule condition** (ADR-133):
   - Sentence rules gain "when the connection strength between …" and "when the shared-attribute
     rarity between …" "… reaches X". These are previewable like the others and judged as the rule's
     author.
   - A rule's preview and its alerts use the strength the author may see, so a rule never fires on
     evidence its author could not read.
9. **Explaining a strength.** The Inspector shows, for a selected link:
   - its strength in words: its count against what is heavy for its type, its recency, and the rule
     and version applied;
   - each influencer that changed it, naming the evidencing record kind;
   - for a pair, their shared attributes ranked by rarity.

   It never shows a corpus-wide count.
10. **Documentation and demonstration:**
    - **User guide:** a section "How connection strength is worked out" (the three ideas, influencers,
      the legend, the filters, why rarity can differ between analysts).
    - **Developer guide:** the formula, the influencer schema and its resolution order, read-time
      application under access, the rarity query, and how to ship influencers in the weights file.
    - **Spec 01 §6.1** is updated.
    - **Decks:** a slide in the Product Overview and the prison decks (step 10).
    - **The Prison Intelligence demo** shows influencers in the legend, an assault-evidenced link
      drawn stronger, a direct call against a shared address, a rare shared contact ranking above a
      common one, the two new filters dimming the canvas, and a monitoring rule on strength. Each is
      captured in both brands.

**Tests that would fail if this were violated (rule 12):**
- **Monotonicity:** adding occurrences never lowers strength, over a grid with each influencer kind on
  and off.
- **Triggers:** an influencer applies only when an evidencing record has the named value; a direct
  influencer applies only to its named link types.
- **Hidden evidence:** an evidencing record the viewer may not see changes nothing (planted: applying
  it regardless).
- **Rarity:** the score with a hidden entity sharing the attribute equals the score in a world without
  it.
- **The Glass's payload** carries no count from beyond the filter.
- **Maker–checker:** an installation-wide influencer has no effect until a second person approves, and
  its proposer cannot approve it.
- **Case overrides:** they apply only in their case, and the resolution order holds.
- **The legend** lists exactly the active influencers.
- **Monitoring:** the rule condition raises an alert on the author's visible strength and not on hidden
  evidence.
- **Keyboard:** steps for the new filters, the legend and the influencer editor.

**Consequences.**
- Weights version 3 stays the stored basis, and no recompute is needed.
- The client's exact sizes can be entered as an installation-wide influencer version once known, with
  no code change.

### ADR-139, Amendment 1 (2 November 2026) — step 9f as built, and how it read the decision

Status: built on 2 November 2026 (build-order step 9f), on the branch `connection-strength`; open to
the owner's review. Each item is how the build read a point the decision left open, or what it found.

**As built:**
1. **The arithmetic.** An influencer's change is applied to the stored weight's pre-logistic score,
   recovered exactly by the logistic's inverse (`raw = midpoint + scale · ln(w/(1 − w))`, the one
   deployment-wide `midpoint` and `scale`; a weight of exactly 0 or 1 is read as 10⁻⁹ from it). Adds
   are summed, then multipliers multiplied, then the logistic; then floors (the highest); **then an
   exclusion, last**, so "no stronger than the base" caps a floor too. Nothing applying leaves the
   stored weight exactly. A structural link's fixed weight is treated the same way (its inverse is a
   finite score), so an influencer can change a structural link if it names one; the shipped ones
   name none. Monotonicity (decision's first test) is held over a grid of every combination of the
   four changes, with and without evidence; shown red by a boost given only to links below the
   midpoint.
2. **"Evidences".** A record evidences a link when it is at one end of the link (a `ROLE_IN` to the
   incident) or linked to both ends by links the reader may see (two people in one incident). This is
   one hop each way; a record two hops away evidences nothing.
3. **The trigger's property is `category`.** The decision says an Incident's `incident_type`; the NIEM
   pack (version 3) declares `category`, with the values `assault`, `disorder`, `find`, `other` and
   `throw_over`, and no `incident_type`. The shipped influencer and the demo use `category`.
4. **The link types an incident evidences** in the shipped ontology, for the shipped
   `incident-source` influencer: `ROLE_IN` (the incident at one end), and the person-to-person links of
   people involved in one: `IN_CONFLICT_WITH`, `ASSOCIATE_OF` and `SHARED_CELL_WITH`. Left out:
   `OCCURRED_AT` (a fixed fact, ADR-120 Amendment 9), `FAMILY_OF` and `CO_DEFENDANT_OF` (not evidenced by
   an incident), `VISITED` (a visit is not), and `PASSES_ITEMS_TO` (inferred).
5. **Sizes.** Both shipped influencers add 0.1348: how far doubling an ordinary link's count, from the
   default rule's heavy count (10) to 20, moves its pre-logistic score, α·(ln 21 − ln 11)/ln 11. A
   test holds the file to the derivation. Marked "to be confirmed with the client".
6. **Any trigger-less influencer marks its link types direct** in the legend, as decision 1 defines
   direct links; a trigger-less floor on money therefore lists money as direct.
7. **The right `manage_strength_influencers`** (ADR-112's I10) is held by the **Analyst** and **Admin**
   roles: the decision has analysts propose and approve, and the administrator runs the installation's
   settings. It is a system-wide right with no case level, as L9 is. The case's own reads
   (`connection-strength`, `rarity`, `strength-influencers` GET) need `investigate` at Viewer; the case
   override needs `investigate` at **Author** (the decision names the Author and no right).
8. **Maker–checker** follows ADR-133 stage (d): a proposal is a whole new set (the version), `pending`
   until a second holder approves it; one version waits at a time (`409`); the proposer may withdraw it
   (send it back) but never approve it (`403 own_change`); the version in force is the latest approved,
   and before any is approved the weights file's are. A version names its proposer and decider by name
   (ADR-106), resolved when served. Each step is audited (`strength_influencers_proposed`, `…_approved`,
   `…_sent_back`, `case_strength_influencers_set`). An influencer naming a type, property, value or link
   type the ontology does not declare is refused `422`, in words.
9. **Rarity's attribute nodes** are every visible node linked to both entities except an `Alert` (the
   weights file's `rarity.exclude_types`): a cell, a phone, a visitor, a report, a group and the
   establishment all count, and the inverse frequency makes the common ones score near zero. Pairs
   are of one entity type only (a pair of different types has no score). **Per dataset** means each
   dataset both entities and the attribute belong to, the highest kept and named; two sharing no
   dataset have no score there. A pair the Glass asks for that is not in the reader's view is answered
   as one naming nobody (no score, nothing shared), its own ids echoed. Past 2,000,000 pair
   contributions the read is refused `limit_exceeded` (`cap_kind: "pairs"`, a new value).
10. **Not built: the count-based rarity** (decision 4's last bullet, "a higher number of incidents").
    It is the same measure over a link's occurrence count against its type's visible distribution;
    nothing in the Glass or the rules asks for it yet. Recorded as an open question.
11. **The Glass.** *Connection strength* and *Shared-attribute rarity* join the Metrics panel's ranking
    and filter metrics; a node takes its strongest link (strength) or its rarest pairing with another of
    its kind in view (rarity); the strength filter also dims each link below the threshold. The Matrix's
    link table sorts by **Strength** and **Rarity** (of the link's two ends). The legend's *Connection
    strength* part, the Inspector's *Connection strength* section (a link) and *What these two share*
    (two nodes selected). The influencer editor is a **Monitoring** tab, *Connection strength*, beside
    the rules it changes, since analysts hold the right: the Admin area is the administrator's alone.
12. **Rules.** A sentence's `strength` blank: "the connection strength between it and [a type, or
    anything] [by a link type, or any] reaches X" (X in (0, 1]), judged on the subject's links read as the
    author (`expand`, then `connection_strengths`), the strongest kept; or "the shared-attribute rarity
    between it and another of its type reaches X", per dataset or across the case. Either runs after
    commit or on a schedule, never before commit. A run with no influencer store (a KYC sweep, a list's
    re-screening) judges with the weights file's influencers alone.
13. **Stored weights stay version 3**, and the weights file gains two top-level keys beside `versions`
    (`influencers`, `rarity`), which the loader now accepts; the frozen versions are unchanged.

**Tests**, each shown red first in the code's own shape (evidence `s9f_*`): the pure arithmetic,
triggers, resolution order and legend (`tests/ontology/test_influencers.py`); the conformance cases
(`connection_strengths` and `shared_attribute_rarity`, including both hidden-world cases and the cap);
the case reads under access with a hidden record and a hidden entity, and the payload's field walk
(`working_set/test_connection_strength_access_control.py`); maker–checker and case overrides
(`test_strength_influencer_routes.py`); the rule condition as its author (`test_strength_sentence_rules.py`);
the demo's claims on the plan (`scenarios/test_pid_connection_strength.py`); the Glass's units; keyboard
(`strength.spec.ts`, and cases in `metrics-panel.spec.ts`, `matrix.spec.ts`, `inspector.spec.ts`) and
axe states.

### ADR-127, Amendment 42 (2 November 2026) — the storyline gains a connection-strength scene

Status: added with ADR-139's build (step 9f); the scene is J6b of `PRISON_DEMO_SCRIPT_v4_PROPOSED.md`
and Part C of `CAPTURE_RUNBOOK_v4.md`, not yet rehearsed.

**No generated data changed.** The case already holds each of the scene's ideas, proved on the plan at

2. **A direct call against a shared address:** cellmate_1 and cellmate_2 held cell F1-03 at different
