     wherever the runbook is followed. A block fenced `bash platform` runs only on the client's
     platform (the Terraform pull requests and the AWS accounts' own commands); a rehearsal on a
     local cluster supplies its stand-in instead. `harness.cloud_platform.runbooks.command_blocks`
     reads the blocks back, so a rehearsal can run the text the client's team reads; until one
     has, the tests check the blocks' syntax, order and rights only.
   - No block ends the reader's shell (`exit`), each block parses as shell, and the rehearsal's
     blocks call neither the AWS command line nor Terraform. Each of these is a test.
   - **Every command runs with a namespace tenant's rights.** Nothing cluster-wide is listed or
     changed: no volume objects, and no listing of every kind there is. The namespace is listed
     one kind at a time, for the kinds the deployment makes. The disks are read from the account
     by the namespace tag the EBS CSI driver gives each one, in a block of the platform's
     (`test_no_command_needs_more_than_a_namespace_s_rights`).
   - **The install** renders the plan unpinned, signs in to the registry (the platform's block),
     runs `ospreyflow images push`, renders again pinned, so the values name ours by the digest
     the registry holds (decision 8), then installs the chart. It ends with the sign-in step,
     `python -m harness.cloud_platform.identity`, which does what the cluster's own install does
     once Keycloak answers. It gives the identity provider the deployment's settings together
     with our Secret, since the realm's sign-in reads ConfigMap settings (the dashboards' address
     among them), then makes the first administrator, `admin`, and prints the one-time code they
     sign in with once. P10's sign-in replaces it.
   - **The decommission removes what `helm uninstall` keeps:**
     - each StatefulSet's claims, selected by the release's label, which the StatefulSet
       controller gives every claim it makes;
     - the shared claims, by name;
     - our Secret.
   - **It then empties what the namespace's Terraform cannot remove while it holds anything**,
     before the pull request that removes those resources: every bucket, of every object and
     every version (`media` is versioned), and every ECR repository the render names, a hundred
     images a call (they have no `force_delete`).
   - **Its last block runs the decommission check** (`harness.cloud_platform.decommission_check`).
     The check names anything of the deployment's still in the namespace (by the chart's label,
     Helm's release annotation, our Secret's and the kept claims' names, and each StatefulSet's
     claims), and any disk made for one of its claims. In the Terraform state it counts only the
     resources the rendered `terraform/` declares: the namespace's folder holds the platform's
     own resources too, which are listed as left alone. An IAM role or policy, and a KMS key
     alias, are named as such, since each outlives the namespace (the render makes no KMS key
     today). Each leftover is planted in the shape its source prints it, each branch red alone
     (`tests/cp_policy_check/test_cp_decommission_check.py`).
8. **The profile's ceiling** (decision 10; Amendment 2's carry for P7, closed here). On this
   profile a deployment that names no `deployment.highest_marking` is held to OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE,
   not the handling scheme's highest; one that names its own keeps it
   (`test_the_ceiling_is_official_sensitive_unless_the_deployment_names_its_own`, red first at
   SECRET).
   The orchestrator accepted this default, and with it that the poc shape's kind run seeds only the
   packs declared at or below OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE (HMP, declared SECRET, is not among them).
   `deployment.highest_marking`'s own description now says so, and with it both settings
   appendices. The poc shape's lock names only the images its pods run, so it has no Keeper of its
   own (`test_the_lock_names_only_the_images_a_poc_pod_runs`), and `make cp-policy-check` holds
   every poc container to a CPU limit (point 5) in Helm's own output.
9. **`ospreyflow images push`'s refusal**, with no render to push, names a command that works as
   given from `OspreyFlow_Core` (`PYTHONPATH=.:packages .venv/bin/python -m harness.render`). A test
   runs the command its words give.
10. **No OpenSearch domain in the poc shape** (the orchestrator's ruling). No pod reads it, and it
    is a paid domain on the client's own install, so the poc shape's Terraform makes none
    (`test_the_poc_shape_makes_no_opensearch_domain`). The standard shape's is carried (below).
11. **A first render into a new folder** writes every artefact. `harness.render.write` made the
    output folder but not `terraform/`, so the first render stopped on `terraform/ecr.tf`. Each
    artefact's folder is now made, readable as the rest
    (`test_a_first_render_into_an_empty_folder_writes_every_artefact`).
12. **One digest from the image plan to the values** (decision 8). The install renders twice: first
    `--allow-unpinned`, since our images are not in the namespace's registry until `images push`
    puts them there, then pinned. The first render named the third-party images by tag, so the push
    copied them by tag and the pinned render resolved each tag afresh. A tag moved in between
    pinned a digest the registry's copy does not have. Now:
    - on this profile, the render resolves the third-party images even when unpinned (only ours
      may stay unresolved);
    - `images push` refuses an image named by its tag alone;
    - the pinned render pins each image the previous plan copied by the digest it copied
      (`harness.cloud_platform.carry`).
    A test drives `harness.render.main` twice with a stand-in registry that moves every tag between
    the two renders (`test_a_tag_that_moves_between_the_two_renders_keeps_the_digest_that_was_copied`).

**Open question for the client's platform team** (Amendment 1's list gains it): what LimitRange
and ResourceQuota the namespace carries, and in particular whether the quota sets `limits.cpu` or
the LimitRange a default CPU limit. Until then the standard shape names no CPU limit (point 6).

**Left, and why.**
- The acceptance scenarios on kind in the poc shape, both runbooks run end to end there (the
  install's blocks, then the decommission's, with the decommission check green at the end), and
  the final render they run, all come after P11's and P12's part 2s land, since the shape renders
  what they leave. Under point 8's ceiling the run seeds only packs declared at or below
  OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE. Until then the runbooks are checked by tests for their syntax, their order
  and the rights they need, and nothing more: no block has run against a cluster or an account.
  The rehearsal supplies the files the platform's blocks write (`state.txt`, `buckets.txt`, and
  `volumes.json` in place of the disks). The identity step has never met a real Keycloak, and its
  reading of an existing administrator ("Conflict detected") is unproven.
- `scripts/seed_internal.py` checks a pack against the ceiling it reads from `deployment.env`, which
  this profile has none of, so before seeding it judges against the scheme's highest. Only the
  engine's refusal at each write holds the ceiling there. Carried to the seeds' owner.
- Carried by name:
  - the standard shape's OpenSearch domain (`opensearch.tf`), which no pod reads
    (`opensearch-output`), left unchanged by the orchestrator's ruling;
  - a gateway for an engine first added in *Admin › Models*, which the render leaves out when the
    install declares none, so that engine has no gateway until a re-render. That is P11 part 2's
    own item (the gateway rendered by default), and P7b's final render picks it up when it lands.

**After the orchestrator's review of P7b (11 November 2026).**

13. **The decommission check names what the namespace's Terraform writes**: the managed stores'
    Secrets (the database's password among them) and the bucket role's service account carry no
    label of the chart's, so they are ours by name. It also names Helm's own release record, and
    gives each removal with its API group (Calico's `networkpolicy.projectcalico.org`). It refuses,
    rather than reads as nothing left, a disks listing that holds no `Volumes`, or that was taken
    in another region or another account than the cluster's. The runbook wraps the listing with
    the account `aws sts` answers for and the region it asked. A disk counts as ours by its
    namespace's tag and one of our claims' names together. In the Terraform state, only the
    folder's root (or the module the environments repository names, `--module`) holds ours; a
    resource of the same type and name in another module is the platform's.
14. **The decommission's AWS steps.**
    - Every AWS call names its region.
    - The deployment's buckets are checked one by one, by name (`head-bucket`), not listed
      account-wide.
    - The buckets are emptied five hundred keys a call, versions and delete markers apart, each
      listing sliced in its query (`--max-items` counts the versions alone, so it cannot cap the
      delete markers). The images go a hundred a call, buildx's tagged indexes before the untagged
      images they hold.
    - A step stops, and ends on having stopped, on a listing that fails, a call that answers exit 0
      with per-key `Errors` or `failures`, and a listing that comes back the same after a delete. A
      loop that cannot finish never runs on, and each loop's block ends on its own result, so a
      pasted block never carries on past a stop.
    - These steps are run under bash in the tests, against a stand-in `aws` that refuses what AWS
      refuses: more than a thousand keys, a 403 against a 404 from `head-bucket`, a failing
      listing, and exit 0 with errors. Each branch is shown red
      (`tests/harness/test_cloud_platform_decommission_aws.py`).
    - Its first step is the last backup, to a place outside the buckets it empties (refused if it
      is inside them). The command is P9's backup, added there by P9's diff, with the poc shape's
      Ingest claim in its set.
15. **The runbooks are bash**, fenced `bash` and `bash platform`.
    - Each says what it needs: the release's checkout at its tag, whose Dockerfiles and source
      `images push` builds from; its environment (`.venv`); the `ospreyflow` command; Docker with
      `buildx`; and bash.
    - The install's header names the render that works before the push (`--allow-unpinned`).
    - The tenant's-rights test reads every `kubectl` and `helm` call wherever it stands in a
      line, every AWS call for its region, and the Python steps' own `kubectl`.
16. **The poc shape refuses `components.search: opensearch`** in words: it makes no domain for one.
    The poc fixture names `postgres-fulltext`.
17. **The ceiling has one source**, `harness.site.highest_marking`, which holds each profile's own
    default (`PROFILE_CEILINGS`, OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE for this profile) and refuses one the handling
    scheme does not hold. The render reads it for the deployment as it is. The change to
    `harness/site.py`, studio-b's file, was made at the orchestrator's word.
18. **A render removes what its last render wrote and this one does not**, by the manifest it
    leaves (`.rendered`), and never a file it did not write, so a standard shape's
    `terraform/opensearch.tf` does not survive a poc render to be applied.
19. **The standard shape is left out of the configuration's copy** in the values. The copy is in
    the ConfigMap whose checksum restarts every pod, so a P7 deployment does not restart on
    upgrade for a setting it never wrote.

20. **A decommission keeps the backups** (the orchestrator's ruling from P9's work): the backups
    bucket and its key are the decommission's one named exception, so no decommission makes a
    retained backup unreadable. P9 (ADR-148 Amendment 7) holds the rule, in
    `harness.cloud_platform_backups`: the bucket's name after the prefix (`BUCKET_SUFFIX`) and its
    kept resources (`KEPT_AT_DECOMMISSION`). Its diff to this step's decommission check and runbook
    is applied at merge, once both steps have merged. The check then reports the bucket and those
    resources as kept, and only when the render declares them; anything else of ours, the backup
    role among it, still fails. The runbook takes the last backup into that bucket, takes the kept
    resources out of the state before the removal, and says how they are removed when the
    retention ends. That diff was shown here to apply cleanly to this step's files and to pass
    (66 tests, with P9's module beside them).

21. **Egress is each workload's own** (the orchestrator's ruling from case-b's P12 review, for both
    shapes). P7 rendered one Calico Allow selecting every pod (`all()`, order 100). It gave every
    workload every other workload, the managed stores' networks and every host, and the namespace's
    Kubernetes policies, at Calico's order 1000 after the deny, never decided egress.
    - Now DNS is the one policy that selects every pod, and it allows DNS alone.
    - Each workload has its own policy, `default.ospreyflow-egress-<workload>` (order 100, selecting
      its own pods by `app.kubernetes.io/name`). It allows the namespace's workloads it calls, on
      their Services' ports; the managed stores' networks if it reads a store, on their ports
      (RDS's 5432, ElastiCache's 6379, and the OpenSearch domain's 443 where the Terraform makes
      one); and the hosts of each kind it is given, each on its own ports, TCP.
    - A host's ports come from the settings the render already reads, in one parse: 443 for S3,
      STS and an engine kind's host; an address's own port or its scheme's (80 for http) for an
      engine's or a map source's; `mail.port` for the mail server; and a connector host's
      `host:port` from `cloud_platform.connector_hosts`, a bare host on 443 (the final review of
      P7b, item 5, as agreed with the orchestrator). A SQL connection needs its database's port
      there, or its connection times out. A host given twice with two ports is reached on both.
      The Conduit's allow-list (`OSPREY_CONNECTOR_EGRESS`) holds the hosts alone and the egress
      the hosts and their ports, so a connection to a listed host on an unlisted port passes the
      Conduit and times out at the egress. The render says, in words at the head of
      `values.yaml` (and in the poc shape's INSTALL.md), which hosts are named without a port and
      so reached on 443 alone. An IPv6 literal is refused in its own words: a host is named.
    - The deny runs at order 200, before the place Calico gives the namespace's Kubernetes
      policies (1000). On this profile the cluster's `ospreyflow-internal` policy is not rendered
      at all, so no Kubernetes policy here types Egress (the final review, item 1).
    - The rows are `profile.yaml`'s `egress.reach`, `egress.managed` and `egress.paths`.
      - The paths come from the addresses each workload's environment names.
      - S3 and STS go to the bucket role's pods, and to ClickHouse for its `BACKUP TO S3` (P9).
      - A model engine's host goes to the gateway alone, a proxied map source to the Conduit,
        the mail server to Keycloak, and a connector host to the Conduit and the workers.
      - The Glass and the recogniser reach DNS and their own targets, nothing outside.
    - The gateway, which signs Bedrock's calls by its own role (P11 part 2), reaches STS alone
      (`egress.identity`), never S3.
    - P9's backup and restore pods (`backup`, `backup-claims`, `restore`, `restore-claims`) are
      rows by their own pods' names (`egress.others`), which the render gives to
      `egress_policy(..., others=...)`, since they render beside the workloads. A row whose pod is
      not rendered selects nothing. Each admits nothing and reaches S3 and STS. The backup and the
      restore also reach ArcadeDB and ClickHouse, which admit them, and a restore alone the
      cluster's API by the `kubernetes` Service (the path target `kube-api`), to see that the
      writers have stopped. The claims' runs reach none of ours: a claim is a mount, not a path.
      No row names KMS: S3 calls it on the backups' behalf (SSE-KMS), so a row to it would be a
      path never used (the orchestrator's ruling with case, 11 November). Calico matches networks,
      not names, so an STS or regional range that also holds KMS is not excluded (a question for
      the platform team, below). No lane renders a Calico
      policy of its own: every path is a row, and a later workload (case-b's Laurium) is a row,
      not a template edit.
    - Point 22's whole-secret rule is about our Secret alone. A Secret of its own (P9's ClickHouse
      backup user's password, read by ClickHouse and the backup and restore pods) passes it,
      whole or by key.
    - `make cp-policy-check` refuses an Allow beyond DNS under a policy selecting every pod
      (`wide-egress`); a deny with no order, or one at 1000 or after (`deny-order`); an Allow
      without its protocol and ports (`allow-ports`), the rule to the API server by its
      `kubernetes` Service alone excepted, matched exactly, as Calico takes no ports there, and
      each port a single number (a range such as `"1:65535"` or a named port is refused); and a
      selector it cannot narrow (`unreadable-selector`): an empty one is every pod, and `has(...)`,
      a part-of label or `all()` in a rule is refused, as is a rule's `notSelector`,
      `notNamespaceSelector` or `serviceAccounts.selector`. A DNS rule names the platform's DNS's
      namespace, or it is no DNS rule. An ingress peer names workloads by name alone, or it is
      `wide-ingress` (an `Exists` expression, an instance label, the part-of label, every pod).
22. **Our Secret only to what reads it** (the same review). P7 gave the whole deployment Secret to
    every workload that reads the settings (`envFrom`), the stores' passwords and the gateway's
    master key among them, with only the model keys blanked.
    - Now the Conduit, the workers and the report sync read it whole (`secrets.whole`).
    - Superset is given by name only the keys it reads (`secrets.named`).
    - The Glass and the recogniser get the ConfigMap alone (the chart's `noSecret`).
    - `make cp-policy-check` refuses our Secret whole to any other pod, and any key outside a
      named allowance (`whole-secret`). The allowance is default-deny (the orchestrator's ruling,
      11 November): a pod not listed in the check may hold no key of ours, so a new workload
      (case-b's Laurium) is refused one until it is listed, with no other edit to the check. The
      list holds the keys the render gives each store, Keycloak, the gateway and Superset. The
      gateway also holds this deployment's keyed engines' keys, read from its own `osprey.yaml`
      in Helm's output (`model_key_variables`), never by a prefix or a fixed name: an IAM-role
      engine's held key is refused it, and so is `OSPREY_MODEL_PROVIDER_KEY` when the single
      `models.provider` is an IAM-role one (ADR-135 Amendments 4 and 7).
    - The ceiling (`OSPREY_HIGHEST_MARKING`) is the ConfigMap's alone, in no key of our Secret, so
      the Secret the Conduit and the workers read whole cannot say otherwise.
    - Our Secret is whatever the values name it (`secrets.name`), as the chart reads it, and it
      is held however a pod reads it: `envFrom`, a key, a `secret` volume (whole or by items), or
      a `projected` volume's `secret` source (the final review, item 2).
23. **Ingress is the paths turned round** (the orchestrator's ruling). Each workload's Kubernetes
    policy, `ospreyflow-ingress-<workload>`, admits only the workloads whose paths name it, on its
    own ports, rendered from the same rows as their egress so the two cannot drift. A workload
    nothing calls admits nothing in the namespace. The front doors keep the ingress controller's
    namespace (`ospreyflow-from-ingress`).
    - On this profile `ospreyflow-internal` is not rendered (point 21); the cluster's render is
      unchanged.
    - `make cp-policy-check` refuses an ingress rule admitting every pod of ours (`wide-ingress`).
    - The evaluator (`tests/cp_policy_check/test_cp_egress_order.py`) applies Calico's order to
      egress and the Kubernetes policies to ingress, over Helm's own output. It checks every
      workload against every other workload, the managed network, each host, the internet and DNS,
      both ways, against the rows.
24. **A token only where the API is called** (the orchestrator's ruling from case-b's P12 part 2).
    Kubernetes mounts a pod's service-account token by default. On this profile every pod and Job
    says whether to mount it: only a pod given an account of its own does. Today that is IRSA's
    pods (the Conduit, the workers, the report sync, for their web identity) and, with Bedrock,
    the gateway. P9's backup and restore pods have accounts of their own; a restore also asks the
    API whether the writers have stopped. Every other pod has `automountServiceAccountToken:
    false`: the Glass, the recogniser, the dashboards, Keycloak, the stores and their Keeper, the
    gateway without Bedrock, the Jobs, and case-b's Laurium when it lands.
    - `make cp-policy-check` refuses a mounted token (`token`) on any pod not in its own list, held
      in the check and not read from the render, and on a listed pod under any account but its
      own: IRSA's (the platform's `secrets.irsa.service_account`) for the Conduit, the workers and
      the report sync, the gateway's own for the gateway, one of their own for P9's pods; never
      the namespace's `default`. An account named by the older `serviceAccount` field counts as
      one named by `serviceAccountName`. The bucket role's account on any other pod, or the
      gateway's on any but the gateway, is refused whether or not a token is mounted: IRSA's
      webhook gives a pod its role by the account alone (the final review, item 6).
    - The other profiles' renders are unchanged: the chart writes the setting only when the render
      gives it.

**Open question for the client's platform team**, added to Amendment 1's list: the storage class's
volume binding. The poc shape's Conduit mounts two ReadWriteOnce claims, the shared one and the
Ingest root's. With `WaitForFirstConsumer` both are made in its node's zone. With `Immediate`
they may land in two zones, and no node could mount both.

**Open question for the client's platform team**, the same list: whether the networks the
platform names for STS, or any regional range a pod is allowed, also hold KMS's addresses. No row
names KMS (point 21), but Calico matches networks, not names, so a shared range would not exclude
it.

**The tests that would fail.** `tests/harness/test_cloud_platform_poc.py` (the shape, the stores,
the claim, the CPU limits, the runbooks), `tests/cp_policy_check/test_cp_policy_check.py` (every
planted fault refused in the poc shape's own render, the claim rendered, mounted and refused
ReadWriteMany), `tests/cp_policy_check/test_cp_decommission_check.py`,
`tests/harness/test_cloud_platform_identity.py`, the ceiling's, the first render's and the moving
tag's cases in `tests/harness/test_cloud_platform_render.py`, and the refusals' in
`tests/cli/test_images_verb.py`; for points 21-24, `tests/cp_policy_check/test_cp_egress_order.py`
(the evaluator over Helm's own output, every pod against every pod, host, port, network, the
internet and DNS) and `tests/harness/test_cloud_platform_egress.py` (the rows, the ports, the
token, the ceiling and `connector_hosts`).

### ADR-148, Amendment 6 (11 November 2026) — Entra ID's claims as built (P10 part 1): mapped by settings, one construction path, the tenant, issuer, client and scope pinned, a principal keyed by `oid` within its tenant

*Entra ID's claims as built (P10 part 1), by the admin lane; two independent review rounds.*

Decision 9 says the claims are mapped, not assumed, by named claim or by Entra group table. Built in
`packages/principal_auth` (`ClaimMapping`, `principal_from_claims`):

1. **One source per claim.** Clearance, organisational unit and handling codes each come from **either** a token claim
   **or** a group table, never both. A setting naming both or neither fails to load, and so does an unknown key or a
   group granting an empty value. Different claims may use different kinds of source. A clearance or unit table maps
   a group to **one** value; a list there fails to load.
2. **A mapping other than the fixed names is an Entra mapping.** It names its tenant (`tenant_id`, a GUID) and the
   Glass's app registration (`client_id`, a GUID). Its `scope` setting names the one delegated scope the Glass asks
   for (default `access_as_user`). With `tenant_id` set:
   - the token must carry `oid` and `exp`;
   - its `tid` must equal the tenant;
   - the resolver refuses to start unless `OIDC_ISSUER` and `OIDC_AUDIENCE` are set.

   All Entra tenants share one set of signing keys, so a signature alone proves nothing about the tenant. The issuer
   is the configured one, because v1.0 and v2.0 tokens have different issuer forms (see the assumptions below).
3. **Refused, never guessed.** Each of these is a 401, never a default:
   - a missing clearance or unit;
   - groups granting more than one clearance or more than one unit;
   - a value of the wrong type (a clearance or unit must be a non-empty string);
   - a group overage (`_claim_names` naming the groups claim, or `hasgroups: true`), and a groups list longer than
     Entra's cap of 200, which is no token Entra issues;
   - a handling code or role that is empty (`""`, alone or in a list).

   **A token carrying `tid` under the fixed names (the Keycloak handling) is refused**, with fixed words ("token
   carries tid: an Entra ID token is refused without an Entra claim mapping"). Keycloak never emits `tid`. Without
   this refusal, an Entra token on a deployment with the default mapping would skip the tenant, `oid` and scope
   checks, and an Entra app role named `osprey-admin` would make an administrator.

   For two clearances the answer is refusal, not the lowest: `principal_auth` holds no marking scheme to order them,
   and a person in two clearance groups is a directory error. Two groups granting the same value resolve. Handling
   codes from groups are the union of the mapped groups' codes. A code named twice in a claim is kept once, as the
   group path does. An unmapped group grants nothing.
4. **Roles are not read from an Entra token.** Its `roles` are app roles an Entra administrator assigns, and decision
   9 keeps roles in Admin › People. Where Admin › People keeps roles on this profile, with no Keycloak, is P10 part 2
   (an access decision held for the owner).
5. **The default mapping is the fixed names**, so deployments that set nothing behave as before. Three tightenings
   apply to every deployment:
   - a string of handling codes or roles is one value, not its letters;
   - a claim of the wrong type, or an empty code or role, is a 401 instead of being `str()`-ed, dropped or causing
     a 500;
   - a code or role named twice is kept once.
6. **The principal's id.** For an Entra mapping, `Principal.id` is the token's **`oid`**. That is the orchestrator's
   ruling of 11 November 2026, on its own recommendation; the owner may overrule it. The reasons:
   - Entra's `sub` is pairwise per application (ADR-112 Amendment 3's rejected alternatives already say so), so a second
     client id would split one person into two principals;
   - Graph gives `oid`, so Admin › People can assign roles before a person's first sign-in.

   `oid` is unique within a tenant, and the tenant is pinned (point 2), so `oid` alone names one person. A token
   with no `oid`, or one that is not an object id, is refused. For the fixed names (Keycloak), `Principal.id` stays
   `sub`, which PyJWT requires and refuses unless it is a string.
7. **An app-only token is no person.** In Entra mode a token with no delegated `scp`, or with `idtyp: app`, is
   refused.
8. **Who the token was issued to, and for what** (decided by the admin lane; the owner may overrule):
   - **The client is pinned.** A v2.0 token names its client in `azp`, a v1.0 token in `appid`. Whichever is
     present must equal `client_id`, and a token with neither is refused. Without this, any other application in
     the tenant that obtains a token for this API would be a Glass session. Recommended by the orchestrator.
   - **`scp` must include the configured `scope`**, as a whole word of its space-separated list (`access_as_user`
     is not satisfied by `access_as_user_extra`). Any other delegated scope (`User.Read`, `openid` alone) is a token
     meant for something else.
   - **Guest (B2B) accounts are refused**: `acct` of `1` (as a number or as text), or an `idp` present and different
     from the issuer (Entra emits `idp` only when the user is homed in another tenant or provider). An
     intelligence workspace admits members of the client's own directory by default, and admitting a guest is a
     decision for the deployment, not something a token can make. Admitting guests would need a new setting and a
     new amendment. `acct` is an optional claim the app registration must ask for, so `idp` is the check that works
     without configuration.
9. **The settings are checked where they are used.** Group-table keys must be group ids, `groups_claim` must be named,
   and the resolver validates again whatever mapping it is given, because `model_copy` and `model_construct` skip
   validation.

**Assumptions, each to be measured in P10 part 2 against the client's development tenant** (CLAUDE.md rule 15: the
token shapes above are as Microsoft documents them, not yet measured):

- **v1.0 or v2.0 access tokens.** An app registration with `accessTokenAcceptedVersion` null (the default) is issued
  v1.0 access tokens. Their `iss` is `https://sts.windows.net/{tid}/`, not `https://login.microsoftonline.com/{tid}/v2.0`,
  their `aud` may be the `api://` application id URI rather than the client id, and they name the client in `appid`.
  The code takes the issuer and audience from settings and reads `appid`. Test:
  `test_a_real_tenant_token_matches_the_configured_issuer_and_audience`. It puts a real token through the profile's
  `OIDC_ISSUER` and `OIDC_AUDIENCE` and shows it resolves. It is red with the other version's issuer configured.
- **Directory extension names.** In a JWT, an extension attribute is assumed to arrive as
  `extension_<application id without hyphens>_<name>`. Through a claims-mapping policy it may arrive as
  `extn.<name>` instead. The mapping names whatever the real token carries. Test:
  `test_the_real_directory_extension_names_reach_the_mapping`. It takes the names from a real token's keys, maps them
  and shows the principal resolves. It is red with the other naming form.
- **A claims-mapping policy's signing key.** An application with a claims-mapping policy has its tokens signed with an
  app-specific key, published at the JWKS URL with `?appid=<client id>`. `OIDC_JWKS_URL` must then carry that query.
  Test: `test_a_claims_mapping_policy_token_verifies_against_the_app_specific_jwks`. It is red with `?appid=`
  removed.
- **Guests and `acct`.** Test: `test_a_real_guest_token_is_refused`. It shows a real guest's token carries `idp` (and
  `acct` 1 where configured) and is refused, and that a member's token resolves.
- **Access tokens, not ID tokens.** The Glass is assumed to send access tokens for this API. ID tokens carry no `scp`
  and would be refused as app-only (point 7). Test: `test_the_glass_sends_an_access_token_for_this_api`.

**Carried to part 2**, each with its test named in `process/lanes/admin/SERVER_LOG.md`:

- the profile's `claims:` settings, with `tenant_id` and `client_id` required;
- `ApiConfig` and its callers passing the mapping;
- Keycloak not rendered on the profile;
- roles and owner resolution on Entra;
- three readers of `roles` outside `principal_auth`, with no issuer or tenant check. Each comes under the rule or is
  shown not rendered on the profile:
  - `harness/webapp_auth.py:135`;
  - `deploy/superset/superset_config.py:89`;
  - `harness/oidc.py:254`;
- one real token from the client's development tenant, which settles the assumptions above.

Tests: `tests/services/api/test_auth_entra_claims.py`. Planted faults: `process/lanes/admin/P10_P1_RED_RECORD.md`.

### ADR-135, Amendment 9 (11 November 2026) — Laurium wired into the cloud-platform profile as built (P12 part 2): its own service with no Secret in its pod, the review queue's extraction alone, the cloud-platform preset read as a profile default, Admin read-only, its key made at start without stopping the Conduit, and Laurium reading the product's own extraction model

Status: as built by the case-b lane (P12 part 2), after its own lane reviewer's round and the orchestrator's rulings of
11 November, each recorded for the owner. Changes Amendment 5 decision 2 where said (point 5); Amendments 6 and 8
stand. Record: `process/lanes/case-b/P12p2_RED_RECORD.md`.

1. **The setting, and the cloud-platform preset.** `models.extraction_engine`: `deep_read` or `laurium`, and Laurium on
   the `cloud-platform` profile alone (as Amendment 7's engine kinds), refused on any other in words naming the profile.
   **Amendment 5 decision 2 ("the `cloud-platform` profile's pack presets Laurium") named no artefact** (the install's
   answers serve Lite, Small and Enterprise; starters are theme and domain): a rule 11 gap, **closed as a profile
   default** (the orchestrator, on the lane's stop, the owner's decision kept): **left unset, `laurium` on
   cloud-platform and its cluster translation, `deep_read` on every other profile; naming `deep_read` opts out.** It is
   **read, never written** (`OspreyConfig.extraction_engine`, a property): a dump of a configuration that named nothing
   still names nothing, so the set-up console's save and a profile switch never carry a resolved value. Platform's two
   cloud-platform fixtures name `deep_read`, so their tests keep their meaning; P7b's poc fixture leaves it unset and
   renders Laurium. **The owner's question stands in MORNING:** keep the preset, or `deep_read` until point 7's open
   item closes.
2. **Laurium serves document extraction into the review queue alone** (the orchestrator's ruling on the lane reviewer's
   item 2, a rule 11 gap; the orchestrator's round 1 on P12 part 2): `services.api.review.run_extraction` takes
   `laurium_may_read` (default false) and sets the marker (`adapters.extract_laurium.composed.laurium_reads`) only when
   it is true; **the review queue's route (`run_extraction_route`) alone passes it**, and only inside the marker does
   `extract` go to Laurium. Questions, Ask to search, email extraction and a document's content (the last two also
   call `run_extraction`, without the flag) stay with Deep read: Ask to search's schema writes an untyped `items`,
   which Laurium's subset refuses, and Questions joins every document into one call. Composed **inside** the routes
   (`services.api.laurium_start.routed_model`), so Laurium's calls keep their engine, its key and the dataset egress
   rules. **No screen reaches Laurium today** (the orchestrator's round 2): the flagged route has no caller in the
   Glass, whose model extraction is a document's content and email extraction, both Deep read. So on the
   cloud-platform profile, with the preset, **Laurium is rendered and runs while no analyst action reaches it, until a
   screen calls the review queue's route**; the preset's question goes back to the owner with this.
3. **The render.** Laurium is a service only when chosen (`harness/laurium.py`): its own image beside the Conduit's,
   so `ospreyflow images push` copies it; its port; **no `env_file`, so on a cluster no `envFrom` of the deployment's
   Secret** (which holds the gateway's master key and every store's password): its environment is its gateway's address
   alone. The Conduit is told the choice and Laurium's address (`OSPREY_EXTRACTION_ENGINE`, `OSPREY_LAURIUM_URL`). The
   gateway is rendered always (Amendment 8). **`harness/laurium.py` is case-b's** (the orchestrator's ratification of
   11 November), beside platform's folder on the same terms as P9's module: one hook in each of `compose_services` and
   the environment file, and imports one way (the render imports it; it imports nothing of the render). Platform's
   files (`render.py`'s two hooks, `cluster.py`'s port, the profile's image and resources, `model_admin.py`'s two
   lines, the two fixtures) as the lane's diff.
4. **Laurium's key at start** (Amendment 6 decision 8's part 2): made with the deployment's extraction model alone, and
   **every older Laurium key deleted**, by its hash, every page read first, so a key from a master key since rotated is
   not left valid. **A key that cannot be made never stops the Conduit** (the lane reviewer's item 1): tried again in the
   background, each wait twice the last up to ten minutes, as the engines' reconciliation (Amendment 3); until it is
   held, Laurium's calls alone are refused in words. The live suite's factory refuses a gateway already holding
   Laurium's key (a deployment's), looking for it by its hash, never with the key in an address.
5. ***Admin › Models* shows the engine, read-only, on the cloud-platform profile alone**, with Amendment 8's words:
   "chosen at set-up: change it in osprey.yaml, re-render, and have the platform team apply it." **This changes
   Amendment 5 decision 2's "and in *Admin › Models* … changing it is audited behind `manage_models`"** (the
   orchestrator's ruling, as P11's: Admin never offers what the render did not make): Laurium is a service the render
   makes, so a change here could not take effect; there is no write route and so nothing to audit.
6. **Where Laurium's traffic may go is P7b's** (platform, ADR-148 Amendment 5): its row in the per-workload egress,
   `laurium: [litellm]`, and `laurium` in the Conduit's row; ingress derived from the same rows (the Conduit alone
   reaches it; no worker holds a model). **Before P7b, the namespace's `allow-egress` (`all()`, order 100) admits
   every pod to every pod, the managed stores and each allowed host** (the lane's finding of 11 November, measured
   on the rendered chart). **So the default never ships open** (rule 3; the orchestrator's ruling on round 1):
   P12 part 2 merges after P7b, with Laurium's row in the same merge, and its network-policy xfails come off there.
   The merge order: P9, P7b, case's decommission diff, then P12 part 2 with its row.
7. **The exit: Laurium reads a real model's answer.** Leased on stack b (11 November, 18:01 UTC) beside the
   orchestrator's pinned gateway (LiteLLM with its own database) and Ollama: **`qwen2.5:7b-instruct`, the product's own
   extraction model, 3 of 3**; the 0.5B conformance model 0 of 3, the control (part 1's strict xfail on it stays,
   narrowed to its unparseable refusal alone). What ran: that gateway directly, Laurium's own code in-process, a
   one-string schema, its key from `put_laurium_key`; **not** the rendered route, Laurium's image, the Conduit, or the
   review queue's real schema (`process/lanes/case-b/P12p2_RED_RECORD.md`). **The client's own engine is proven at their install (20 November): P12's
   last open item**, and D2c says so.

**Consequences.** Laurium's prompt asks for its format in the prompt alone; a model that does not follow it (the 0.5B)
is refused as `unparseable`, never read as an empty finding. The options for one that does not, recorded not built:
constrained decoding (`response_format: json_schema` bound on Laurium's chat model), JSON mode, a larger model.

**The tests that would fail.** The setting and its preset, read not written: `tests/schemas/test_extraction_engine_setting.py`
(the round trip and a shared `ModelsConfig` planted red). Laurium's render and no Secret in its pod:
`tests/harness/test_laurium_render.py` (`env_file` planted red). The review queue's extraction alone:
`tests/adapters/extract_laurium/test_laurium_reads_findings_alone.py` (the marker left out, and every caller sent, each
red); no other call site, email extraction and a document's content at theirs and every module by scan:
`tests/adapters/extract_laurium/test_laurium_call_sites.py` (the marker back inside `run_extraction`, the route not
passing it, and a planted `laurium_reads()` in `questions.py`, each red). The composition inside the routes, the key at start never stopping the Conduit, the client closed:
`tests/services/api/test_laurium_start.py` (the reversed wrapping planted red). The sweep, every page first:
`tests/adapters/extract_laurium/test_laurium_at_start.py`. Admin read-only:
`tests/services/api/test_admin_models_extraction_engine.py` and `Models.test.tsx`. The platform's rules with Laurium
rendered on three shapes: `tests/harness/test_laurium_cp_policy.py`. Laurium's image unscanned:
`make -C OspreyFlow_Core trivy-image-laurium` in Core's `check`, and CI's `trivy-image-laurium` job. The release
building another set of images than the local release: `tests/test_release_local_matrix.py`. Laurium's traffic, in Calico's order:
`tests/harness/test_laurium_network_policy.py`, strict-xfailed until P7b. The exit:
`tests/conformance/model_port/test_laurium_reads_a_real_model_live.py`, leased.

### ADR-148, Amendment 8 (11 November 2026) — Entra ID's claims wired into the cloud-platform profile as built (P10 part 2): roles kept by the deployment, Keycloak not rendered, every reader of a role through `principal_auth`

*Entra ID's sign-in on the cloud-platform profile as built (P10 part 2), by the admin lane. An access step: two
review rounds, listed for the owner.*

1. **Roles are the deployment's, kept by tenant and object id.** This is the orchestrator's ruling of 11 November
   2026, on the lane's recommendation; the owner may overrule it. Amendment 6 point 4 held the question. Decision 9
   keeps roles in Admin › People, and with no Keycloak there is no user attribute to keep them in.
   - **The store.** `services/api/entra_people.py` keeps one row per person in the deployment's own Postgres
     (`entra_people`), keyed by `(tenant_id, oid)`. Only Admin › People writes roles to it, and every statement names
     the tenant, so a row of another tenant's same object id grants nothing (`test_entra_people_live.py`, rule 3).
   - **One construction path.** The resolver is given the store (`principal_auth.RoleSource`). `resolve_principal`
     checks the token in full first, so a refused token records nobody. It then reads the person within two seconds
     and builds the principal in `principal_from_claims`, the one construction path, from the token's verified claims
     and the stored person.
   - **No cache.** A role taken away holds from the next request.
   - **Refusals.** A read that fails, times out or answers something malformed is `PrincipalLookupUnavailable`: a 503
     (`people_store_unavailable`), never a principal with no roles. The socket closes with 1013. Every read path that
     resolves a session goes through it.
   - **Disable** is the store's flag. The construction path refuses a disabled person (401) from their next request.
   - **The delta socket outlives the request that opened it**, so it asks the store too: at connect (a ticket minted
     before a change is refused before the snapshot is sent) and before every message. It closes 1008 when the person
     is disabled, no longer recorded, or their roles changed (they sign in again, and the one construction path builds
     their principal afresh), and 1013 when the store cannot answer. Found by the lane's own review.
   - **The synchronous `resolve`** refuses an Entra mapping, and `principal_from_claims` refuses an Entra principal
     with no stored person. Each guard is shown red alone.
2. **Who appears in Admin › People.**
   - A person is recorded, with no roles, at their first sign-in.
   - An administrator may add one by object id ahead of it (`POST /v1/admin/people/by-object-id`, behind
     `manage_people`, audited as `add_person_by_object_id`). The Entra admin centre shows object ids (Amendment 6 point 6). The id is
     validated as an object id, and one already recorded is a 409 that names it.
   - The first administrators are named by object id at install (`cloud_platform.claims.first_administrators`,
     rendered as `OSPREY_FIRST_ADMINISTRATORS`) and given the Admin role once. Taking it away later is not undone at
     the next start, except when nobody can manage people (point 10).
   - An empty list is refused when the settings load, and the Conduit refuses to start without one. It is never read
     as "everyone".
3. **What Entra holds is refused in words** (409 `entra_holds_accounts`):
   - invite, and reset a sign-in;
   - access (clearance, unit and codes come from Entra's claims);
   - remove (the person would return, with no roles, at their next sign-in; disable instead);
   - join an organisation account;
   - register a dashboard identity.

   People on Entra says so (`GET /v1/admin/sign-in` tells the Glass the kind, behind `manage_people`). It offers *Add
   a person by object id* in place of the invite, and no Access, Reset sign-in or Remove.
4. **Owner resolution is unavailable on Entra.** Entra has no impersonation exchange. `resolve_for_owner` answers
   none (ADR-044's path: the run is marked stopped), whatever exchange endpoint is configured. Carried to a later step.
5. **The service identity on Entra** (CARRIES, P10 round 2). A run API caller's token must be all of these:
   - an app-only token of the pinned tenant, with the configured issuer and audience;
   - `tid` the tenant;
   - no delegated `scp` (a person's token is 403), and `idtyp` `app` where present;
   - its client in `azp` or `appid` (the same if both), an application id that is neither the Glass's nor this API's
     own. The mapping carries the API's own application id (`api_client_id`), so on v1.0 tokens, whose audience is the
     `api://` URI, the API's registration is still refused.

   Under Keycloak's handling a token carrying `tid` is refused. The verifier is judged by the resolver's own mapping.
6. **Every reader of a role or principal on the profile goes through `principal_auth`**, or is not rendered there:
   - `harness/webapp_auth.py` (the set-up console's `/admin`) and `harness/oidc.py` (the realm's sign-in) refuse an
     Entra token (one carrying `tid`). Neither is a cloud-platform workload.
   - **Report sync and Superset are not on this profile until their own step** (the orchestrator's ruling (a), 11
     November 2026). Both signed in through Keycloak: report sync with a client-credentials token, which the Entra
     resolver refuses as no person's, and Superset through Keycloak as its OAuth provider. Both are off by default, so
     the bare profile renders. An explicit `reporting.sync` or `reporting.superset` is refused in words naming the
     later step (CARRIES). Superset's own configuration still reads no token role when told `SUPERSET_SIGN_IN=entra`,
     so its step starts from everyone Gamma.
   - The Glass shows and gates on `GET /v1/me`, the resolved principal: id, clearance, unit, roles and codes, its own
     only. It fails closed: while `/v1/me` is asked, or when it does not answer, there is no clearance, no role, no
     account menu and no `isAdministrator`. When it does not answer, the person is told so in words, with *Try
     again* and *Sign out* (point 9).
   - No ID-token role or access claim is read anywhere in the Glass. A source check over `apps/workspace/src` is
     shown red on each shape.
   - The display principal's id is the Conduit's (the object id), never Entra's pairwise `sub`.
   - A person disabled in this deployment is told so ("Your account is disabled in this deployment. Ask an
     administrator."), only when the Conduit's 401 carries `principal_auth`'s own words exactly, and no renewal is
     tried. Any other refusal keeps its own words. A test holds the two languages' words equal.
   - `harness/verify.py`'s resolver uses the Keycloak mapping. The deploy's verify stage is no cloud-platform
     workload.
   - ADR-106's display names (`PrincipalNameDirectory`) have no source on Entra and show the object id. Carried: the
     people store's names could serve it (CARRIES).
7. **The profile** (platform's files, applied from the lane's diff):
   - **`cloud_platform.claims`** names, and the render refuses without it:
     - the tenant;
     - the Glass's registration (`client_id`) and the API's (`api_client_id`, optional `api_id_uri`);
     - `token_version` (2.0 or 1.0);
     - `scope`;
     - the three claim sources and `groups_claim`;
     - the first administrators;
     - `claims_mapping_policy`.

     `principal_auth.ClaimMapping` must read it, or the render refuses in words. The rendered mapping carries the
     Glass's and the API's application ids.
   - **The issuer, audience and keys follow the version**:
     - v2.0: `login.microsoftonline.com/<tid>/v2.0`, with the API's id as the audience;
     - v1.0: `sts.windows.net/<tid>/`, with its `api://` URI as the audience.

     The keys are `…/discovery[/v2.0]/keys`, with `?appid=<api_client_id>` under a claims-mapping policy.
   - **Keycloak is not rendered**: not its workload, its database step, its realm and theme files, its door, its
     group 0, nor its resources, secrets (`OSPREY_KEYCLOAK_*`, `OIDC_TOKEN_EXCHANGE_CLIENT_SECRET`) or settings
     (`OIDC_TOKEN_EXCHANGE_*`, `OIDC_ADMIN_USERS_URL`, `OSPREY_IDENTITY_ORIGIN`). No rendered value names Keycloak or
     the `id.` host (the deployment's own `osprey.yaml`, mounted as written, keeps its settings' defaults).
     `cp-policy-check`'s `GROUP_ZERO_ALLOWED` is empty. The realm's secrets are taken out by a **deny-list**
     (`REALM_SECRETS`: the three `OSPREY_KEYCLOAK_*` and `OIDC_TOKEN_EXCHANGE_CLIENT_SECRET`), not by an allow-list
     of what this profile needs. A Keycloak secret added to the install later would be rendered here until named in
     it; the render test's "no rendered value names Keycloak" case catches one with Keycloak in its name, and
     nothing catches one without. Kept as it is (the orchestrator's review of 3848c32).
   - **The set-up console** (`python -m harness.webapp`) is no pod, image, command or door of the render, on all
     five fixtures (`test_the_set_up_console_is_no_part_of_the_render`), so `webapp_auth`'s Keycloak-only role
     check never stands between an Entra token and anything on this profile.
   - **The install runbook's step 6** (P7b's `INSTALL.md`) is Entra's: the client's app registrations (the Glass's,
     and the API's exposing the scope) and the first administrators the settings name, then a check that the Conduit
     reads Entra's settings. P7b's Keycloak step (the `identity` module of the cloud-platform harness) and its test are removed. This
     lane's, sent as `runbook.diff` with the render diff regenerated on P7b (the orchestrator's ruling, 11 November
     2026).
   - **The Glass's `deployment.json`** carries `sign_in` (Entra's authority, the Glass's registration, and `openid
     profile <api_id_uri>/<scope>`) in place of the realm's address, only on this profile. Every other profile's file is byte
     for byte as main rendered it (a golden from main's own module).
   - **Egress.** `login.microsoftonline.com` is the one host P10 adds, a kind of its own in P7b's per-workload egress
     (`egress.sign_in`) that the Conduit alone reaches, since it alone verifies tokens. `always` is unchanged. Its
     networks are the deployment's (`egress_nets`), or the render is refused (the docs lane's gap (a)). Keycloak's
     rows are gone from P7b's reach, managed, paths and CPU-limit tables, and nothing reaches the mail server, which
     only Keycloak's sign-in mail used.
8. **The carries of part 1, settled.**
   - **The guest check compares the tenant `idp` names to `tid`**, in either Entra issuer form. An `idp` naming no
     Entra issuer of our tenant is a guest. That includes a Microsoft account and a federation's own issuer, so a
     federated member, should Entra send one, is refused until a later setting admits it.
   - **`client_id` or a non-default `scope` without a tenant is refused** when the settings load.
   - **The scope check is typed on its own**, so the app-only cases are red by the app-only words.
   - **`sub` stays required of an Entra token** (PyJWT's `require`): Entra issues it in every access token, and the
     docs lane's guide (1.81 §6a.8) says so. The docs lane's gap (b), recorded here.

9. **The orchestrator's review of 3848c32 (12 November 2026)**, its rulings marked for the owner.
   - **The way back in**: as amended by the second review (point 10), which replaced this round's "holds no role"
     rule.
   - **Locking everyone out** (`leaves_no_people_manager`) counts only an enabled manager who has **signed in at
     least once** (`PersonAccount.signed_in`, from the store's `first_seen`). A person added by object id who never
     signed in is no proof anyone can administer.
   - **Stale access** (the orchestrator's ruling, for the owner): on Entra ID a clearance or unit is the token's,
     recorded at sign-in (`access_read_at`, refreshed at most hourly while the person is active). One read more than
     **24 hours** ago (above Entra's longest access-token lifetime, with a margin) is not trusted for what is given
     to a person in their absence: a case transfer to them is refused in words ("their clearance and unit were last
     read from Entra ID over a day ago: they sign in again first"), and a promotion's ageing alert leaves them out,
     its log saying how many and why (`recipients`, `recipients_of`; `cleared_to` then never sees such a
     clearance), and they are not named a case's Author (point 10). Display elsewhere is unchanged. Keycloak's
     people (no `access_read_at`) are always current.
   - **The signing keys** (`principal_auth.SigningKeys`): as the second review left them (point 10).
   - **The token check on Entra**: RS256 alone, whatever `OIDC_ALGORITHMS` says; a leeway of 60 seconds on the
     times; the service identity's token must carry `exp`.
   - **The Glass asks for `openid profile`** and the API's scope, for the names it shows. When `/v1/me` does not
     answer it says so, offers *Try again* (which asks again) and keeps *Sign out* within reach, with nothing
     role-gated offered meanwhile.
   - **A bearer header at the delta socket's connect** whose stored roles cannot be read closes 1013, a refused one
     1008 (point 1's claim, now tested).
   - **`BOOTSTRAP_SQL`** runs under a transaction-scoped advisory lock, so two Conduits starting together make the
     table once.
   - **Carried**: the service identity's app-role check (requiring an orchestrator's application to hold an app role
     this API defines), measured on the client's tenant first (CARRIES).

10. **The orchestrator's second review of 67f3d2a (12 November 2026)**, its amended ruling marked for the owner.
    - **The way back in, amended** (the orchestrator's ruling, for the owner as amended): at start, a named first
      administrator is given Admin again **only when nobody can manage people** (`people_managers` empty: no enabled
      person who has signed in holds `manage_people`, by their roles and the custom roles' rights), added to what
      they hold. Each Admin role a start gives (the install's, and a way back in) writes an audit row,
      `grant_first_administrator`, by `first-administrators` (`user_id` and `roles`, as `set_person_roles` writes;
      named on purpose in the audit census's words-shown list). Written by the system, it is in the audit log but,
      like every entry the system writes, not shown in Admin › Audit (audit_section's rule for an entry with no
      person's unit). Otherwise an administrator's change stands, a named
      person's roles cleared on purpose included. The seed runs under `PEOPLE_LOCK`, the lock every change that could
      leave nobody able to manage people takes. The runbook's recovery step says so.
    - **The signing keys** (`principal_auth.SigningKeys`, which replaced `PyJWKClient`): kept for
      `OIDC_JWKS_TTL_SECONDS`, counted at the server (N sign-ins, one fetch). One thread fetches while the others use
      the last good set. Past the keys' time a failed fetch leaves the last good set in use for
      `KEYS_GRACE_SECONDS` (an hour, logged), then a 503. A key id not held is fetched for at most once in five
      minutes; a set fetched in the same call opens that window. **A key Entra publishes within five minutes of
      such a fetch is refused (401) until the next fetch is due or the keys' time is up**: pinned by a test, and
      carried to the live checks. Each fetch is bounded by five seconds and runs in `KEYS_EXECUTOR`, the keys' own
      four threads, never `asyncio.to_thread`'s shared pool. Every way the identity provider can fail to give keys
      (unreachable, a refusal, a body that is not JSON, a set with no usable key) is `SigningKeysUnavailable`, a 503
      in words, never a 500 nor a 401 that signs people out. The URL must be http or https. The run API's verifier
      shares the person path's set (one cache, one fetch limit), with its own 503, RS256 pin and leeway tested.
    - **Owner resolution on Keycloak**: the exchanged token is checked in the keys' threads, and its keys
      unreadable is `PrincipalExchangeUnavailable` (ADR-044's path: the run marked stopped), as before this step,
      never an exception the scheduler, a monitor, a screening run or a recipe run does not expect. That it runs in a
      thread is not shown red on this path alone (the same `in_keys_thread` is, on the person path).
    - **`access_read_at` refreshed at most hourly** while the person is active: tested live both ways (two hours
      old, refreshed; thirty minutes, not).
    - **An open socket** closes with the code its admission gives: 1013 when the store cannot answer, 1008 when the
      person is disabled, gone, their roles changed or their case level lost (point 1, now as the code does).
    - **Name an Author** refuses a person whose access was read over 24 hours ago (409 `access_out_of_date`, in the
      transfer's words), so the rule fails closed the same way everywhere a unit or clearance is trusted in the
      person's absence.
    - **The transfer's markings check** no longer reads the stale set: `check_transfers`, run first, refuses a stale
      recipient, so that branch could not be reached.
    - **The account-unread notice** is its own component (`src/auth/AccountUnread.tsx`), with a keyboard spec
      (`account-unread.spec.ts`, registered as `ACCOUNT_UNREAD_ACTIONS`) and an axe scan in dark, light and GOV.UK
      (`account-unread-harness.html`), each shown red.
    - **The bootstrap's advisory lock** is shown deterministically: while another session holds it, `connect` waits.

11. **The orchestrator's third review of e8d5874 (12 November 2026).**
    - **The five-second bound is total**: `in_keys_thread`'s own wait (`KEYS_TIMEOUT_SECONDS`) bounds the whole fetch,
      a name that does not resolve and a body that trickles in under each read's own timeout included. A fetch
      still running past it is **abandoned**: who fetches is an owner with a deadline (not a lock held across I/O),
      so the next caller takes the fetch, and the abandoned one's late answer is dropped. Point 10's "each fetch
      bounded by five seconds" meant each read; it now means the whole.
    - **The unknown-kid window** opens only on a fetch that succeeded: an unreachable identity provider is a 503
      every time, never a 401.
    - **A rotated-out key** stays valid for up to the keys' time (`OIDC_JWKS_TTL_SECONDS`) plus the grace hour while
      Entra cannot be reached, since the last good set is what is held.
    - **Concurrent sign-ins** finding the keys out of date fetch once: each reads the set's age once, before
      anything else. Measured: twelve at once with nothing held, against a slow identity provider, make one
      request, and twelve once the keys' time is up make one more.
    - **A set with no key a token can be checked by** (every key for encryption, or none with a key id) is a 503,
      with the other failure classes.
    - **The run API's sign-in** (`get_service_identity`) is async and reads its keys in the keys' own threads,
      never anyio's shared pool.
    - **The start's grant and its audit row** are one transaction on one connection (`audit_log` is in the same
      database): an audit write that fails takes the grant back. The custom roles' rights are read on that
      connection inside `PEOPLE_LOCK`, and the lock is planted.

**Still to measure against the client's development tenant**, unchanged from Amendment 6's list (rule 15): the token
version, the extension names, the claims-mapping policy's keys, guests and federated members, and the Glass's access
token. Also the `aud` of a v1.0 token, which this amendment takes as the `api://` URI.

### ADR-132, Amendment 7 (12 November 2026) — The phase banner's words are the deployment's to set (`appearance.banner_text`)

Status: as built by the platform-b lane (step gate-b), at the owner's request of 12 November 2026
(about 23:15), for the demonstration on Friday 13 November. The owner's wording, used on the
demonstration's deployment: **"Demonstration only: this is not a government service, and all data is
synthetic."**

1. **`appearance.banner_text`** in `osprey.yaml`: one line of at most 200 characters, never blank
   (refused in words otherwise). It replaces the banner's fixed "This is a new service.".
2. **Where it shows:** the Glass's banner (`PhaseBanner`, in `BrandFrame`, under either brand) and the
   GOV.UK sign-in page (`harness/govuk_chrome.js`, given it as `bannerText`). At `alpha` or `beta` the
   words follow the phase's tag; at `live` or `none` they are shown **alone**, in the same "Service
   phase" region. Always set as text, never as markup. The OspreyFlow-branded sign-in page has no
   banner and is unchanged.
3. **Unset, nothing changes:** the setting is left out of `/deployment.json` and of the sign-in
   theme's settings (never written as `null`), so every deployment that does not set it renders byte
   for byte as before (`gate/B-unset-renders.raw.txt`, every profile and fixture).
4. **Tests:** `PhaseBanner.test.tsx`, `brand.test.tsx`, `BrandFrame.test.tsx`,
   `tests/harness/test_banner_text.py`, `test_keycloak_theme_govuk.py`,
   `keycloak_theme/govuk_sign_in.test.mjs`; by keyboard and axe in the dark, light and GOV.UK themes
   (`keyboard/shell.spec.ts`, `a11y/every-harness.spec.ts`'s `shell-harness.html?banner=1`); each red
   first (`process/lanes/platform-b/gate/A*`).

### ADR-114, Amendment 41 (12 November 2026) — A shared key asked by the front proxy, on all three names, against a bcrypt hash set on the server

Status: as built by the platform-b lane (step gate-b), at the owner's request of 12 November 2026, for a
deployment shown to people who are not its users (the demonstration). Small only.

**Decision.**

1. **`network.access_key: true`** in `osprey.yaml` (default false) says the deployment's front proxy
   asks every browser for a shared key, the browser's own user name and password box (HTTP Basic), on
   **all three names** (the Glass, `id.` and `bi.`), before any page, asset, sign-in or API answer.
   **Small only** (refused in words for any other profile): its proxy is the product's own, and its
   address is always `https://`, so the key, which a browser sends again with every request, only
   ever travels over TLS.
2. **The key is never stored; its bcrypt hash is set on the server**, never in `osprey.yaml`, the
   repository, a message or a log. The owner runs `python -m harness.access_key set <the deployment's
   folder> [--user demo]` on the server: it reads the key twice without echo (at least 12 characters,
   no spaces at either end), hashes it with **the proxy image's own `caddy hash-password --algorithm
   bcrypt`** (the key on standard input, never a command line), and writes
   `access-key.caddy.pending` (`600`): the user name, the hash and a new random pass. It says to run
   `ospreyflow apply`, which carries it into place as `access-key.caddy` (moved with the staged
   files, preflight reading it there) and, the proxy's mounted file having changed, restarts the proxy.
   The pending file is removed once in place. Setting the key again replaces the hash and the pass.
3. **The render never reads the file.** The Caddyfile `import`s it from `/etc/caddy/access-key.caddy`,
   mounted read-only into the proxy alone, so no rendered file, change preview or drift report holds
   the hash. A deployment that asks and has no file set does not start its proxy (Caddy refuses a
   missing import): it fails closed. Preflight (`access-key`) says so first, and refuses a file others
   may read or one edited by hand, never quoting it.
4. **The pass.** Once a browser has answered with the key, Caddy gives it a session cookie
   (`osprey_pass`, `Domain=<host>`, HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Lax), a random value set with the hash
   (not the key), so it is asked **once** for all three names, and its own requests that carry a token
   of their own (the Glass's API sends `Authorization: Bearer`, which a browser sends in place of the
   key), its WebSocket and its frames still pass. The pass is given only when the key was checked.
   **The key's own `Authorization` is taken off** before anything behind the proxy sees it (on the
   identity provider, except at a token endpoint, where a client may sign in with Basic).
5. **What goes without the key**, every one checked live: a CORS preflight (`OPTIONS`, which never
   carries a credential), and on the identity provider the three answers the Glass asks from its own
   origin, where a browser sends no stored credential and no cookie: `/realms/osprey/protocol/
   openid-connect/token`, `.../certs` and `/realms/osprey/.well-known/openid-configuration`. Each
   answers nothing without a code, a refresh token or a signature to check. **The sign-in page, the
   master realm and the admin console stay behind the key.** The loopback doors and the proxy's own
   health answer are not public names and are not asked. The server-side calls (the Conduit's and
   Superset's to Keycloak) go by the internal network, never through the proxy.
6. **`X-Robots-Tag: noindex, nofollow`** on every answer of a deployment that asks, a refusal and a
   redirect to `https://` included.
7. **The tools on the server** that reach the deployment by its names (`apply`, the sign-in
   registration, backup and restore, through `harness.site.deployment_origins` or `carry_the_pass`)
   present the pass from the same file, which only its owner can read, on those three names alone.
8. **Unset, nothing changes**: no import, no mount, no header; `access_key` is left out of every dump
   of the settings while false (the cluster's and cloud platform's values carry `osprey.yaml`), so every
   profile's and fixture's render is byte for byte main's (`gate/B-unset-renders.raw.txt`; the first
   run found `access_key: false` in those values, fixed before the commit).

**Tests.** `tests/harness/test_access_key.py` (the setting, the render, the helper, preflight, the
carry and the restart, the tools' pass) and `tests/harness/test_access_key_proxy.py`, **the
access-control test of each name** (rule 4), against the real Caddy 2.11.4 running the rendered
Caddyfile and the helper's file: no key and a wrong key or user refused; the key let in, given the
pass, its `Authorization` never reaching behind; the pass with a Bearer token; another pass refused;
the open answers given no pass for an unchecked key; the sign-in page, a path that climbs out of the
token endpoint, the master realm and the admin console refused; no key file, no start; unset,
answered as before. Red first: the real proxy against seven planted defects and the unit cases
against nine (`process/lanes/platform-b/gate/B-*-plants.raw.txt`). `test_access_key_proxy.py` needs a
`caddy` binary (`OSPREY_TEST_CADDY`) and is skipped in words without one, as on GitHub's runners.

**Cost.** A browser's first request is answered 401 until the key is given; an organisation's own
sign-in that returns by a cross-site POST (SAML) would be asked for the key again, since a SameSite=Lax
pass is not sent there; none is in use on the demonstration. The pass lasts until the browser closes.
